--- Page 7 ---
<meta>This page contains the introductory dedications for the 1546 French edition of the "Hypnerotomachia Poliphili". The layout consists of two distinct addresses: a French dedication by the translator/editor Jean Martin to a high-ranking nobleman, and a Latin preface by the scholar Jacques Gohory to the general reader. Both establish the book's pedigree and its focus on architecture and ancient wisdom.</meta>

->TO MY LORD, THE LORD<-
->*Count of Nanteuil-le-Haudouin, Messire Henry de Lenoncourt,<-
->*Knight of the Order, Governor of Valois, and Captain of<-
->*fifty men-at-arms.*<-

**M**y Lord, although I know your lordship to be continually occupied with the great affairs in which it pleases the Majesty of the King to employ you, such that there is little or no time to devote to matters of pleasure, I shall not fear to dedicate to you this *Poliphilo* <note>The protagonist of the book; the title "Hypnerotomachia Poliphili" translates to "Poliphilo's Strife of Love in a Dream."</note>, which in the year 1467 was composed in Italy by a learned gentleman of an illustrious house, and recently translated into French by another virtuous gentleman of good knowledge. The translation was given to me by a friend of mine, so that I might review it and lend a hand in bringing it to light <note>i.e., publishing it</note>. This is a task I believe I have performed as faithfully as I would wish someone to do for me, should I leave behind any works of my own.

The reasons (My Lord) that move me to dedicate it to you are, in the first place, the improvement of architecture or the art of building well, which could hardly be bettered; and thus I am of the opinion that it is due to you, considering that you take as much pleasure in it as a lord of your quality might, as you have shown in effect in your beautiful edifice of Nanteuil. You yourself devised the arrangements for it, so convenient and well-understood that there is now no architect in this Kingdom who would not consider himself honored if these inventions had issued from his own mind. The second cause is that this book is so abundant in singular and diverse things that we have nothing to which it can be compared; and you delight yourself marvelously in hearing such readings when your convenience allows. Then the third and principal reason is so that this *Poliphilo* may not go wandering through the world like an orphan destitute of a protector, but rather that under your acknowledgment and the safeguard of those lords and gentlemen who bear you friendship, he may receive the customary welcome given to things coming from friends. Be favorable to him then, My Lord, and receive him (if it please you) as humanely from me who presents him to you, as the gift is made to you with most humble and entire affection. With which I pray the Creator to give you, My Lord, in perfect health, a very long and very happy life. From Paris, this 13th day of August, 1546.

->Your most humble and most obedient<-
->servant, Jean Martin.<-

<column-break/>

->*Jacques Gohory of Paris, Greetings to the Reader*<-

**I**t is a wonder, Reader, that Francesco Colonna <note>The Dominican friar credited with writing the original Italian text.</note> assumed the name of Poliphilo: I believe either so that, while living, he might remain hidden and hear the opinions of men after the manner of Apelles <note>A famous Greek painter who hid behind his paintings to hear critiques.</note>, or because, following the example of the Gnidian Architect, he placed his hope for praise and glory in the opinion of posterity. For just as that man had inscribed on a notable stone: *Sostratus of Gnidus, son of Dexiphanes*, and then over it wrote the name of the Egyptian King in plaster <note>A reference to the Lighthouse of Alexandria; the plaster eventually fell off to reveal the architect's true name.</note>; so this man has silently noted in the first letters of each chapter: **BROTHER FRANCESCO COLONNA GREATLY LOVED POLIA.** <note>original: "FRATER FRANCISCVS COLVMNA PERAMAVIT." This is the famous acrostic hidden in the book's initials.</note>

He seems to assert his homeland by his very surname, being (I believe) from that illustrious family <note>The Colonna family of Rome.</note> which, along with famous men, perhaps devised this work in this manner. Using the Greek, Latin, and Tuscan <note>Italian</note> languages, he reached for the knowledge of many peoples through his divine wisdom, as if consecrating himself to immortality in various perennial monuments. They say it is in the interest of the state that the secrets hidden under these coverings of architecture and ceremonies should not be known by the common people, but only by those who have withdrawn into the service of a more sacred Philosophy. For a dream of this kind—the forest, the spring, the monster of the journey, the obscurity and difficulty of almost all labors—is perennial. For there are certain hidden fiery things which he sold to art, and often from his eyes... <note>The Latin text here becomes somewhat fragmented or metaphorical regarding the visual nature of the work.</note> he had vehemently requested to read carefully. For this work my close friend (of Jacques Kerver the printer) gave to me readily; being filled with its abundance and variety, we cannot regret how much one may profit in reading it. FAREWELL.

<meta>This page follows the title page and contains the introductory material for the 1546 French edition of the "Hypnerotomachia Poliphili." It includes a Latin address to the reader by Jacques Gohory and a French dedication by the translator, Jean Martin.</meta>

*Jacques Gohory of Paris greets the Reader.*

<note>original: "Iacobus Gohorius Parisiensis Lectori S." Gohory was a noted Parisian scholar and alchemist who helped edit this work.</note>

Who would find this strange, Reader? The letter "F" stands for the name of Francesco Colonna, who assumed the name of Poliphilo <note>The "Lover of Polia"</note>: I believe he did so either to remain hidden while alive, or so that, following the custom of men, he might hear himself praised as an Apollo; or perhaps because, following the example of the Architect of Cnidus, he placed his hope for praise and glory in posterity through his own judgment. For, just as that architect had inscribed on a famous stone: *Sostratus of Cnidus, son of Dexiphanes*, and then covered it with plaster bearing the name of the Egyptian King <note>A reference to the lighthouse of Alexandria; the plaster eventually fell away to reveal the true builder's name</note>. So has this author silently noted in the first letters of each chapter: FRANCESCO COLONNA LOVED GREATLY. <note>original: "FRANCISCVS COLVMNA PERAMAVIT." This refers to the famous acrostic formed by the decorated initials of the book's chapters.</note> His homeland, Venice, seems to claim him by his surname, being (I believe) from that illustrious family; and this work was perhaps devised in this way so that through the Greek, Latin, and Tuscan languages, a knowledge of many peoples might reach his divine wisdom, to be consecrated to immortality as monuments of his memory. They say it is in the interest of the state that the architectural secrets hidden beneath these things should not be known by the common people. But they have hidden the family of more sacred Philosophy from contemplation by these means alone. For a dream of this kind—the forest, the fountain, the monster of the journey, the sequences, the hieroglyphic characters, and finally the delay in obtaining Polia—is the womb of this book. A Knight of Malta, a man of easy and cultivated genius, had first sketched it out; but soon after he and I were led away from here by our respective fates. Jean Martin <note>original: "Ianus Martinus"</note> took up the task of polishing the work (as is noble to do upon request). Indeed, there is such a wealth of excellent things here that even the most skilled readers cannot regret how much they profit from reading it. FAREWELL.

<column-break/>

->TO MY LORD, MY LORD THE<-
*Count of Nanteuil-le-Haudouin, Sire Henri de Lenoncourt,*
*Knight of the Order, Governor of the Île-de-France, and Captain of*
*fifty men-at-arms.*

My Lord, although I know your lordship to be continually occupied with the great affairs in which it pleases the Majesty of the King to employ you, such that there is little or no time to attend to matters of pleasure, I shall not fear to dedicate to you this *Poliphilo*, which in the year fourteen hundred and sixty-seven was composed in Italy by a learned gentleman of an illustrious house, and recently translated into French by another virtuous gentleman of good knowledge. The translation was given to me by a friend of mine, so that I might revise it and assist in bringing it to light: a task I did not wish to acquire as easily as I would desire others to do to complete this unfinished undertaking. The primary reasons (My Lord) that move me to dedicate it to you are, in the first place, the excellence of the subject and the argument of architecture, or the art of building well, which could hardly be bettered. Therefore, I am of the opinion that it is due to you, considering that you take as much pleasure in it as a lord of your quality should, as you have shown in effect in your beautiful building of Nanteuil, for which you yourself devised the arrangements, so convenient and so well understood that there is now no architect in this Kingdom who would not consider it a great work if such or similar inventions had come from his own mind. The second cause is that this book is so abundant in singular and diverse things that we have no other in our language today that can be compared to it; and you take marvelous delight in hearing such readings when your convenience allows. Then the third and principal reason is so that this *Poliphilo* should not be wandering through the world like an orphan destitute of a protector, but rather that under your endorsement and safeguard, he may be received by the gentlemen who bear you friendship with as good a face as one is accustomed to welcome things that come from friends. Be favorable to him then, My Lord, and receive him (if it please you) as humanely from me who presents him to you, as the gift is made to you with very humble and entire affection: with which I pray the Creator to give you, My Lord, in perfect health, a very long and very happy life. From Paris, this 13th day of August, 1546.

->Your very humble and very obedient<-
->servant Jean Martin.<-

<meta>This page serves as the translator's preface to the French edition of the "Hypnerotomachia Poliphili" (The Dream of Poliphilus). The translator, Jean Martin, addresses the readers to summarize the complex allegorical journey of the protagonist, Poliphilus, through a world of classical architecture and romantic trials.</meta>

# JEAN MARTIN, SECRETARY TO MY LORD
# THE MOST REVEREND CARDINAL OF LENONCOURT.

## TO THE READERS.

If you desire (my Lords) to understand in a few words what is contained in this work, know that Poliphilus says he saw in his dream admirable things, among which he describes many ancient remains worthy of memory, such as Pyramids, Obelisks, great ruins of edifices, the differences between columns, their measurements, pedestals, bases, and capitals <note>The decorative top part of a column.</note> with which they are adorned. Then the architraves, friezes, cornices, and frontispieces with their workmanship. A great horse, an Elephant of marvelous size, a Colossus, and a magnificent gate, with its ground plan, arrangement, moldings, and carved work. Afterward, how five beautiful Nymphs led him to the baths: and meanwhile he does not forget to mention an excellent fountain. Further, he describes the Palace of Queen Eleutherilide <note>Her name is derived from the Greek word for "Liberty."</note>: who for love of him has a solemn feast prepared, in which one can learn many things beneficial to human health. After, he specifies the diversity of precious stones, with their natural virtues: the means of cutting them: and the diversity of the pastime of a dance: and consequently depicts three gardens, of which one is of glass, the other of silk, and the third made into a Labyrinth. In the middle of this peristyle <note>A courtyard surrounded by columns.</note> is seated a pyramid engraved with Egyptian characters, which are called Hieroglyphic letters. Departing from there, he goes to the three gates, and enters the middle one, where he finds his beloved Polia, whose beauty, grace, and the fashion of her garments he expresses. This Polia makes him see four triumphs of the great Jupiter: then shows him the mortal ladies with whom the gods were in love: together with the beloveds of the Poets: and there one recognizes the affections and various effects of love. After follows the triumph of Vertumnus and Pomona <note>Roman deities of seasons and fruit trees.</note>, together with the great god of gardens <note>Priapus.</note> with his sacrifices: and having said that, the author comes to describe a temple made of rich materials, and conducted by good industry, where many other sacrifices are made following the order of ancient religion and ceremonies. Which being completed, Polia leads her Poliphilus to the seashore to await the coming of the god Cupid: and meanwhile she persuades him to go see the antiquities that are in a destroyed temple: which he does: and finds there a great number of Epitaphs, at which he remains for a long time, until he comes to encounter a Hell painted in Mosaic work: looking at which, a sudden fear comes over him, which makes him depart from there, and return to his Polia: to whom he has no sooner arrived, than Cupid arrives in a Boat furnished with many exquisite things, and steered by six damsels trained in the office of rowing. Therein enter Poliphilus and his beloved: whereby Love suddenly sets sail, spreading his golden wings embellished with all colors. Love navigates them; the sea gods and goddesses, nymphs, Tritons, and other monsters do honor and reverence to Cupid, recognizing him as lord. Finally, this god descends on the Island of Cythera <note>The sacred island of Venus.</note>, which the author describes
and distinguishes into small groves, gardens, rivers, and fountains, in such a way that he makes it more beautiful than the Elysian fields of which the Greek and Latin Poets have made such great mention. There the amorous Nymphs make several beautiful presents to Cupid, which he receives and accepts: then he goes on a triumphal Chariot to the middle of the Island, to the marvelous Theater situated in the middle of the Island, at the center of which is the fountain of Venus, surrounded by seven columns of precious stones. There the author recounts all the mysteries that were performed nearby, then how for the coming of the god Mars, he and his beloved were constrained to retire with the Nymphs, who led them to another fountain, near which was the sepulcher of Adonis, in commemoration of whom the goddess Venus has a funeral pomp <note>A solemn procession.</note> held every year, and she herself assists there, performing the office of Prioress. The Nymphs being seated around the foot of this fountain, they request Polia's pleasure be to tell them from what race she is descended, and how she became amorous, together with the discourse of her loves, and there ends the first book. In the second, this same Polia, to satisfy the request of the Nymphs, relates to them entirely her parentage, and does not fail to say how the city of Treviso was first built. Then she pursues the difficulty there was before she could condescend to become amorous, and then the happy success she has in her loves with several notable accessories. Poliphilus wakes up at the song of the Nightingale.

You may believe, my Lords, that beneath this fiction there are many good things hidden, which it is not permitted to reveal, and also you would have no pleasure if they were specified to you particularly: for you would never taste the flavor of the fruit that can be gathered in this reading: wherefore I will tell you nothing else of it, but rather refer the whole to the exercise of your studies. Nevertheless, to make known to you the name of the author of the first volume, and what must be followed from the beginning to the end, the capital letters enriched with Arabesque leaves, and those will instruct you in what you desire <note>The first letters of each chapter in the original Italian edition formed an acrostic: POLIAM FRATER FRANCISCVS COLVMNA PERAMAVIT (Brother Francesco Colonna loved Polia dearly).</note>. Regarding that of Polia, she herself explains it at the beginning of the second book, where she says she bears the name of the Roman woman who killed herself for having been violated by the son of a proud King <note>Lucretia.</note>: and not with the ancient nobility of her race, she dedicates her founder of Treviso to the domain of the Venetians.

You see, my Lords, that such a work has not had as good a destiny as its subject deserves, because it did not fall at the first stroke into the hands of the true French Cicero, who is Nicolas de Herberay, Lord of Essars, who made a Castilian Amadis speak <note>Herberay was famous for translating the Spanish chivalric romance "Amadis de Gaula" into elegant French.</note>: I do not know if those of our posterity will be able to follow him, much less would I say surpass him. In truth, if this book had at first sight fallen into his hands, and he had wished to employ his style for what it contains, it is my opinion that it would now be the pearl of all those that for twenty years have been communicated to us in this language: for as for those from before, I do not think much account should be made of them. Nevertheless, I still wish to testify that whoever the gentleman was who first translated it into our common speech, he is worthy...

->a iij<-

->JEAN MARTIN, SECRETARY TO MY<-
->LORD the Most Reverend Cardinal of Lenoncourt.<-

->TO THE READERS.<-

| If you desire (my Lords) to understand in a few words what is contained in this work, know that Poliphile <note>The protagonist; his name means "lover of many things" or "lover of Polia."</note> says he saw in his dream admirable things, among which he describes several antiques worthy of memory, such as Pyramids, Obelisks, great ruins of edifices, the variety of columns, their measurements, pedestals, bases, and capitals with which they are adorned. Then the architraves, friezes, cornices, and frontispieces with their carvings. A great horse, an Elephant of marvelous size, a Colossus, and a magnificent gate, with its plan, arrangement, moldings, and stonework. Afterward, how five beautiful Nymphs led him to the baths: and meanwhile he does not forget to mention an excellent fountain. Further, he describes the Palace of Queen Eleutherilide <note>Her name is derived from the Greek word for "freedom."</note>: who for love of him had a solemn feast prepared, in which one can learn many things beneficial to human health. After that, he specifies the diversity of precious stones, with their natural virtues: the means of cutting them: and the diversity of pastimes in a dance: and consequently illustrates three gardens, of which one is of glass, the other of silk, and the third made into a Labyrinth surrounded by a Peristyle or enclosure of columns made of terracotta. In the middle of this peristyle is seated a pyramid carved with Egyptian characters, which are called Hieroglyphic letters. Departing from there, he goes to the three gates, and enters the one in the middle, where he finds his beloved Polia, whose beauty, grace, and the fashion of her garments he expresses. This Polia shows him four triumphs of the great Jupiter: then shows him the mortal ladies with whom the gods were in love: together with the beloveds of the Poets: and conducts him by good industry to where several other sacrifices are made following the order of ancient religion and ceremonies. These being completed, Polia leads her Poliphile to the seashore to await the coming of the god Cupid: and meanwhile she persuades him to go see the antiquities that are in a destroyed temple: which he does: and finds there a great number of Epitaphs, at which he remains for a long time, until he comes to encounter a Hell painted in Mosaic work: looking at which, a sudden fear comes over him, which makes him depart from there and return to his Polia: to whom he has no sooner arrived, than Cupid arrives in a Boat furnished with many exquisite things, and steered by six damsels trained in the office of rowing. Into this Poliphile and his beloved enter: wherefore Love suddenly sets sail, extending his golden wings embellished with all colors. Before the voyage, the sea gods and goddesses, nymphs, Tritons, and other monsters do honor and reverence to Cupid, recognizing him as lord. Finally, this god descends on the island of Cythera <note>The mythical island of Venus.</note>, which the author describes | describes and distinguishes into small groves, gardens, rivers, and fountains, in such a way that he has made it more beautiful than the Elysian fields of which the Greek and Latin Poets have made such great mention. There the amorous Nymphs make several beautiful presents to Cupid, which he receives and accepts: then he goes on a triumphal Chariot to a marvelous Theater situated in the middle of the island, at the center of which is the fountain of Venus, surrounded by seven columns of precious stones. There the author recounts all the mysteries that were performed nearby, then how for the coming of the god Mars, he and his beloved were constrained to retire with the Nymphs, who led them to another fountain, near which was the sepulcher of Adonis, in commemoration of whom the goddess Venus has a funeral pomp performed every year, and she herself assists, performing the office of Prioress. The Nymphs being seated around the foot of this fountain, they request Polia that it be her pleasure to tell them from what race she is descended, and how she became amorous, together with the discourse of her loves, and there ends the first book. In the second, the said Polia, to satisfy the request of the Nymphs, relates to them entirely her parentage, and does not fail to say how the city of Treviso was first built. Then she pursues the difficulty there was before she could condescend to become amorous, and then the happy success she has in her loves with several notable accessories. --- Page 11 ---
<meta>This page continues the translator's preface to the French edition of the "Hypnerotomachia Poliphili." The previous page likely introduced the work's origins; here, the translator justifies his stylistic choices and describes the collaborative effort to bring the text into French.</meta>

...worthy that one should be grateful to him for it, especially seeing that he extracted it from an **Italian** language mixed with **Greek** and **Latin** <note>original: "Italien meſlé de Grec & de Latin"</note>, so confusedly put together that even moderately learned Italians cannot derive any structure from it: and furthermore, he has reduced it to a **French** brevity which will satisfy many people. But if there are some who are annoyed that I have not entirely restored it according to the **Italian**: so that they do not blame me, I wish to beg them to understand how I was induced to set my hand to this work.

Immediately after I had published my *Arcadia* by **Sannazaro** <note>Jacopo Sannazaro (1458–1530), an Italian poet whose pastoral work "Arcadia" was immensely influential.</note>, a friend of mine who had the copy of this book brought it to me to share it with me; and after several remarks, he prayed me that for love of him I would be willing to take the charge of revising it. This I granted him, as to one for whom I would wish to do much greater things: and in fact, finding myself for the hour with a little leisure, I began in his presence to change not only some spellings which are no longer used by us, but furthermore to transpose some words which still retained something of the **Italian** phraseology, so corrupted that truly I marveled how this gentleman had been able to succeed so well with it: and certainly that made me so scrupulous <note>original: "religieux" - meaning meticulous or conscientious in this context</note> toward him, that I never wished to amplify nor diminish anything in the clauses he had made, except at times to change their order, to the end of making them easier. This, **My Lords**, is how the interpretation and printing of this book proceeded: which you will receive, if it please you, with as good affection as it is presented to you.

This book

<column-break/>

### This excellent and new book,
### Comparable to the ancients,
### Contains all that is beautiful
### Upon the fertile and arable earth,
### But it would have been miserable
### If its second loving father
### Had not, by his helping hand,
### Restored it to the world, and made it happy.

**Poliphilo** <note>The protagonist of the story, whose name implies "lover of many things" or "lover of Polia."</note> first
Gave it what is called essence:
And the other, secondly,
Guarded it from death by his power,
Which was taking enjoyment of it
By plunging it into the river of forgetfulness <note>A reference to Lethe, the mythological river of oblivion.</note>.
But he brings it into knowledge
To be ennobled by praise.

The **French** will now read it,
Who did not think it was in the world:
And many praises they will speak
Of chaste, pure, and clean friendship:
In which, when a good heart is founded,
Nothing but good can come to it:
Whereas he who abounds in lewdness,
Cannot attain to honor.

**Bacchus** <note>The Roman god of wine and theater; the poet refers to the myth of his double birth (first from Semele, then from the thigh of Jupiter).</note> was fathered twice,
As the **Poets** tell us,
And this book speaks with two voices,
At the very least to those who read it.

Now, since foreigners prize
These two, I am quite deceived,
And I shall say that the stars are harmful,
If its discourse is not well received.

->a .iii.<- <note>Signature mark for the printer to keep the pages in order.</note>

<meta>This page continues the translator's preface, discussing the linguistic challenges of the original text and the transition into a poetic commendation of the work.</meta>

worthy of gratitude, especially considering that he extracted it from an Italian language mixed with Greek and Latin <note>original: "Italien meslé de Grec & de Latin"</note>, so confusedly put together that even the Italians themselves—unless they are highly practiced—[would struggle]; but furthermore, to transpose the structure: and yet so fashioned by the rules of Art, that it is reduced to a French brevity which will satisfy many people. But if there are some who are annoyed that I have not entirely restored it according to the Italian: so that they do not blame me, I wish to pray them to understand how I was induced to set my hand to this work.

Immediately after I had brought to light my *Arcadia* by Sannazaro <note>Jacopo Sannazaro (1458–1530), an Italian poet whose "Arcadia" was a major influence on Renaissance literature</note>, a friend of mine who had a copy of this book brought it to me to share it with me; and after much discussion, he prayed me that for the love of him I would take the charge of revising it. This I granted him, as to one for whom I would wish to do much greater things: and in fact, finding myself for the hour with a little leisure, I began in his presence to change not only some spellings which are no longer in use among us, but furthermore to transpose some words which still retained the Italian phrasing <note>original: "fraze Italienne"</note>, so corrupted that truly I was amazed how this gentleman had been able to come through it so well: and certainly that made me so scrupulous <note>original: "religieux"</note> in his regard, that I never wished to amplify nor diminish anything in the clauses he had made, except sometimes to change their order, to the end of making them easier. This, My Lords, is how the interpretation and printing of this book proceeded: which you will receive, if it please you, with as much good affection as it is presented to you.

<meta>This page serves as the introductory front matter for the famous architectural romance, the "Hypnerotomachia Poliphili." It features a sonnet in Italian followed by its French poetic paraphrase (Exposition), and begins the Table of Contents. The tone is celebratory of human intellect and the arts.</meta>

->SONNET.<-
Behold the other Column that sustained
That beautiful model of ancient memory:
Every figure, every mass, and structure:
And various styles of signs it contained.

That which a thousand eyes, and thousands upon thousands of pens:
And that which they have written with great toil,
In a dream is all here explained,
And I understand what happened to the author.

O coarse minds, and men only in part:
And you who are intent on vile profit,
These papers are heavy burdens to you.

O pure spirits, and noble Frenchmen:
By God, see in these learned papers
How much genius and art are worth and can achieve.

->*Heaven, not earth.*<-
<note>original: "Cælum, non solum." A Latin motto suggesting the work's aspirations are spiritual or intellectual rather than merely worldly.</note>

->EXPOSITION OF THIS SONNET.<-

<insert>ornamental initial V</insert>iew here the most high column,
Where the most ancient knowledge is marked.
Every stroke, every plan, every work beautiful and good,
And many a fragment is well-applied there.

That which a thousand eyes and hands have practiced
With great labor, is given in this book
Easily, explained through discourse
Under a brief dream, which the author ordains.

O thick wits whom reason abandons,
And you who are focused on miserable gain,
This book is such that its weight <note>The French "paix" is likely a variant or typo for "poix" (weight/pitch) or "prix" (value), matching the Italian "pesi" (burdens).</note> astounds you.

But O Frenchmen, beautiful and prudent spirits,
See how much can be achieved in a person
By art and spirit when they are in accord.

Poliphilo recounts how it was advised to him in a dream, that he slept, and while sleeping found himself in a valley enclosed by a great wall in the form of a pyramid, upon which sat an Obelisk of marvelous height, which he regarded with admiration. **3.**

Poliphilo recounts the excellence of the Queen, the place of her residence, with her magnificent preparation and sumptuous banquet, and how the Queen commanded two of her young ladies, that they should make him see more amply the whole state of her palace: also how he was instructed by her on certain doubts he had: then led to the three gates in which he entered, and remained in the middle one with the amorous young ladies. **39.**

->BOOK ONE<-

## Of the sleep that took Poliphile, & how
### IT SEEMED TO HIM WHILE SLEEPING THAT HE
*was in a desert country, then in an*
*obscure forest.*

**P**OR one morning in the month of April around the dawn of the day, I, Poliphile, was in my bed, without other company than my loyal guard Agrypnie <margin>Agrypnie, that is to say, without sleep, or vigilance.</margin>, who had kept me all that night in many conversations, and took pains to console me: for I had declared to her the occasion of my sighs. At the end she advised me to forget all <margin>by sickness.</margin> to remedy all my grief: then knowing that I ought to rest, she took her leave, and left me alone. Whereby I remained fantasizing, and consuming the rest of the night by myself. If love is never equal, how is it possible to love that which loves not? and in what manner can a poor doubtful soul resist, fought by so many assaults? considering especially that the war is interior, and the enemies familiar and domestic, along with being continually occupied by very variable opinions. After this there came to my memory the miserable condition of lovers who, to please another, desire sweetly to die: and to satisfy themselves, are content to live in unease, not satiating their famished desire, except with vain, dangerous, and painful imaginations. I labored so much at this discourse, that my spirits, weary of this frivolous thinking, received a false and feigned pleasure, and from the divine object of my lady Polia (the figure of whom is engraved in the depths of my heart) sought thereafter nothing but natural rest, so as not to find myself entirely overtaken by sleep, and I fell asleep. O Jupiter, sovereign God, shall I call this vision happy, marvelous, or terrible, which is such that in me there is no part so small that does not tremble and burn in thinking of it? It seemed to me (certainly) that I was in a spacious plain, sown with flowers and greenery: the weather was serene and temperate, the sun bright, and softened by a gracious wind: whereby everything there was marvelously peaceful, and in silence: of which I was seized with a fearful admiration: for I perceived there no sign of human habitation, nor even a haunt of beasts: which made me hasten my steps, looking here and there. Nevertheless, I could see nothing else except leaves and branches which did not move at all.

## BOOK ONE OF
(Image of a forest scene with figures)

But at last I journeyed so far that I found myself in a forest, great and dark; nor can I remember in what manner I could have gone so astray. Nevertheless, however it happened, I was assailed by a grievous and sudden terror, so much so that my pulse began to beat beyond its usual rate, and my face grew pale. The rays of the sun could not penetrate through the foliage, which made me fear I had arrived in the Black Forest <note>original: "forest noire," likely referring to the Hercynian Forest</note>, in which none dwell except wild and dangerous beasts. For fear of these, I strove with all my might to find a quick exit, and I set myself to running without keeping to any way or path, nor knowing toward what part I should direct myself, often stumbling among the trunks and stumps of trees that were there at ground level. I went forward at times, then suddenly turned back, now to one side, now to the other, my hands and face torn by brambles, thistles, and thorns. And what made it worse for me than all else was that at every step I was held back by my robe, which caught on the bushes and thickets. The labor I had from this was so great and so excessive that there was no more counsel left in me; and I knew not what to do, except to complain in a loud voice. But all that was in vain, for I was heard by no one, except by the beautiful Echo, who answered me from the hollow of the forest; which made me reclaim the help of the piteous Ariadne <note>The Cretan princess who helped Theseus escape the Labyrinth</note>, and desire the thread she gave to the disloyal Theseus to guide him through the Labyrinth.

## OF POLIPHILUS. VI.
[[page number: 2]]
### Poliphilus, fearing the peril of the forest, made his
->PRAYER TO JUPITER: THEN FOUND<-
*the exit, all parched with thirst. And just as he wished to refresh himself at a fountain, and had abandoned the water ready at hand, he heard a melodious song, by following which he found himself afterward in greater anguish than before.*

Befogged in my understanding, without being able to know what part I should take—whether to die in that strayed forest or to hope for my uncertain salvation—I made every effort to get out. But the more I entered into great darkness, very weak and trembling for the fear I had; for I expected nothing but that some beast would come to confront me to devour me, or that striking my foot against a trunk or root, I would fall into some abyss and be swallowed by the earth, as was Amphiaraus <note>A hero of Greek myth who was swallowed by the earth while fleeing battle</note>. In this manner was my understanding troubled, without hope and without reason, wandering without way or path. Wherefore, seeing that in my case there was no other remedy, I betook myself to recommend my soul to the divine mercy, saying: "O Diespiter <note>An archaic Latin name for Jupiter, meaning 'Sky Father'</note>, most great, most good, most powerful, and most helpful, if by humble and devout prayers humanity can merit the help of divine aid and ought to be heard by you, I, at present repentant and sorrowful for all my past frailties and offenses, beseech and invoke you, sovereign eternal father, ruler of heaven and earth, that it please your incomprehensible deity to deliver me from these perils, so that I may finish the course of my life by some other happy end." Hardly had I finished my prayer, made from the depths of my quite humbled heart, my eyes full of tears—firmly believing that the gods help and save those who invoke them with pure will—than I found myself out of the forest. Whereupon, just as if from a cold and humid night I had arrived into a clear and serene day, my eyes emerging from such darkness could not well (for some time) endure the brightness of the sun. I was tanned <note>or "weather-beaten"</note>, sad, and anxious, so much so that it truly seemed I was stifling from a foolish faintness, almost entirely broken and slowed of heart; in short, I esteemed nothing of all that was present to me. Furthermore, I had such a great thirst that the fresh and delicate air could in no way refresh me, nor satisfy the dryness of my mouth. But after having regained a little courage, I deliberated by all means to appease this thirst; wherefore I went searching through that country, until I found a great vein of fresh water, gushing and bubbling in a beautiful fountain, which flowed by a small brook, which became a noisy river across the stones and trunks of trees fallen and overturned in its channel, and against which the water surged back as if angry and vexed that they thought to delay it—it which was augmented by several other rivulets, along with some torrents engendered from the snows.

to approach, I placed both knees on the ground upon the bank of the fountain: and from the hollow of my two hands I made a vessel which I filled with this liquor. But as I intended to bring it to my mouth to quench my burning thirst, I heard a song so powerfully melodious that it exceeds the power and the knowledge to declare it: for the sweetness of this harmony gave me much more delight than the drink which was stayed from me, so much so that I lost my senses, thirst, and understanding: and as if I had been overwhelmed, the water that I had already drawn spilled out through the gaps between my fingers, so much did I find myself destitute of strength. I was (believe me) so diminished in strength that I could hardly draw breath to warm it within my stomach, where a tiny bit of heat remained, ready to expire and depart, leaving me entirely insensible. **L** Having passed through the terrifying forest, and after having left that first region through the sweet sleep that had then overtaken me, I found myself all anew in a place much more delectable than the first. For it was bordered and surrounded by pleasant green hillsides, populated with diverse kinds of trees, such as oaks, beeches, planes, elms, ashes, hornbeams, limes, and others, planted according to the aspect of the place. And down across the plain, there were small bushes of wild shrubs, such as broom, juniper, heather, and tamarisk, laden with flowers, among the medicinal meadows—namely, the three comfreys, elecampane, chervil, lovage, Macedonian parsley, peony, marshmallows, plantain, betony, and other simples <note>Medicinal herbs</note> of all sorts and species, many of which were unknown to me. A little further than the middle of this plain, there was a sandy area mixed with small green mounds and full of fine grass, and a small wood of palm trees, from which the Egyptians gather bread, wine, oil, clothing, and timber for building. Their leaves seemed like sword blades and were laden with fruit. There were large, medium, and small ones, and the ancients gave them the title of signifying victory, because they resist every charge and heavy weight without being able to be cast down. In this place there was no habitation; however, while walking among these trees on the left hand, a wolf appeared to me

<column-break/>

On the side where this edifice was, the hills rose a little higher and seemed to join the building which was situated between two mountains, serving as an enclosure to a valley. Therefore, estimating it to be a thing worthy of seeing, I directed my path that way; but the more I approached it, the more the desire grew to look at it. This edifice was a magnificent work, and a marvelous obelisk, founded upon a great heap of stones, the height of which exceeded without comparison the mountains that were on both sides. When I had approached quite near, I stopped to contemplate at more leisure such a great insolence <note>In the sense of "extraordinary boldness" or "grandeur"</note> of architecture which was half demolished, composed of blocks of white marble joined without cement, and so well fitted together that where it was still entire, the point of a needle could not have entered between two stones. There were all sorts of columns, partly fallen and broken, partly whole; and in their places, with their capitals, architraves, friezes, cornices, and bases, of singular invention and workmanship, with several other pieces of noble sculpture, totally beyond recognition of what their carving had been, and almost reduced to their first form, tumbled and scattered here and there across the countryside.

The terrifying forest having been passed by me, and after having left that first region through the sweet sleep that had then seized me, I found myself all anew in a place much more delectable than the first; for it was bordered and surrounded by pleasant green hillsides, peopled with various kinds of trees, such as oaks, beeches <note>original: "faux"</note>, plane trees, elms, ashes, hornbeams, lindens, and others, planted according to the aspect of the place. And down across the plain, there were small thickets of wild shrubs, such as broom, junipers, heather, and tamarisks, laden with flowers; among the meadows grew medicinal herbs, namely the three comfreys <note>original: "consolides"</note>, elecampane, honeysuckle, bear's breech <note>original: "branche ursine"</note>, plantain, betony, and other simples <note>medicinal plants</note> of all sorts and species, many unknown. A little further than the middle of this plain, there was a sandy area mixed with small green mounds, and full of tiny grass, and a small grove of palm trees, from which the Egyptians gather bread, wine, oil, clothing, and timber for building: their leaves looked like sword blades, and they were laden with fruit. There were large, medium, and small ones, and the ancients gave them the title of signifying victory, because they resist every charge and heavy weight without being able to be cast down. In this place there was no habitation; nevertheless, while walking among these trees on the left hand, there appeared to me a wolf running

running with its mouth full, at the sight of which the hair stood up on my head: and I wanted to cry out, but I found I had no voice. As soon as it perceived me, it fled into the woods: seeing which, I returned somewhat to myself, and raising my eyes toward that part where the mountains met, I saw a little to the side a great height in the form of a tower, and nearby a building which seemed imperfect; nevertheless, from what I could judge of it, it was of ancient structure.

(Image: A traveler, Poliphilo, stands in a landscape of scattered ruins and lush trees. A wolf flees into the woods on the left. In the background, a massive, stepped pyramidal structure supports a towering obelisk, flanked by mountains.)

On the side where this edifice was, the hills rose a little higher, and seemed to join the building which was situated between two mountains, and served as a closure to a valley: whereby, estimating that it was a thing worthy to be seen, I directed my way that way: but the more I approached it, the more I discovered this magnificent work, and my desire to look at it grew, for it no longer resembled a tower, but rather a marvelous obelisk, founded upon a great heap of stones, the height of which exceeded without comparison the mountains that were on the two sides. When I had approached quite near, I stopped to contemplate at more leisure such great insolence <note>In this context, "insolence" refers to an overwhelming or extravagant display of architectural grandeur.</note> of architecture which was half demolished, composed of blocks of white marble joined without cement, and so well fitted together that where it was still entire, the point of a needle could not have entered between two stones. There were all sorts of columns, partly fallen and broken, partly whole: and in their places, with their capitals, architraves, friezes, cornices, and bases <note>original: "soubassemens"</note>, of singular invention and workmanship, with several other pieces of noble sculpture, totally beyond recognition of what their carving had been, and almost reduced to their original form, tumbled and dispersed here and there, through the countryside.

amidst which, and between these fragments, many wild plants, herbs, and trees of various kinds had sprung up, such as myrtles, mastic trees, wild olives, centaury, vervain, gooseberry bushes, and capers. Then, against the ruined walls grew houseleek, polypody, scolopendrium—or hart's-tongue fern—senna, <term>faune</term><note>likely a local variant of "faunée" or a similar wild herb</note>, and pellitory. Thus, at the principal front of this great edifice, I beheld an exquisite portal, well-proportioned to all the rest of the structure. The section of the wall continued from one of the mountains to the other, and was six <term>stades</term><note>An ancient Greek unit of distance, roughly 600 feet</note> and twenty paces in length, as I was able to conjecture. The alignment of the mountains was plumb from the top to the bottom of the site. Therefore, I remained quite pensive and amazed as to how, with what iron tools and implements, with what labor, and by what human hands such an edifice had been constructed, at such great expense and consumption of time.

This wall had (in my judgment) the fifth part of a stade in height from the last cornice down to the foot and level of the pavement. It was made (as I have said) to enclose this valley, into which one could neither enter nor exit except through this gate, upon which was founded the great pyramid—so marvelous that I estimated the expense to be inestimable and the length of time to make it incredible. The multitude of men who worked on it was innumerable and infinite; for if merely looking at it confounded my understanding and dazzled my sight, what could it do to the intelligence of the building itself? Now, so that I do not fail to describe what I have seen, I will state its form in very few words. Each face or side of the square of the <term>plinth</term><note>The heavy base or platform supporting the structure</note> where the alignment of the steps forming the pyramid began, was six stades in length; these, multiplied by four for the circuit of the four equal squares, make twenty-four stades. The height was constructed in this manner: drawing the sloping lines A B and A C along the four corners from the plinth up to the highest of the steps, where they joined to form the pyramid. The <term>cathetus</term><note>original: "cathet" - a vertical line</note> or perpendicular line A D, being in the middle of these and falling straight upon the center of the plinth at point D, where the diagonal lines crossed, had a height of five parts, of which the sloping and collateral lines had six.

## BOOK ONE OF
The pyramid was constructed in the form of a flight of steps, containing one thousand four hundred and ten steps, of which the last ten were converted into a marvelous cube or massive stone, forming the reduction and narrowing of the pyramid. It was so large that it was impossible to believe that human hands could have raised it so high; it was made of that same marble stone as the steps and placed there as the base and foundation for the obelisk, of which I shall speak hereafter. It measured four paces in diameter on each of its square faces. At the four upper corners, following the diagonal lines, were six feet of Harpies <note>Mythological monsters with the bodies of birds and faces of women</note>, hairy and clawed, made of the finest cast metal, ending toward the top in an antique interlaced foliage that embraced the foot of the obelisk. The obelisk was supported on these four feet or paws of Harpies, which were fourteen paces in height; the foot of the obelisk had the same proportion, so that being placed so high in the air, its length was seven times as much, tapering at the point. It was made entirely of a single stone of Theban *pyropoecile* <note>original: "Pyropecile Thebaique"; likely referring to red granite or porphyry from Thebes</note>, inscribed with Egyptian hieroglyphic letters on its four faces, and on its sides it had a well-polished mirror.

At the very tip was placed a nymph of gilded copper, set upon a rotating vase in the shape of a pyramid, to the astonishment of all who beheld her. For the nymph was made in such proportion that, being placed so high in the air, it was a strange thing to consider how she had been raised and carried so high. Her garment fluttered around her as if lifted by the wind, leaving part of her thigh uncovered. She had two wings extended and open, as if she were ready to fly, toward which her gaze was turned. Her hair fluttered over her forehead in great abundance, but the back of her head was bald and without hair <note>This is a classic depiction of Occasio or Opportunity, who must be seized by the forelock before she passes</note>. In her right hand, facing the pyramid, she held a horn of plenty, full of all good things; the other hand rested on her breast, turned toward the earth, which was bare. This statue was easily turned by all the winds, along with its base which was of bronze and hollow, such that no such sound was ever heard. I do not think there has ever been such an obelisk; certainly that of the Vatican in Rome was not its equal, nor that of Alexandria, nor even those of Babylon. It possessed within itself such a height of wonder that I was ravished with amazement in contemplating it, and even more so for its inestimable size, for I could not well understand how it had been raised so high.

But upon a great plinth <note>The heavy square slab forming the lowest part of a column or pedestal</note>, massive as I have said, which was fourteen paces high and six stades <note>An ancient Greek unit of distance, roughly 600 feet</note> in length, forming the substructure of the first and lowest step. This plinth had not (in my judgment) been brought there from elsewhere, but was carved from the same rock in this form, and adapted in its natural place for this great structure. The remainder of the steps were made of blocks of marble, assembled and arranged in order. The plinth did not touch the long walls but was distant from each side by the length of ten paces. On its face toward the side from which I came, and in the middle of its square, was carved in

high relief, the terrifying head of Medusa, a horrible monster, living and crying out (as it seemed) by a furious demonstration, scowling, with sunken eyes, hanging eyebrows, a wrinkled and frowning forehead, and an open maw, which was hollowed and pierced by a small vaulted path passing into the middle of the edifice. To this opening of the mouth (which served as a door to enter this path), one climbed by the interlacings of her hair, which were formed with such regularity and geometric precision that they served as steps. And instead of tresses, they were twisted with long revolutions of serpents that wrapped around and bit one another, extending around the head and face down to beneath the chin. They were so gravely made that the material seemed quite truly to maintain the appearance of the work, such that they gave me great fright; for their eyes were sunken, made of shining stones, so that if I had not been certain the material was marble, I would not have dared to approach so easily.

The path carved inside the mouth led straight to the top of the cube. Then I climbed inside by a spiral staircase and continued from one to the other toward the top where the obelisk was seated. But the pyramid was illuminated throughout by clear light that the ingenious architect had, by a singular instrument, made in several places of the building—certain secret conduits that corresponded directly to the aspect of the sun as it made its high, low, and middle course. The lower part was lit by the conduits from above, and the upper part by those from below, being illuminated by the completion of light through reflection and reverberation. The building was so well calculated according to the three faces—Western, Southern, and Eastern—that at all hours of the day the pyramid was lit by the sun, as its conduits were made in the form of air-vents and distributed in their places all around the pyramid from the cube down to the plinth, where I climbed by a straight and massive square step on the same rock. On the right side, to my thinking, the mountain came to fail below the foot of the obelisk by ten paces. When I had come before the head of Medusa which served as steps (as I said above) to look down: for all that could be seen starting from the middle of this pyramid seemed like a great flow from this spiral staircase upward, with balusters and spindles placed in pairs; they were half a pace in height, linked and continued one to another toward the point by a crown of hedge and enclosure at the opening of the base, which they surrounded all about, except for the side where one climbs so high; and the turning atop the obelisk was an admirable dizziness. <gloss>Lixas of Libya, architect, has raised me.</gloss> <note>original: "ΑΙΧΑΣ Ο ΑΙΒΥΚΟΣ ΛΙΘΟΔΟΜΟΣ ΩΡΩΞΕΝ ΜΕ." The French gloss translates the Greek inscription provided in the text.</note>

On the first face of the plinth <note>The heavy square slab serving as the base of a column or pedestal.</note> upon which the pyramid was founded, there was carved a cruel battle of Giants, who lacked nothing but life, for they were so excellent in the prompt swiftness of their bodies and in the amplitude of their monstrous frames, that it seemed they were unburdened by nature; it was so well made and arranged that it is impossible to declare it: for nature was followed and imitated, and its effects so properly expressed, that it seemed they wished to set their feet upon those who had fallen, stumbling in great numbers. Others there were unbridled and furious, breaking through the press and the fray. Also, some of these Giants had thrown down their arms and were embracing in the form of wrestling: many had fallen, whom others pulled by the feet, others trampled and stepped over: Giants among the dead beneath the horses, some of whom strove to rise again, and placed their targets <note>Small shields.</note> before the blows of swords, or otherwise ancient scimitars, very artistically figured. The majority fought on foot, in confusion, and in troops. There were enough of them armed with hauberks <note>Chainmail shirts.</note>, cuirasses, and helmets, enriched with various crests, plumes, and devices: others were all naked, who seemed to assail their enemies with an inflamed courage: many were portrayed in a fearsome likeness as if crying out: others in an obstinate and furious figure, some ready to die, others entirely dead, manifesting their robust limbs, such that one could see the raised muscles, the joints of the bones, and the extended nerves. The combat seemed so terrifying and horrible, that one would have estimated that Mars had assembled for battle against Porphyrion and Alcyoneus <note>Two of the Giants who fought the Olympian gods in Greek mythology.</note>. The figures were in half-relief of white marble, and the background of jet-black touchstone, to give grace and luster to the images, and to make the work stand out. There could be seen strange bodies, extreme efforts, passionate acts, diverse deaths, and uncertain victory. Alas, that my weak and labored understanding, confused by the continual distraction of such marvelous things, cannot suffice to declare the whole, nor to well express the smallest part of this so noble sculpture. God, from whence proceeded such great audacity and presumption with the disordered will to assemble stones in such a great heap? With what rollers, with what chariots, and other traction machines were these blocks of incredible size raised so high to erect such a marvelous pyramid? Certainly, Dinocrates <note>The architect who proposed carving Mount Athos into a statue of Alexander the Great.</note> never proposed more superbly to the great King Alexander the form of his concept and design for the structure of Mount Athos. In truth, this one exceeds the insolence of the Egyptians, the miracle of the Labyrinth of Crete, and the fame of the Mausoleum: also without any doubt,

it never came to the knowledge of him who wrote of the seven wonders of the world. At no time was such an edifice seen or even imagined. <insert>L</insert> It is right that I be permitted to say that in all the universal world there were never works so magnificent made, nor contemplated by mortal eye, nor (what is more) imagined by any human understanding: and I would almost frankly dare to affirm, that it is not in the knowledge or power of man to raise or define such a great excellence of building. I was truly so surprised by admiration, and so occupied in looking at it, that no other thing (though it were comforting and pleasant) could enter my imagination, except when, in considering all the parts of this beautiful and fitting composition, I saw the statues made in the forms of maidens. Then I sighed so loudly, that my sighs echoed through this deserted and solitary place, obscured by a thick and heavy air, because of the memory I had of Polia, my best beloved. The idea of her is imprinted in my heart: upon which my soul has made its nest, and rests as in a sure sanctuary. Alas, she had not abandoned me in this so strayed journey. On the first face of the plinth <note>the square block serving as a base</note> upon which the pyramid was founded, there was carved a cruel battle of Giants, who lacked nothing but life, for they were so excellently figured with the movement and great promptness of their dead bodies, that it is impossible to be able to declare it: for nature was there so well glimpsed and counterfeited, and its effects so properly expressed, that it seemed their feet strove with their eyes, and that they ran here and there. There were some unbridled and furious, breaking through the press and the fray. Some of these Giants had thrown down their arms and embraced each other in the form of wrestling. Many had fallen, who were being pulled by the feet, others trampled and stepped over, lying among the dead beneath the horses, from which some tried to rise again, putting their shields in front, or otherwise ancient scimitars, very artistically figured. The majority fought on foot, in confusion, and in troops. There were enough of them armed with hauberks <note>coats of mail</note>, cuirasses, and light helmets, enriched with various crests, plumes, and devices: others were all naked, who seemed to assail their enemies with an inflamed courage: many were portrayed in a fearsome effigy by striking out in another obstinate and furious figure. Some were ready to die, others entirely dead, manifesting their robust limbs, such that one could see the raised muscles, the joints of the bones, and the extended nerves. The combat seemed so terrifying and horrible, that one would have estimated that Mars had assembled for battle against Porphyrion and Alcyoneus <note>Giants from Greek mythology who warred against the gods</note>. The figures were in high relief <note>original: "demy bosse"</note> of white marble, and the background of jet-black touchstone, to give grace and luster to the images, and to make the work stand out. There could be seen strange bodies, extreme efforts, affectionate acts, diverse deaths, and uncertain victory. Alas, that my weary and labored spirits, my understanding confused by continual doubt, troubled by such marvelous things, cannot suffice here for everything, but only to well express the smallest part of this so noble sculpture. God, from whence proceeded such great audacity and presumption with the disordered will to assemble stones in so great a heap? With what rollers, with what chariots, and other traction machines were these blocks of incredible size raised so high, to erect such a marvelous pyramid? Certainly, Dinocrates <note>Alexander the Great's architect</note> never proposed more superbly to the great King Alexander the form of his concept and design for the structure of Mount Athos. When I had passed beyond, I found a marvelous Colossus, having the pieces without joints, the legs upright and empty, and likewise all the rest of the body up to the head, which could not be looked upon without horror. Then I conjectured that the wind, entering through the opening of the feet, had caused this sound in the form of a groan, and that the craftsman had made it so quite intentionally. This colossus was lying on its back, made of bronze or cast metal, and forged with excellent skill. When I had come that far, I emboldened myself to enter inside; then, descending by a small stairway, I went down into the throat, then into the stomach, and from there through all the other parts of the body, even into the bowels and entrails. O marvelous concept of human understanding, an enterprise more than admirable! I saw all the internal parts of the natural body open and passable, the name of each written in three languages, namely Chaldean <note>likely referring to Hebrew or Aramaic</note>, Greek, and Latin, along with the diseases that can be bred...

...to observe <note>The text begins mid-word, likely completing "regarder" (to look at/observe) from the previous page</note>, and by the same means, find the cause and the remedy. Everywhere there was a passage, so that one could clearly see bones, arteries, nerves, veins, muscles, and intestines; for it was furnished with several small secret windows which gave sufficient light. Not a single vein was missing, no more than in a perfect man. When I was at the level of the heart, I perceived the place where love forges its sighs, and the spot where it offends most grievously. Then I uttered a great lament, calling "Polia!" so loudly that I felt the whole machine resound, which frightened me. Then I began to weigh the excellence of such an invention, by which, without dissection <term>anatomy: here meaning the surgical study of a corpse</term>, a man could make himself excellent and singular. Oh, noble spirits of antiquity! Oh, truly Golden Age when virtue was equal to fortune; you have left only ignorance and avarice as an inheritance to this unhappy century. 

After I had come out of this colossus, I saw the forehead and the top of the head of another; but it was in a feminine form, the rest of which was buried under those ruins, so that I could see no further. For this reason, I returned to the first place, where I contemplated a great Elephant of black stone, sparking with flecks of gold and silver like powder scattered over it. The stone was so polished and clear that it reflected everything around it as if it were a mirror of fine glass; however, some parts were missing where the metal had tarnished it with its green rust. This Elephant had on the top of its back something like a saddle or copper covering, tied with two wide straps tightened <gloss>by</gloss> below and surrounding the entire belly. Between these was made a square pillar in the form of a pedestal, of a size corresponding to the thickness of the obelisk standing on the animal's back—because nothing of great weight should be seated in vain, for it could not be durable. 

The three faces of this pedestal were engraved with Egyptian letters <note>Hieroglyphs, which in the Renaissance were viewed as mystical, symbolic riddles</note>, and in the fourth was the door to enter it. The elephant (in truth) appeared so perfectly rendered that nothing was lacking in its craftsmanship. Its saddle or covering was adorned with small figures and stories in half-relief <term>demy bosse: a sculptural technique between low and high relief</term>. And right in its middle could be seen erected an obelisk of green Lacedaemonian stone <note>original: "pierre Lacedemoniẽne verde," a rare green porphyry or serpentine marble found near Sparta</note>, which had on its equal faces a width of one pace at the diameter of its base, and seven other geometric paces in height. It tapered to a point, and at the summit was fixed a ball of clear and transparent material. This great animal was supported by a base or counter-base of Porphyry <note>A prized, hard igneous rock, usually deep purple or red</note>. The two large tusks protruding from its mouth were made of white stone, shining like ivory. To its covering was attached, with rich gilded buckles, a breastplate of the same copper, in the middle of which was written in Latin letters: THE BRAIN IS IN THE HEAD <note>original: "CEREBRVM EST IN CAPITE"</note>. Likewise, the point where the neck joins the head was surrounded by a beautiful band, from which hung an ornament in the form of a chanfron <term>chanfrein: a piece of armor designed to protect a horse's forehead</term> cast over the beast's forehead, composed of two perfect squares and bordered with antique foliage, also made of copper.

# THE FIRST BOOK OF THE STRIVING FOR LOVE IN A DREAM

...in the middle of which were carved Ionic <note>referring to Greek characters</note> and Arabic letters, which said: **Labor and industry.** <note>original Greek: *πόνος, καὶ εὐφυΐα*</note>

The proboscis or snout did not touch the pedestal, but was slightly raised and turned back toward the forehead. It had hanging ears, wide and wrinkled in a strange manner, showing by its size that it exceeded the natural order. The pedestal was oblong <note>original: *berlong*</note> and oval, carved with Egyptian <term>hieroglyphic</term> characters <note>In the 15th century, hieroglyphs were viewed as sacred, mystical symbols whose phonetic meaning had not yet been rediscovered</note>, and decorated with its moldings. The length was twelve paces, the width five, and the height three. On one of the sides I found a small door, and a climb of seven steps: by which I arrived on the platform of the pedestal: and saw that in the square block positioned under the belly, another small door was hollowed out. In the hollow of this Elephant there were metal rungs, fixed on both sides in the form of steps, by which one could easily climb and pass through this hollow machine <note>The author uses "machine" to describe any complex, large-scale construction</note>. This made a desire take hold of me to see it, so much so that I entered by this door: then climbed by the rungs into this marvelous body, entirely hollowed out, except that they had left as much mass inside as there was below on the outside to support its obelisk: and there was so much space on each side of the Elephant's flanks that a man could pass through there at his ease. From the vault of the back, toward the rear, hung a burning lamp, attached to bronze chains, which never went out, and illumi-

At this I was completely astonished, and somewhat seized by fear. These things were quite new to me, especially the riddles, which I read and re-read several times, thinking to understand them: but their meaning seemed very ambiguous to me, and such that I did not know how to interpret it. Furthermore, I did not dare to undertake anything, for I was overcome by a **reverent dread** <note>original: *horreur deuote*—a mix of religious awe and physical fear common in Renaissance descriptions of ancient ruins</note> in this dark place, having no light except from two lamps. Moreover, the great desire I had to contemplate the beautiful gate at my ease was the reason I did not stop further, and I departed, intending however to return to consider it more at leisure. Thus I descended by the place where I had entered, and looked at this **great beast** <note>the stone elephant</note> from the outside, thinking what human boldness had been so reckless as to undertake such a high task; what chisels, what tools and ironworks could have penetrated a material so hard and so resistant, especially since all the carvings on the inside corresponded to those on the outside. After I had descended all the way to the bottom onto the pavement, I examined the base that supported it, around which were attached such <term>hieroglyphs</term> <note>symbolic picture-writing which Renaissance scholars believed held secret, divine wisdom</note>.

These most ancient and sacred writings, after having thought well upon them, I interpreted in this manner:
**From labor, sacrifice liberally to the god of nature; little by little you will bring back a mind subject to God, who, mercifully governing the firm guardianship of your life, will hold and preserve it unharmed.**

That is to say:
Sacrifice liberally of your labor to the God of nature; little by little you will bring your spirit into subjection to God, who by His mercy will be the sure guard of your life, and in governing it, will preserve it safe and sound.

I left this beautiful figure with great difficulty, so much did it please me; and then I returned to look at the great horse, which had a dry and lean head, proportionately small, and very well formed to resemble an <term>inconstant</term> <note>meaning lively, spirited, or restive—as if the statue might move at any moment</note> creature. One could almost see its muscles tremble, and it seemed more alive than artificial. On its forehead was engraved this Greek word **GENEA**.

<meta>This page continues the architectural analysis following Poliphile’s encounter with the symbolic "hieroglyphs." He has now reached a magnificent portal and shifts from interpreting symbols to analyzing the geometric principles of classical design, contrasting ancient mastery with the "unlearned" practices of his own time.</meta>

->POLIPHILE.<-

...have you carried with you into the grave the wealth of our riches? <note>This continues the lament from the previous page regarding the loss of ancient knowledge.</note>

When I arrived before the gate—which well deserved to be studied carefully for the excellence of its workmanship—I felt a desire to understand the proportions and measurements that the craftsman had observed there. To find them, I quickly employed this method: I measured one of the squares that supported the double columns on each side, and by that, I easily understood its underlying logic.

First, he had created a square figure **A B C D**, divided by three straight lines and three crossing lines, equally distant from one another, composing sixteen smaller squares. Then, he added onto this square figure one of its halves, which, being divided by the same measurements, made twenty-four squares in total, including the sixteen from the first square figure. Then, drawing two diagonals in the first figure **ABCD**, which were marked by two lines crossing through the middle, he created four squares, each having its own diagonal or transverse line. Furthermore, he fashioned a **Rhombus** <term>Rhombus: a diamond shape</term> or lozenge above the large square, by tracing four lines within its void across the four principal points that equally divide the four sides of the void. After I had conceived this figure in my mind, I thought to myself:

"What can modern architects do, who consider themselves learned, yet are without letters and without doctrine, and even work without rule or measure? For this reason, they corrupt and deform all manners of buildings, both private and public, despising Nature who teaches them to do well, if only they would imitate her. Nevertheless, they may enrich their work, and add or diminish to satisfy the eye, provided that the **massif** <term>Massif: the core structural body or framework of a building</term> remains whole, to which all parts must agree. By this *massif*, I mean the body of the edifice, which even without ornaments makes known the knowledge and the spirit of the master; for it is easy to enrich a thing after it has been invented. However, above all, one must value the distribution, partitioning, and arrangement of the members. From this, one must conclude that it is a common and practiced thing for every workman, even down to the apprentices, to know how to ornament a work; but to *invent* certainly lies within the heads of the learned."

To return, then, to our subject: by taking the large square and its half, and removing the rhombus and the diagonal lines, leaving only the three perpendiculars and the three transversals—except for the middle one which ends at the center of the perpendiculars, cut into four parts and portions—by this rule, you will find two perfect squares, one at the top and the other at the bottom, each containing four small squares which form the door. Now, if you take the diagonal of the bottom square, it will teach you what thickness must be given to the **fintre** <note>original: "fintre," an archaic form of "cintre," referring to the arch or the wooden centering used to build it</note> of the portal, if you set it upright toward the line **A B**, which will serve as the **architrave** <term>Architrave: the main beam resting across the tops of columns</term>. And the midpoint of the upper square will show you the arc and curvature that must be given to the door by turning one point of the compass in a semi-circle, which will rest on the transverse line that cuts the square-and-a-half into two equal parts. But if it is made by any other way, I do not consider it perfect.

It contains diagonal lines forming an X in the lower square and a diamond (rhombus) shape inscribed within the overall frame, illustrating the architectural proportions described in the text.</image-desc>

->### POLIPHILE.<-

C

This measurement was invented by ancient craftsmen well-versed in masonry <note>original: "massonnerie"</note>, and observed in their arches and vaults to give them grace and strength. The pedestal or base of the columns began at the level of the pavement with a plinth; and the whole was one foot high, decorated with its moldings and their astragals or beads <note>original: "astragales ou fuzees"</note>, following the alignment of the building and serving as a base for the side-posts or jambs of the door. The space contained between lines A, B, E, and F was divided into three parts: one for the architrave <term>architrave: the main beam resting across the tops of columns</term>, another for the frieze <term>frieze: the wide central section of an entablature, often decorated with sculpture</term>, and the third for the crown or cornice, which had one part more than the other two; that is to say, if the architrave has five parts, and the frieze the same, the cornice must have six. In this work, the cornice exceeded that measure, because the expert craftsman had made a projection of half a foot on the cymatium <note>original: "cymaise" — the uppermost molding of a cornice</note> of the cornice, so that the overhang of its moldings would not obstruct the view of the sculptures placed above—though one could also enlarge the architrave and the frieze with their ornaments, as the work requires.

Beneath the cornice, there was a square on each side as wide as its projection. The frieze below was as wide as half of this square, or a third of one of the twenty-four squares. The space between the two squares was divided into seven parts: the middle one, which aligned vertically with the door opening, was used for a niche to hold the figure of a nymph. On each side, three parts remained for other sculptures.

The projection of the highest crown or cornice can easily be found by forming a square from the line of its thickness, the diagonal of which will be its projection. Now, considering the entire figure of the twenty-four squares together, you will find that it contains a perfect square and a half. Divide the half that sits upon the square into six parts using five horizontal lines and five vertical ones; draw a line from the middle of the fifth crossing line to the corner of the large perfect square **A**, where the architrave begins; then raise it perpendicularly above the keystone of the curved architrave or vault of the door. And it will show you the regular height of the frontispiece <note>original: "frontispice" — here referring specifically to the triangular pediment crowning the structure</note> or pediment above, the extremities of which must join and relate to the projection of the final cornice or cymatium, and with similar moldings.

The central part of the frieze features a niche intended for a statue. The drawing includes geometric lines indicating the calculation of the pediment's height and the projection of the cornices.</image-desc>
