->OF POLIPHILO.<-

This gate was built of squared stones, so perfectly joined that it seemed to be made of a single piece. On either side of it, at a distance of two paces, lay two great columns, almost entirely buried in the ruins, which I uncovered somewhat; I saw that the bases and capitals were made of copper. I measured the height of one base, and by doubling it, I found the diameter of the foot of the column, and by that same measure I inferred its length, which exceeded twenty-eight cubits. Of the two columns closest to the gate, one was of Porphyry <note>A hard purple igneous rock highly prized by the Romans</note> and the other of Ophite, or serpentine <note>A green, mottled stone resembling snakeskin</note>; the other two were fluted Caryatids <note>Columns carved in the figure of women</note>. On both sides there were several others, some arranged in pairs, others placed at equal intervals, made of dark green Laconian stone. The half-diameter of the foot of the column formed the height of the base, which consisted of a torus, a scotia, and a plinth <note>Poliphilo uses the terms "bozel" (torus/rounded molding), "contrebozel" (scotia/concave molding), and "plinthe" (the square block at the bottom)</note>, formed in this manner: dividing the height of the base into three parts, one was given to the plinth, which had a width of one and a half diameters of the foot of the column. The two remaining parts were divided into four: one part was for the upper torus; the other three were divided in two, one for the lower torus and the other for the scotia. The fillets <note>Small, flat decorative bands</note> each had a seventh part of the whole. Such measurements were observed by the ancient Architects, because they seemed to them good and regular. Upon the capitals of all the columns was placed a beautiful architrave or epistyle <note>The main beam resting on the columns</note>, made with three faces: the first at the bottom was adorned with a molding of a cord of beads in the shape of paternosters <note>Prayer beads</note>; the second was of this same work, except that after two round beads, there was a long one in the shape of a spindle; the third was made with "ears of *forys*" <note>likely a corruption of 'fores' or 'folia', referring to leafy architectural ornaments</note>, split and carved in the manner of foliage. Above was the frieze or zophore <note>The central part of the entablature, often decorated with figures</note>, carved with ancient branches and flowers, interlaced with vine branches and various herbs, interspersed with several kinds of birds. After that there was an order of mutules or modillions <note>Decorative brackets under a cornice</note> resembling heads of foliage projecting from the wall in various ways, upon which began the moldings of a great cornice. The rest of the building from there upward was demolished and fallen, but there appeared to be large double windows, stripped of their ornaments, somewhat showing what the building had been in its entirety. Beneath this architrave, the point of the pediment of the gate met at both sides; within these, which had the form of two scalene triangles <note>original: "triangles dipleures" — triangles with two equal sides, i.e., isosceles</note>, were carved two rounds enclosed by moldings and surrounded by triumphal wreaths made of Oak leaves. Tied with silk ribbons, inside these were made two high-relief figures <note>original: "figures de bosse"</note> emerging from the flat or concave surface of the rounds from the waist up, having their chests covered with a mantle knotted on the left shoulder in the ancient fashion; one had a mixed beard, both were crowned with Laurel, and in their gaze presented great majesty. On the projections of the frieze resting above the columns were carved certain eagles, holding their wings open and perched on festoons of greenery interspersed with fruit, hanging slightly toward the middle; the ends of which seemed to be attached on both sides to ribbons in half-relief, with many folds pierced through like lace. Opposite this gate was situated a great colonnade. And because I have sufficiently...

-># POLIPHILO. <-

This gate was built of squared stones, so perfectly joined that it seemed to be made of a single piece. On either side of it, at a distance of two paces, lay two great columns, almost entirely buried in the ruins, which I uncovered somewhat; I saw that the bases and capitals were made of copper. I measured the height of one base, and by doubling it, I found the diameter of the foot of the column, and by that same measure I inferred its length, which exceeded twenty-eight cubits. Of the two columns closest to the gate, one was of **Porphyry** <note>A hard purple-red stone highly prized in antiquity for imperial monuments</note> and the other of **Ophite**, or serpentine <note>A green, mottled stone resembling snakeskin</note>; the other two were fluted **Caryatids** <note>Columns carved in the shape of female figures</note>. On both sides there were several others, some arranged in pairs, others placed at equal intervals, made of vibrant green Laconian stone <note>A prestigious green marble from Laconia, Greece, also known as *verde antico*</note>. The half-diameter of the foot of the column formed the height of the base, which consisted of a torus, a scotia, and a plinth <note>Poliphilo uses the terms "bozel" (torus/rounded molding), "&nbsp;contrebozel" (scotia/concave molding), and "plinthe" (the square block at the bottom)</note>, formed in this manner: dividing the height of the base into three parts, one was given to the plinth, which had a width of one and a half diameters of the foot of the column. The two remaining parts were divided into four: one part was for the upper torus; the other three were divided in two, one for the lower torus and the other for the scotia. The fillets <note>Small, flat decorative bands</note> each had a seventh part of the whole. Such measurements were observed by the ancient Architects, because they seemed to them good and regular. 

Upon the capitals of these columns was placed a beautiful **architrave** or **epistyle** <note>The horizontal beam that rests directly upon the columns</note>, made with three faces: the first at the bottom was adorned with a molding of a cord of billets in the form of prayer beads; the second was of this same work, except that after every two round beads there was a long one in the shape of a spindle; the third was made with door-frame projections <note>original: "oreilles de forys," referring to *crossettes* or decorative "ears" on a frame</note>, split and carved in the manner of foliage. Above this was the **frieze** or **zophoros** <note>A long horizontal band of sculpted decoration, often depicting animals or figures; from the Greek *zoophoros*</note>, carved with ancient branches and flowers, interlaced with vine branches and various herbs, interspersed with several kinds of birds. After that there was an order of **mutules** or **modillions** <note>Decorative brackets supporting the weight of the upper cornice</note> resembling leafy heads, projecting from the wall at equal distances, upon which began the moldings of a great cornice. The rest of the building from there upward was demolished and fallen, but there was the appearance of large double windows, stripped of their ornaments, showing somewhat what the building had been in its entirety. 

Beneath this architrave, the point of the **frontispiece** <note>A pediment or decorated triangular gable</note> of the gate came to rest; on its two sides—which had the form of two **isosceles triangles** <note>original: "triangles dipleures," which the author helpfully defines as having two equal sides</note>—were carved two rounds enclosed by moldings and surrounded by triumphal crowns made of oak leaves, tied with silk ribbons. Inside these were made two figures in high relief, emerging from the background or concave of the rounds from the waist up, having their chests covered by a mantle knotted on the left shoulder in the ancient fashion. One had a mixed beard; both were crowned with laurel, and in their gaze they presented great majesty. On the projections of the frieze resting upon the columns, certain eagles were carved, holding their wings open and perched on festoons of greenery interspersed with fruit, hanging slightly toward the middle. The ends of these seemed to be attached on both sides to bundles in semi-relief, with many folds pierced through in the manner of ribbons. Opposite this gate was situated a great course of columns. ...sufficiently (as it seems to me) specified these principal members <note>In classical architecture, the "members" are the primary structural components like columns, architraves, and walls</note>. It remains now to describe its enrichments: for the Architect must first conceive and arrange in his mind the solid mass of the entire work, and only afterward consider the ornaments. These are but accessories to the main structure; it is in the former that the skill and experience of the master is recognized, while the latter is easy and common even to apprentices.

BEFORE proceeding further, I wish to beg the favor of lovers who (perhaps) expect to hear from me things more pleasing to them, such as the thoughts with which they sustain their hearts. I ask them to excuse me if I dwell a little long on this description; I hope later to satisfy their desires. To conclude my undertaking, then, I stated above that the principal part of the Architect's task is the invention of the solid body of the entire building. He can then easily reduce it into smaller divisions, much like a musician who, having invented the tone for a specific time based on a "long" or "maxima" <note>In early music notation, a *longa* or *maxima* represented the longest possible note durations</note>, then proportions it into <term>chromatic minims</term> <note>Smaller, faster musical notes; Poliphilo is comparing the subdivision of a building's space to the subdivision of a musical beat</note>—that is, temporal divisions—which he relates back to the firm and solid note <note>original: "note ferme," referring to the *cantus firmus*, the foundational melody in polyphonic music</note>.

Thus, in the Architect's invention, the principal and most necessary rule is the square. Once this square is distributed and divided into several other small squares, one finds the harmony and proper proportion of the entire building, so that all the accessories correspond to their principal structure. And so was this gate made. First, on the right side, was a pedestal decorated with its moldings, taller than it was wide—specifically, of <term>diagonal proportion</term> <note>A rectangle where the height is equal to the diagonal of its square base (a 1:√2 ratio)</note>. Indeed, it is necessary for me to use terms known among men of the craft, even if they are not common. For we have degenerated and lost much of that ancient treasury of language which could properly express every detail of such work; thus, I must speak with the rough and ill-suited words that remain to us.

Now, within the square of this pedestal was carved in <term>alabaster</term> <note>A soft, translucent white stone often used for fine carving</note> stone—diaphanous or transparent—a man slightly past middle age. He had a robust and rustic face, a hard, strong, and bristling beard with straight, rough, and stinging hairs, so that his chin resembled the back of a boar. He sat upon a stone, wrapped in a goatskin, the hind legs of which were tied at his sides, with the neck hanging between his legs and the hair turned toward his skin. ## BOOK ONE OF
## THE STRIFE OF LOVE IN A DREAM
<note>original: "LIVRE PREMIER DE POLIPHILE"</note>

The structure was dedicated to both sexes of the gods, namely to god and goddess, as to male and female, husband and wife, or other such pairings. It was understood that the channels <note>the fluting of the columns</note> were attributed to the feminine sex, and the filling <note>the solid core or perhaps the astragal</note> to the masculine. These fluted columns were first made for the temple of a goddess, intended to represent the capitals with their volutes or scrolls to signify their hair, just as the Greeks wear it—that is to say, tucked up above the ears. The **Caryatid** columns, which have for a capital the head of a woman adorned in her finery, were first made to the shame of the rebellious people of **Carya**, a city of the **Morea** <note>The Peloponnese peninsula in Greece</note>, who allied themselves with the Persians against the other Greeks of their own nation. This was done so that it might serve as a perpetual memory to condemn the more-than-feminine inconstancy of those people of Carya. The bases of these four columns were of copper, enriched with work of oak leaves and garnished with acorns. The capitals were of the same material, covered with notched **abaci** <note>the flat slab on top of a capital</note>, and in the middle of each notch was a beautiful lily flower. The vase of the capital was clothed in two rows of **Acanthus** leaves, each row containing eight leaves, in the Roman and Corinthian fashion. From these leaves issued small volutes, which met in the middle of the vase and composed the lily placed among the notches or arcs of the abacus. The remainder closed itself in the manner of scrolls at the four corners of this work. **Marcus Agrippa** had such as these placed at the portal of the great **Pantheon** temple in Rome. To each capital was attributed for its height one entire diameter of the foot of the column, observing the proportion and measure of all its parts and accessories. The threshold of the door was made of a large green stone, speckled with spots of white, black, yellow, and other diverse and imperfect colors, upon which were placed and seated the doorposts or jambs. These had as much width as the threshold, plus one pace more, in which (nor likewise in the side-posts) there had never been hinges or bolts. Above the vaulting of the door was the architrave with moldings and ornaments, such as billets or beads, "mouse ears," and others. The key or wedge of the arch or vault was of a very black agate stone, carved in the form of an eagle, almost entirely free from the solid block, having its wings extended and holding a child between its talons, directly by the navel, so discreetly fashioned that it seemed the bird feared to wound him. You would have said, seeing his little face, that he was afraid of falling, for which reason he had extended his arms and grasped the wings of the eagle at the thick bones joining the shoulder, and drew his little legs upward over the tail, reaching beneath the vault. It was certainly so perfectly counterfeited from the white vein of the agate (or onyx) and the eagle from the slate-colored part (which is the other nearby vein in the same stone) that I remained quite astonished, thinking in what manner the ingenious workman had imagined applying that stone to such a beautiful invention. Seeing the feathers that the bird had ruffled around its neck, its beak open, and its tongue panting, you could have known that it was smitten with love for this child. The rest of the underside

This is the corrupted and depraved [style] used by modern idiots, ignorant of the true situation of the places and parts of a building; for the wise and expert master compares it to a well-proportioned and properly clothed human body. The remainder of the enclosure on both sides showed in appearance that it had been an excellent edifice; this could be easily understood by certain works that remained whole in several places, even the lower parts, such as the **naturalistic columns** <term>Telamones<gloss>Architectural supports sculpted in the form of men, similar to female Caryatids</gloss></term> figured in the form of hunched men, sustaining the heaviest load. The measure of these could not be known, for they were made as required by the proportion sufficient for the weight, the ornament, and the reason comprised and drawn from the human likeness; because just as a man sustaining a heavy burden holds his feet bent under his legs, in this manner the naturalistic columns applied under the greatest weights were shortened. But the **Corinthian** and **Ionic** columns, which are slender, were placed there for decoration and beauty; wherefore the composition of this building was accomplished with all the required perfections, as much in the diversity of marbles of different colors—such as white, black, porphyry, serpentine, and alabaster, diversified with mixed and confused veins—as in several laudable ornaments.

I saw there (certainly) a form of **pulvinated bases** <term>Pulvinated<gloss>A term describing a convex, pillow-like swelling in an architectural element</gloss></term>, which upon the **plinth** or elevation had two **tori** and **scotiae** <note>original: "contrebofelz & trochiles, ou naffelles," referring to the rounded and hollow moldings of a column base</note>, separated by the interposition of two fillets to distinguish the moldings. Similarly, many shrubs grew between the cracks of the stones, such as **Houseleek**, **Erogene**, **Pellitory**, **Celandine**, **Chickweed** or **mouse-ear**, **Polypody**, **Maidenhair fern** (or Venus’s hair), and **Ceterach** <note>A type of fern often called Rustyback</note> rusted on one side, along with the great **Moonwort**, and others always living, loving and haunting the old walls; together with **Golden Maidenhair**, the green **Wild Olive**, and **Capers** inhabiting the rocks and ruins, by which almost all the marbles and works were covered and reclothed. There was such a great number of columns overturned one upon the other that they seemed like great heaps of trees fallen inside a thick forest. And likewise a great quantity of statues and figures in all forms, naked and clothed, some planted on the right foot, others on the left, having their heads...

...plumb with the center of the heel, one foot planted and the other raised, the length of which was the sixth part of the total body height, proportioned at four cubits <note>A cubit is an ancient unit of length, based on the distance from the elbow to the tip of the middle finger, approximately 18–20 inches.</note>. Several statues stood entire upon their platform; others sat in chairs and seats of honor in various manners, with innumerable trophies, spoils, and infinite ornaments: horse and ox heads, from whose horns hung bundles of greenery with festoons of fruit and foliage, slender and thin at the ends but thickening toward the middle, with small children <note>Often referred to in art as "putti," these are chubby male infants, common in Renaissance decoration.</note> mounted atop them and playing nearby. The whole was so ingeniously perfect that one could rightly judge and know that the spirit and industry of the Architect were most excellent; for, to the pleasure and contentment of the beholders, he had so properly expressed the concept and intention of his imagination—both in the proportion and measurements of the building and in the perfection of the art of sculpture—that if the material had been not marble, but soft wax or clay, it could not have been better guided or crafted. 

This is the true art that discovers and exposes our presumptuous ignorance, or our detestable presumption, which is a public and harmful error. It is the clear light that sweetly ravishes us in its contemplation to illuminate our darkness; for none remain blind with their eyes open, except those who flee and refuse it. It is this art which accuses that cursed avarice that destroys all virtue, even gnawing incessantly at the heart of the one it possesses and holds captive, because it is entirely contrary to noble spirits and a mortal enemy of noble and worthy Architecture, even though in this present age everyone holds it [avarice] as their idol, offering it honors and sacrifices—a thing unworthy, evil, and greatly pernicious. 

O dangerous and mortal poison, you make miserable the one afflicted by you. How many magnificent works have perished and been suppressed by you? In this manner, I was ravished and seized by a sovereign pleasure, contemplating the relics of holy, venerable antiquity, so much to be esteemed, that I found myself uncertain, inconstant, and insatiable, looking here and there, accompanied by a continual affection and admiration, thinking within myself what the significance of these narratives <note>original: "histoires," referring to the scenes depicted in the sculptures</note> might be, which I found quite obscure, considering the whole attentively. And I could not satisfy my desire to look at them—a desire that was distracted and secluded from all other human thought, except for Lady Polia, who frequently returned to my memory; but that passed in a moment, and so I suddenly returned to my undertaking, persevering in the contemplation of this building, so perfect and well-ordered.

# How Poliphile entered a short way into the gate described above,
*looking at its beautiful ornaments: then, wanting to turn back, he saw a great Dragon that wished to devour him, for fear of which he began to flee through hollow and subterranean ways: so that finally he found another exit, and arrived at a very pleasant and delightful place.*

It would be a very great and praiseworthy thing to be able to easily declare the unparalleled work and singular composition of this so exquisite building, along with the grandeur of the edifice and the excellence of the gate, full of every wonder: for the pleasure I took in looking at it exceeded my astonishment. Without any doubt, I truly thought in my heart that no workmanship is strange or difficult for the gods; and I almost suspected that such an incomprehensible work could not have been composed by human hands, nor such concepts so well expressed, nor such a magnificent novelty invented by any mortal understanding—and yet, at the same time, so perfectly finished. For I have no doubt that if the natural historian <note>A reference to Pliny the Elder (23–79 AD), whose *Naturalis Historia* was the primary source for Renaissance knowledge of ancient art and wonders.</note> could have seen it, he would have made little account of Egypt or its workmen. Those craftsmen, though separated from one another and assigned to different places—each having taken a limb to carve according to the measurement given to them—found when they later brought their finished pieces together that they all fitted the composition of a great colossus as perfectly as if they had been carved by a single workman. 

He would also have held in low esteem the great industry of Satyros the Architect <note>One of the architects of the Mausoleum at Halicarnassus, one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World.</note>, together with the work of the great Memnon, who fashioned three figures of Jupiter from a single massive stone, one of which, being seated, had a sole of the foot seven cubits <note>Approximately 10.5 to 11.5 feet long.</note> long. Likewise, he would have made little case of the marvelous figure of Queen Semiramis <note>A legendary Queen of Babylon.</note>, composed at Mount Bagistan <note>Now known as Behistun in modern-day Iran; the "figure" refers to the massive rock reliefs there.</note>, spanning seventeen stadia <note>An ancient Greek unit of distance; seventeen stadia would be roughly two miles, a vast exaggeration typical of ancient traveler's tales.</note>. For the pyramids of Egypt, the theaters, amphitheaters, baths, temples, aqueducts, and colossi so renowned—neither the great figure of Apollo transported to Rome by Lucullus, nor the Jupiter dedicated to Claudius Caesar, nor even that of Lysippos at Tarentum, nor the masterpiece of Chares of Lindos <note>Original: "Cares Lydien." Chares was the sculptor of the Colossus of Rhodes.</note> at Rhodes, nor that of Xenodorus made both in Gaul and in Rome; nor likewise the Colossus of Serapis, being nine cubits long and made entirely of emerald stone; nor the Labyrinth of Egypt, nor the image of the brave Hercules at Tyre <note>Original: "Sur."</note>—were almost nothing in comparison to this beautiful work. Therefore, he would easily have passed those over in silence and employed his style and great eloquence to describe and highly praise this single work, which exceeds them beyond comparison,

...beyond all others that were ever made. I could not (in truth) satisfy my eyes with seeing such marvelous things, and I said to myself: "If the fragments of holy antiquity, if the ruins and broken pieces, indeed almost the very dust of it, give me such great contentment and admiration, what would it be if they were whole?" Then I thought again without delay: perhaps inside these deep and hollow places lies the altar of sacrifices and the holy flames of the goddess Venus, or her statue and Aphrodite <note>The author often uses multiple names for the same deity to evoke a sense of ancient mystery.</note>, together with Cupid her son. 

While in this thought, I set my right foot upon the threshold of the door, and suddenly a white mouse crossed my path; nonetheless, I passed onward without thinking further on it, and found that the inside was no less rich than the outside. For the side walls were of white marble, and right in the middle of them, on each side, was set a large circle of jet <term>Jet (jayet): A dense, black, polished gemstone formed from fossilized wood.</term>, surrounded by a triumphal wreath made of green jasper. This circle was so black and so polished that one could see oneself in it as in a crystalline mirror. I would have passed by without noticing, but when I was between the two, I saw my reflection on either side, which made me somewhat frightened, thinking they were two men. 

Beneath these circles, along the side walls, were marble seats two feet high, upon a pavement of mother-of-pearl <term>Mother-of-pearl (nacre): The iridescent inner lining of shells, prized for its lustrous glow.</term>, clean and without any stain; and likewise the vault <note>The arched ceiling of the entry passage.</note>, in which one could not see a single spiderweb, because a fresh wind always blew through it. The vault was joined to the side walls by a belt <note>A decorative molding or cornice running along the top of the wall.</note> that began at the capitals of the pilasters <term>Pilaster (arrierecorps): A rectangular column that projects slightly from a wall.</term> of the door, continuing to the end of the entrance, containing in length (as I could judge by the rules of perspective) twelve paces, or thereabouts. 

In this belt were carved in half-relief several small sea monsters, swimming in the water, fashioned in the form of men from the navel upward, while the rest ended in twisted fish tails, upon which sat naked women of the same nature and figure, embracing the monsters and likewise being embraced by them. Some blew into trumpets made of snail shells <term>Buccines: Ancient spiral-shaped trumpets or conches used by sea deities.</term>; others held strange and wonderfully fantastic instruments. Many were crowned with the flower and herb of the nymph-leaf <term>Nymphée: The water lily (Nymphaea).</term>—called by the French "white or yellow water-flower," and by the Arabs "Nenufar" <note>original: "Nenufar"</note>—seated in chariots made of great sea-shells, drawn by dolphins. Some were loaded with baskets full of fruit; others carried horns of plenty. You would have seen some fighting one another with handfuls of reeds and rushes, others girded with thistles and mounted on sea-horses, making shields from tortoise shells, all different in action and form, even making such vividly expressed efforts that they seemed almost to move. 

The vault was divided into two squares, separated by a frieze two feet wide, which served as a border running all around, passing along the belt and following the arch of the vault, constructed entirely of mosaic <term>Mosaic (musaique): Decorative patterns made of many small pieces of colored glass or stone.</term> made of small squares of colored glass, so neatly that it seemed to have been made that very hour. It was a foliage of greenery as vivid as emerald, the underside of which (where it happened to fold back) was of a crimson color like ruby, and the flowers were azure blue...

...set with stones like sapphires, so appropriately scattered through the work that you would have said they were born there. In one of the square panels was depicted the beautiful **Europa** crossing the sea upon the false bull <note>In Greek mythology, Zeus transformed himself into a bull to carry off the princess Europa.</note>, and King **Agenor** her father, commanding his sons, **Cadmus**, **Phoenix**, and **Cilix**, to go and seek their sister. It showed how, in their search, they courageously slew the scaly dragon they found near the fountain; then, by the counsel of **Apollo**, they built a city where the ox stopped, and gave to that region the name **Boeotia**, after the lowing of the oxen <note>original: "du blugement des bœufs"; the name Boeotia was traditionally thought to derive from the Greek "bous" for ox.</note>. Afterward, it showed how Cadmus founded Athens <note>While the text says Athens, in traditional mythology, Cadmus is the founder of Thebes.</note>, Phoenix founded Phoenicia, and Cilix founded Cilicia. In the other square was carved the unbridled **Pasiphae**, enclosed within the counterfeit cow with the bull mounted upon her; then the great monster **Minotaur**, shut inside the Labyrinth; and the ingenious **Daedalus**, who fled the prison and flew through the air by means of the wings he had fashioned for himself and his son **Icarus**. The boy, for refusing to heed his father’s advice, fell headlong and was drowned in the sea, to which in dying he left his name. It also showed how the father, having reached safety, hung up his wings in the temple of Apollo and devoutly fulfilled his vow.

These histories were so complete that not a single tile was missing or displaced, so firm was the cement with which they were assembled.

I went step by step, contemplating the excellence of the work and the great knowledge of the craftsman, who had so perfectly observed all the rules of portrayal, painting, sculpture, and **perspective**. For he had drawn the lines of the masonry to the point of their object <note>A reference to the "vanishing point," a relatively new concept in art at the time this was written.</note>, so much so that in some places they vanished from sight. In this way, he gradually reduced imperfect things to their true perfection; and conversely, he made distant things appear close and nearby things appear far away, with a pleasing arrangement of landscapes composed of plains, mountains, valleys, rustic houses, groves, little streams, and fountains, enriched with livestock and small figures <term>Small figures (mannequins): In Renaissance art, these were tiny human or animal figures added to a landscape to provide scale and life.</term>, darkening the colors according to the distances and the appropriate light.

Furthermore, he had fashioned the drapery of the garments so close to nature that one could almost have grasped them. Indeed, in every part he had so closely followed nature that if one had not looked carefully, one would have judged it real and not a fiction. This left me so ravished with wonder and transported by amazement that I could hardly believe I was present there, but felt entirely outside of myself.

Walking thus one step after another, I reached the end of the entrance where the painting finished. Further on it was so dark that I did not dare enter; therefore, I resolved to turn back.

Hardly had I turned my face when I felt, through these ruins, something like a rattling of bones or a clashing of heavy branches, which frightened me greatly.

Soon after, I heard more clearly what sounded like the dragging of some large dead beast, such as an ox or a horse, and this noise continually approached the door.

Then, before long, I heard the **hissing of a serpent**. At that, I lost both heart and voice; my very hair stood up on my head, and I considered myself as good as dead and destroyed.

O poor, miserable, and unfortunate man! Truly, I suddenly saw coming from the light of the doorway—not a limping, complaining lion like the one that met Androcles <note>original: "Androdus"; refers to the classical story of the slave Androcles who aided a lion in a cave.</note>—but a marvelous and horrible dragon. Its mouth was agape and its jaws were clattering, armed with sharp teeth set like those of a saw; it was covered in a thick hide with hard scales, gliding across the pavement, beating its back with its wings, and dragging a great long tail that it went coiling along. Alas, wretched and desolate as I was! It was enough to terrify the great god **Mars**, to make the valiant **Hercules** tremble, and to frighten the giant **Typhon** <note>original: "Typhoeus"; in Greek mythology, the deadliest monster, son of Gaia and Tartarus.</note>, of whom even the gods were horrified. It was enough to stun the proudest heart—even the most stubborn, robust, and steadfast courage of iron ever seen in this world—let alone a young man of weak and frail constitution <note>original: "complexion"; in Renaissance medicine, this refers to the physical and mental state determined by the four humors.</note>, already terrified to find himself in wild and strange places without anyone's aid or help.

### POLIPHILE.

Seeing then that the poisonous and detestable smoke that this **Dragon** spewed out extended nearly to me, I cast myself haphazardly into these thick shadows, considering my life as lost, piteously calling upon the immortal Gods, and fleeing by winding paths where I entirely lost the light. I was so disoriented that I could not tell if I were inside the **Labyrinth of Daedalus** <note>In Greek mythology, an elaborate maze built for King Minos of Crete to house the Minotaur.</note> the ingenious: there were so many twisting roads, paths, alleys, crossroads, doors, and passages, all designed to make one fail and forget the way out, only to return always to the first error and go astray in even deeper obscurity.

I truly feared I had arrived in the hollow rock of **Polyphemus** <note>The one-eyed giant (Cyclops) who imprisoned Odysseus and his men in a cave.</note> the cruel Cyclops, or in the cavern of the malicious thief **Cacus** <note>A fire-breathing giant from Roman mythology who lived in a cave on the Aventine Hill and was killed by Hercules.</note>. Therefore, I immediately threw my arms before my eyes for fear of hitting the pillars that supported the pyramid. I went along groping, turning back many times to look behind me and see if I could still find the place where I had entered, or even if the devouring Dragon was coming after me. But I found that the light had failed me entirely. And to increase my great fear, these dark caves were full of **bats**, which flitted about my ears. Already terrified, I thought that everything I heard, felt, or touched was the cruel Dragon. Although my eyes eventually became somewhat accustomed to these shadows, I still could not see anything; therefore, my arms had to perform the office of my eyes, just like the **snail**, which goes along testing the path with its horns, and if it finds an obstacle, suddenly pulls them back into itself.

In such a manner, I went groping through these blind detours and astray paths, in greater labor and perplexity than **Mercury** when he turned himself into a stork; indeed, even more than the God **Apollo** when he was constrained to guard the sheep in Thrace; or than the beautiful **Diana** when she was changed into a little bird; even in more extreme anguish than **Psyche** after having lost **Cupid** her husband; and in more laborious peril than **Lucius Apuleius** when he was transformed into an **Ass**, and heard the counsel and deliberation of the thieves regarding the imminent act of his death <note>A reference to the 2nd-century Roman novel *The Golden Ass* by Apuleius, where the protagonist is turned into a donkey and overheard his captors' plans.</note>. My fear was more than doubled by the wild flitting and beating of the air by these bats: for when I heard them whistling so close to me, I already thought I was between the teeth of the Dragon.

And although this fright was excessive and almost extreme, it was yet more intense when it returned to my memory that I had seen the **Wolf** <note>Seeing a wolf was often considered a bad omen in classical and Renaissance lore, sometimes thought to strike a person dumb if the wolf saw them first.</note>, which made me presume it was a very bad omen, indeed a manifest sign of my sad and painful end. Therefore, I ran here and there, my ears open and my eyes closed, reduced to such necessity that death was much dearer and more desired by me than life. Nevertheless, I felt a marvelous regret at dying without having obtained the long-desired fulfillment of my love. Alas, if only I had seen my lady **Polia**! Truly, no death would then be grievous or troublesome to me. Shall I then lose, through a single misfortune, two things so very precious: my life and my beloved? Then I muttered between my teeth: "If I die thus in strange misery, who will be the worthy successor of a jewel so worthy and so exquisite? Who will deserve to inherit such a great good? Who will possess this treasure so rich? What serene and purified sky..."

...will I ever acquire and recover this light so very bright? O wretched **Poliphile**, where do you think you are fleeing? You are going to lose yourself. There is no more hope for you. Never (alas) will you see her again. Here is the end of your pleasures, as well as your amorous thoughts. Alas, what misfortune, or what malignant Star has plunged you into such mortal languor: and destined you to serve as fodder for a beast as hideous as this **Dragon**, in whose belly you must be buried? Alas, at least let me be swallowed whole, and in this state go to rot within its poisonous entrails. Oh miserable end, Oh lamentable death. Where are the eyes so dried up and deprived of natural moisture that they should not distill and melt into tears? But here it is, I feel it at my shoulders. Who ever saw a greater cruelty of fortune? Here is spiteful death, and the final hour of that cursed moment when this poor human flesh will be meat for a serpent. What calamity is more strange and rigorous than to live after one's death and remain without burial? O how much more grievous is the misfortune of abandoning one's lady, so loyal! Farewell, farewell then, **Polia**, my heartfelt and singular friend.

Thus I lamented to myself, so weary and altogether troubled that I had nothing left but my spirit wandering through these shadows; with which I took as my last refuge the invocation of the all-powerful Gods of heaven and my good Angel, with a pure and affectionate conscience, believing they would have pity on this sinister accident of mine. Then, while I was in this perplexity, I perceived from afar a small light: so there is no need to ask if I ran toward it with great joy; but for certain, it was short-lived: for when I arrived near, I saw that it was an ever-burning lamp hanging before an altar which (as far as I could understand) was five feet high and twice as wide; and upon it were placed three golden statues. Then I found myself frustrated in my intent <note>Poliphile had hoped the light was an exit, but found only a subterranean shrine.</note> and overtaken by a devout horror <note>In this period, "horreur" often signified a profound, religious awe or a shivering sensation in the presence of the divine.</note>. 

This light was hardly clear, but rather all troubled because of the thick air. Nevertheless, I could somewhat see the arrangement of these subterranean places—namely, the great openings, the dark and deep pathways, with vaults supported by thick pillars of four, six, and eight sides <note>These are polygonal columns: square, hexagonal, and octagonal.</note>, which could not be clearly discerned owing to the weakness of the light; nonetheless, they seemed well-made in suitable proportion to sustain the excessive weight of the great and marvelous pyramid that was above. For this reason, after having said a brief prayer before this altar, I set out again to seek the exit; and I had not traveled far when there appeared to me another small, shining splendor through a narrow hole, almost like the neck of a funnel. Oh, how I celebrated it, and with what a heart I followed it!

I had not (certainly) perceived it before I renounced all those desires for death to which I had previously yielded; and I began my amorous thoughts once more, persuading myself with a feigned and flattering hope that I might yet in time easily acquire what I had lately held for lost. When I had then reached this light, which from afar had seemed so small, I found that it was a large opening through which I exited in great haste, and I began to run without looking back at where I had come from. Then my arms, which had served me as a shield <note>original: "pauois" — a large shield used by medieval infantry, which Poliphile used to feel his way along the walls.</note> to avoid colliding with the pillars, served me as strong

...with strong strides <note>literally "strong oars," a metaphorical expression for the rapid movement of his legs</note> to better hasten my flight: by means of which I did so much that I reached a region beautiful and pleasant. In this place, I did not yet dare to stop, because the memory of that **Dragon** was so strongly imprinted in my mind that it seemed to me I could still feel it at my heels. But the great beauty of the location stimulated me to walk further on, in the hope of finding people and a dwelling where I might rest in safety, and without fearing anything. And in this I was comforted by the vision of the **white mouse**, which I held to be a good omen.

And nonetheless, I had some doubt about arriving in a place where my coming might be poorly received and judged as too great an audacity or a rash presumption, such that some harm might come to me, just as it had already occurred when I entered the beautiful gate. On one hand, I was in great fear, and on the other, I felt regret for having lost sight of such noble and sumptuous buildings, which I had not sufficiently contemplated to my liking. At times, the fancy also came to me that it was all a dream or an illusion. Then I would say: "This is no dream; I am not sleeping. I have seen it and touched it. My memory of it is quite fresh. It is a true and very certain thing. I am mindful and remember it all, and I could recount it specifically, part by part, if there were any need. That beast was neither false nor simulated, but full of natural life." 

And saying this, the hair stood up on my head from having recalled the **Dragon**, and I began to flee again as before. Soon after, I reassured myself, saying: "In a place so beautiful and so delectable, none could dwell but people of good character; and perhaps it is the home of some **divine spirits** and **demigods**, or perhaps they act as its protectors; or it may be the retreat of **Nymphs** and **country goddesses** <note>original: "Deesses champestres"</note>." Therefore, I resolved to follow my path, whatever might happen to me.

Finally, after I had escaped from those dark caverns, which truly resembled a chamber of hell (for my life had been in great danger there, even though it was the most holy **Aphrodisium** <note>original: "Aphrodife"; this refers to the sacred realm or festival of Aphrodite, the goddess of love</note>), and after I had arrived in that graceful country, I turned my head to see from where I had come out. I looked upon a mountain that was not very steep, but moderately sloping in its descent, covered with beautiful green trees, such as Oaks, Maples, Lindens, Ashes, and others like them. Along the plain, it was bordered with Medlars, Hazels, Service trees, and Whitebeams, entwined with Honeysuckle, Privet, Hops, and Bryony. And beneath these grew Polypody, Hart’s-tongue fern, the two Hellebores, Clover, Plantain, Bugle, Sanicle, and many other herbs that thrive in the shade. The opening through which I had emerged was a little high up, and the mountain was all covered in brambles and bushes; and from what I could conjecture, it was opposite the beautiful gate through which I had entered. Therefore, it is to be believed that similarly on this side there used to be an entrance like the other, and that time and old age had reduced it to a heap of ruins, and converted it into a large mound entirely stripped of recognition. For among the stones, several shrubs had risen, so that with great difficulty had I been able to pick out with my eye the hole through which I had issued. And I think that one could not have re-entered it because of the branches, trunks, and roots that occupied it; nor (what is more) find it without difficulty. At least for my part, I do not believe I could have returned there, so secluded and wild was the place.

In one of the faces of the structure, there was a stone of white marble, polished as well as possible, having a height of a square and a half: the width of which (as I was able to estimate) was six feet in measure. At the two sides of this stone, there were two fluted columns with **rudentures** <term>rudentures: also known as "cabling," these are decorative convex moldings that fill the lower parts of the fluting in a column</term> or beadings, furnished with their bases and capitals, and above them the architrave, frieze, and cornice, upon which sat the frontispiece, having a height of the fourth part of the square. Between the two columns within the square was carved a beautiful **sleeping Nymph**, stretched out upon a cloth, part of which seemed bunched up beneath her head, as if it had served her as a pillow. Her other arm was extended along her left hip, down to the middle of the thigh. In front of the fountain, upon a rich pavement between the two basins, there was a small channel in which these two waters joined together, exiting the basins opposite one another: and thus mixed, they made a small stream of temperate warmth, suitable for bringing forth all greenery. The hot water leapt so very high that it could not hinder those who put their mouths to the right breast to suckle from it and drink the cold water. This soil is more blessed and grand than Mount Taurus on its northern slope, though it is said that the grapes it produces there are two cubits <note>A cubit is an ancient unit of measurement, roughly 18 inches; the author uses this to suggest a land of supernatural abundance.</note> long, and that a single fig tree there bears seventy measures <term>muys</term> <note>A "muy" (from the Latin modius) was a large dry measure for grain or fruit; here it emphasizes the miraculous productivity of the flora.</note> of fruit each year. It was an octagonal space—that is to say, having eight angles or sides—on the outside of which were two pillars set upon a single pedestal, which began at the level of the pavement and surrounded the entire enclosure. These pillars emerged from the wall by a third of their width and were enriched with beautiful capitals, above which ran the architrave, frieze, and cornice <note>These are the three horizontal parts of a classical entablature: the beam (architrave), the decorative band (frieze), and the projecting top molding (cornice).</note>. In the frieze were carved little naked children holding belts or cords from which hung beautiful festoons, otherwise known as bunches of greenery. Upon the cornice was placed the *retube* <note>The author likely means a "rotunda" or a vaulted dome.</note>, which is a round vault like an oven-base but made in an octagonal shape to correspond to the rest of the building. Its faces were pierced through with foliage of various designs; the openings were closed with glass or else thin sheets of fine crystal, which from afar had seemed to me to be lead. The pavement at the bottom beneath the water was of <term>mosaic</term> assembled from tiny fine stones, which depicted all sorts and manners of fish. The water was moderately warm, not by artificial heat, but solely by nature; and what is more, it was so neat and clear that, looking into it, you would have judged these fish to be moving and rubbing against the seats where they were portrayed to the life: namely, carp, pike, eels, tench, lampreys, shad, perch, turbot, sole, rays, trout, salmon, mullet, plaice, crayfish, and infinite others, which seemed to stir with the movement of the water, so closely did the work approach nature.

And they, who took good notice of my foolish manners and too-simple countenance, smiled with great pleasure, finding their amusement in me. At this, I was the most content man in the world, as one who desired to please them in every way and everywhere, to win their favor.

Thus I endured this burning passion with marvelous patience, and my suffering was accompanied by a modest shame, knowing that I was unworthy to be in such divine company. Although I frequently refused and made excuses, I was constrained by them to enter into the bath, like a **Jackdaw** <note>original: "Corneille"; a reference to the fable of the bird that tries to pass itself off as a more beautiful species.</note> among the **Doves**. Therefore, I kept myself apart, full of shame, my eyes shifting and restless, not daring to look upon such excellent and singular objects. Then **Osphrasie** <note>Her name is derived from the Greek word for "Sense of Smell."</note> said to me: "My friend, what is your name?" And I answered her with all reverence that I was called **Poliphile**. "It pleases me well," she said, "if the effect matches the name. But what is your lady-love's name?" "**Polia**, my lady," I said then; to which she promptly replied: "Certainly, I thought your name meant *greatly loved* <note>original: "fort aymé"; a play on the Greek *Poly-philos*.</note>, but from what I can understand, it means *the lover of Polia*. By your faith, if she were here, what service would you do for her?" "That, my lady," I responded, "which belongs to her modest chastity, and which would be suitable and worthy to be done in your divine presences." Then she said to me: "Tell me more, I pray you, Poliphile: do you bear her great affection?" "Alas, my lady," I replied, "yes, more than my own life," and sighing, I added, "Truly, more than all the delights, riches, and precious treasures of the world." "Where then have you left," she asked, "a thing so dear and so beloved?" "I truly do not know," I answered, "not even in what place I am now." Then she said, smiling: "What would you give to the person who could make you find her again? Do not worry; be of good cheer and rejoice in your heart, for you shall find her very soon." In such and similar talk, the beautiful Nymphs bathed, and I with them. 

But to continue my discourse: just opposite the beautiful fountain on the outside where the sleeping Nymph and the Satyr (previously described) were located, there was another inside the bath. Its figure was of gilded copper, set upon white marble, recessed in a square and flanked by two columns in half-relief; above was an architrave, frieze, cornice, and frontispiece, carved and cut from the mass of the same stone. In this fountain were two Nymphs, somewhat smaller than life-size, dressed in fluttering garments that were open along the thighs, with sleeves tucked up to the shoulders and arms bare (which was a fine sight to see), supporting a small child who had his two feet placed upon their hands—that is, the right foot on the left hand of one, and the left foot on the right hand of the other. The faces of all three seemed to be laughing in earnest. These Nymphs lifted with their other two hands the clothing of this child, uncovering him to the waist above the navel. He held his little **spout** <term>quynette</term> <note>A playful, diminutive term for the penis of the statue, serving as a water pipe.</note> in both hands and urinated water as cold as ice, which mixed with the hot water to temper it and make it lukewarm. 

I found myself, certainly, in great contentment of spirit; but the principal part of my pleasure was troubled by seeing myself so base and different from the beauty of these Nymphs—**black as an Ethiopian** <note>A common Renaissance literary trope used to emphasize a contrast with idealized, pale skin.</note> amidst such excessive whiteness. At this, **Acoé** <note>Her name is derived from the Greek word for "Hearing."</note>, smiling, said to me with good grace: "Poliphile, take this crystal vessel and bring me a little fresh water." Hearing this, I, who desired nothing but to gratify and please them, and even to make myself a slave and subject to do them some service, ran there without thinking any ill of it. But I had no sooner set foot upon a step to approach the falling water than this little child lifted his **spout** and urinated straight into the middle of my face,

### BOOK ONE OF THE STRATEGY OF LOVE ###

...and they gave me a box. This ointment seemed very beneficial as I came out of the bath, because besides its pleasant scent, my limbs—weakened and debilitated by the hardship I had suffered—were suddenly refreshed. I dressed myself as diligently as I could, but the young ladies remained a long time grooming and adorning themselves. Then they opened their <term>comfit-boxes</term> <note>original: "drageoers"; decorative containers for sweets or spiced seeds used as a digestive or treat.</note> full of perfect preserves, from which we took refreshment, and we drank a delicious beverage of excellent quality. When the snack was finished, they returned to their mirrors and carefully checked their head-dress to see if everything was as it should be. This done, they covered their hair with delicate <term>crepes</term> <note>original: "crespes deliez"; thin, gauzy veils often made of silk or fine linen.</note>, saying: "Let us go quickly, Poliphile, toward Queen Eleutherilide <note>Her name is derived from the Greek *Eleutheria*, meaning "Liberty" or "Freedom." In the allegory, she represents Free Will.</note>, our sovereign princess. You will have more pastime and joy in her company than you have had in this place." 

Then, jesting with me, they said: "Even so, you did get water in your face!" and then they renewed their laughter, sporting with such joyful words, signaling to one another with the corners of their eyes while looking at me sideways, for I was walking in the middle of the troop. Afterward, they began to sing sweetly of a *Metamorphosis*—the transformation of a lover who thought to turn himself into a bird by means of an ointment, but for lack of the right box, he was transformed into a Donkey <note>This is a direct reference to Lucius in Apuleius's *The Golden Ass*, a foundational text for Renaissance literature.</note>. Their conclusion was that some think ointments are for one effect, while they are directly intended for another. 

This gave me a suspicion that they were speaking covertly about me; I was also made to doubt by their countenances and the smiles they cast upon my person at every moment. But at that time I thought no more of it, estimating and believing for truth that the ointment they had given me was for the great benefit of my limbs, which were weary and worn out from pain. But suddenly, I felt myself entirely moved by a lustful heat, so vehement that I could not contain myself. At this, these affected nymphs laughed among themselves with pleasure, knowing my "malady" well enough. It increased to such an extent that I do not know what restrained my disordered appetite from throwing myself among them, like a <term>goshawk</term> <note>original: "Autour"; a bird of prey known for its sudden, forceful strike.</note> into a covey of partridges. And my desire was reinforced all the more because such convenient, even urgent and opportune objects offered themselves to me to give allegiance to my pain. 

Then a "firebrand" of the group, who was called Alphaé <note>Alphaé represents the sense of Touch (from the Greek *Haphé*).</note>, said to me, mocking me: "Poliphile, what is the matter with you? You were jesting just a moment ago, and now I see you completely changed." To which I made this response: "I pray you, forgive me, my lady: for I am twisting like a wicker branch, and am almost a lost man, due to an immoderate burning." At this word, they began to laugh even louder than before, and said to me: "If your Polia, whom you desire so much, were here with us, what would you do to her at this hour?" 

"Alas," I replied, "my ladies, by that divine majesty whom you serve and obey, do not throw oil on my great fire, nor blow upon the flame that burns my heart: for I am totally consumed." At this sorrowful response, they made such a great hue and cry that it was impossible for them to go further; instead, they fell upon the grass as if in a trance or fainting from laughter. Then, through a confidence that had already become private and familiar, I took it upon myself to say to them: "O wicked women, enchantresses who have bewitched me, do you treat me in this fashion? I have a very good reason now to run at you and use force!" Then I made a pretense of grabbing them, as if I had the boldness to execute what in no way...

Immediately after, that lascivious heat was extinguished, so much so that I returned to my former calm disposition. 

Then I walked with them until we arrived at a palace of marvelous sumptuosity. To give a description of it: first, we passed through a beautiful, straight, and wide road, bordered on both sides by tall Cypresses, planted in a line at equal distances, thick and dense with branches and leaves, as much as they could be according to their nature. All the ground outside the path on either side was covered with sky-blue Periwinkle, at least in its beautiful little flowers. This way was about five hundred of my paces in length; and at the end, it finished at the entrance of a beautiful hedge, made with three sides in the form of a wall, having as much height as the Cypresses which served as columns. But it was interspersed with Orange and Lemon trees planted close together and very dense, industriously bent and interlaced with one another. The hedge, as far as I could conceive, was six good feet in width. In the middle of the first side was a large portal where the path led, made in an arch from the very trees thus flexed and bent for the purpose. Above this, in other suitable places, were made windows of the same material, in which no sign of wood, branch, or trunk could be seen from the outside, but only the natural greenery of the leaves enriched with their white flowers, giving off a scent so sweet that one could not have wished for better. Similarly, beautiful fruit hung there—namely, Oranges and Lemons, some ripe, others green, some beginning to form, and others half-formed, and even others ready to be picked. Inside the thickness of this hedge, the branches and trunks were so neatly tightened that one could easily walk on top of them to go to the windows or to stroll around; and the leaves were so very thick that passers-by could not have seen through. Through this portal, we entered the hedge, which was singularly pleasant and delightful to the eye, but more marvelous to the mind: for it served as an enclosure for a rich square palace, which made the fourth side of the courtyard along with these three sides of greenery. Each of the sides of its wall was sixty paces in length. The court was surrounded by this...

### THE DREAM OF POLIPHILUS

...hedge, and in the middle of it a beautiful fountain of water as clear as crystal, which shot upward almost as high as the enclosure, and fell into a large basin of fine Amethyst <note>A purple variety of quartz, prized in antiquity for its beauty and supposed "sobering" properties.</note>, measuring three paces in width across its entire diameter. Its thickness was three inches, tapering little by little toward the rim, which was only an inch thick; and all around the outside of it were carved small sea monsters in half-relief <note>original: "demyboſse"; a sculptural term where the figures emerge halfway from the background.</note> or low relief. It rested upon a pillar of Jasper <note>An opaque, impure variety of silica, usually red, yellow, or brown, symbolizing endurance.</note> of diverse colors, mixed with Chalcedony <note>A translucent variety of quartz with a waxy luster, here described as having a sea-water tint.</note>, diaphanous or transparent, of the color of sea-water, made in the shape of two beautiful vases with narrow necks and wide bellies, placed one upon the other, base against base, and between the two a rounded knob set upon a plinth of Ophite stone <note>A green mottled stone, its name derived from the Greek *ophis* for snake.</note>, perfectly round, and raised about five inches high, enclosed by another basin of Porphyry <note>A hard igneous rock containing crystals, usually purple-red, historically associated with imperial power.</note>, made in the fashion of a tub, rising to a height of three feet. Around the pillar were four Harpies <note>Mythological winged creatures with the faces of women and bodies of birds.</note> of fine gold, having their claws extended upon the Ophite plinth, their backs turned to this pillar, and opposite to one another. The tips of their wings extended up beneath the Amethyst basin, as if to hold it in the air. Their faces resembled maidens, but their tails were of serpents, twisted and ending in antique foliage, which gathered at the very top of the pillar directly under the bottom of this basin, so that they served as a superb and magnificent ornament. In the very center of the large basin, and directly above the pillar, emerged a vase somewhat elongated, intentionally turned upside down on its mouth, and decorated with beautiful foliage made of the same stone as the basin, as prominent on the outside as the basin was deep; and it supported a round base, upon which were placed the three Charites <note>original: "Charites"; the Greek name for the Graces, daughters of Zeus, representing charm, beauty, and creativity.</note> or Graces, naked and life-sized, made of fine gold, joined back to back, spouting water from their breasts like delicate little threads, which looked like rods of fine silver. Each of them held a cornucopia <note>original: "corne d'abondãce"; a "horn of plenty," a symbol of abundance and nourishment.</note>, which all merged into one just above their heads. From among the fruits and leaves emerging from the horns, the water came out through six small pipes, and jetted upward to the height of the hedge or wall of greenery. The craftsman, to preserve modesty, had ensured that each of the three ladies held her left hand over the part that ought to be covered. Upon the edges of the large basin, exceeding the aforementioned Ophite plinth by one foot in width all around its circumference, were six gold Dragons, set upon their feet at equal distances, in such a way and with such skill that the water coming from the breasts of the three ladies fell directly into their heads, which were hollowed and carved out; then the water came back out through their mouths and fell between the Ophite plinth and the porphyry basin, in which there was a channel a foot and a half wide and two deep. The rest of the dragons' bodies lay upon the hollow of the basin, until their tails met and merged into antique foliage, from which the vase supporting the three ladies was made and composed, without the basin being in any way deformed or obstructed on the inside. But the reflection of the greenery from the Orange trees, the luster of the stone, and the clarity of the water caused the onlookers to see a variety of colors, such as those seen in a rainbow. From the belly of the basin on the outside, between two Dragons, emerged Lion heads, discharging through certain small pipes the water that distilled from the Cornucopias; which, after having risen very high, fell back into this basin in the places where these Lion heads were, creating a resonance that was sweet and gracious beyond measure.

The workmanship was so excellent that I do not believe the hands of men could have crafted it; for it is impossible to describe it well, and for the human mind to comprehend it. However, I can say this: that never in all our time, nor before (as far as is known), was a work seen so perfect; nothing else even comes close to its quality. The entire area around the fountain was paved with squares of marble of various colors and patterns. In the middle of each square was inlaid a roundel of jasper, each of a different color. The corners and angles of the squares outside of these circles were decorated with foliage. Between the squares and around the entire pavement were bands or borders to serve as separation, made of fine mosaic. This was a very green foliage, accompanied by many flowers—yellow, blue-grey, crimson, and violet—composed of tiny cubic stones <note>This refers to *tesserae*, the small individual tiles used to create a mosaic.</note>, so artistically joined that it looked like a flat painting. I found myself completely surprised by these things, for I was not accustomed to seeing such excellent works; I would have gladly stopped to contemplate it more at my leisure, but it was then necessary for me to follow the young ladies, my guides and companions.

The appearance and look of this Palace seemed truly to smile at people; therefore, the closer I approached it, the more I found it worthy of contemplation for the richness of the walls, the excellence of the painting, the arrangement of the columns, and the distribution of the sections, such as halls, chambers, galleries, and offices. There were the feats of the magnanimous and powerful Hercules, carved in half-relief <note>Bas-relief sculpture where the figures project from the background.</note>, and so precisely rendered that the figures seemed separated from the backdrop; they were surrounded by spoils, titles, and trophies of an unparalleled and admirable artistry. But what an entrance! What a portico! What a staircase! Certainly, I have nothing to compare it to; for everything was so singular that even the most perfect understanding would be too small and weak to give a full description of it. The spiral staircase and ascent were quite exquisite, considering that the art of Architecture had employed all its knowledge there. The arch of the vaulting of the door was lowered underneath between two moldings, with round and square panels, and inside it was sown with roses and foliage in half-relief, highlighted with gold, and the background laid with azure <note>original: "azur" — likely referring to a deep blue pigment like lapis lazuli.</note>. In front of this gate was hung a curtain woven of gold thread and silk; upon it were portrayed two beautiful images, one with all the instruments suitable for labor <note>Likely representing the Active Life or agriculture.</note>, and the other contemplating the sky <note>Representing the Contemplative Life.</note>. When we arrived before this curtain, the Nymphs took me by the hand to make me enter, saying: "Poliphilus, this is the order that must be observed, and by which one must come into the presence of the Queen, our mistress. It is not permitted or lawful for anyone to enter this first curtain unless he is received by a vigilant lady gatekeeper named <term>Cinosia</term> <note>original: "Cinosie (muable, ou mouuante)" — From the Greek *kinesis*, meaning movement or change.</note>, who heard us immediately and came to us, drawing aside the curtain, whereby we soon entered within." There was a small space there, and after it another curtain, more beautiful than the first, diversified with all sorts of colors and all manners of beasts, plants, herbs, and flowers, of sovereign tapestry. Arrived as I was at the first chamber, she looked at me as if completely astonished: and after I had greeted her, as was fitting, I was received by her with all sweetness, and likewise by her ladies. The walls were covered with the same workmanship and material: and the pavement similar to that of the courtyard outside. The matron porter of the last curtain admonished and warned me that I should be assured and constant, without fearing anything in this world, and should wish to persevere in following and putting into execution these good admonitions and wise counsel of Queen Eleutherilide their mistress: for the end of it could only be good and honorable. Such was the ornament and sculpture of the frieze, upon which stood the cornice, perfected in every excellence of workmanship. Above the last <term>cymatium: a wave-shaped architectural molding that often serves as the uppermost part of a cornice</term>, directly aligned with each pillar, there was an antique vase three feet high. These were made of various materials: some of agate, others of jasper, some of amethyst, garnet, or amber, of diverse colors and different designs. They were solid and turned on a lathe, with handles carved in the shape of serpents, lizards, and other beautiful fantasies. 

Between the spaces aligned with the triumphal wreaths <note>original: "chapeaux de triumphe"; ceremonial wreaths or crowns of victory</note> were planted square joists, set upright and pointed, standing seven feet high. They were all made of fine gold, though hollowed out for fear of too great a weight. Above these were others that crossed the entire court, resting upon other beams reaching to the opposite wall. There were seven in number, serving as main beams crossed by smaller joists and rafters, also all of gold, styled in the manner of the woodwork of a flat trellis. 

From the four vases located at the four corners, large grapevine stocks emerged, along with several other different plants, such as *bindweed* <note>original: "Voluble"</note>, *hops* <note>original: "Hobelon"</note>, *honeysuckle*, *privet*, and other similar plants, all of gold. These spread over the woodwork in many branches and boughs intertwined, embracing one another in a lattice-like pattern with beautiful and singular joints, so that they covered this entire beautiful court with a rich—or rather, priceless—work. 

For the leaves were of emeralds, the flowers of sapphires, rubies, diamonds, topazes, and other precious stones, daintily ordered and arranged according to their colors. Across this foliage, there were also grapes fashioned from amethysts and other exquisite stones, with colors matching their natural appearance. 

The expense of this building was infinite, for the entire trellis shone with a marvelous brightness, not only because of the incomparable material but also because of the matchless artifice. I could never understand by what art or invention this work had been erected, nor certainly determine if it was nailed, soldered, or set <note>original: "enchaffée"; the process of mounting a stone or metal piece into a frame or setting</note>—which are the three ways of joining used in goldsmithing. All three seemed impossible to me for a covering so large, interwoven with such diverse joints and lattices.

Being thus on both knees before such high majesty, I found myself amazed and bashful. Then the Queen questioned my companions about the manner of my arrival, and how I had entered within <note>original: "leans"; an archaic term for "inside" or "within this place"</note>. To which they recounted the whole matter to her, and let her know my name. Hearing this, she said gracefully to me: "Poliphile, be of good cheer. I thanked her for this gracious welcome with the most humble and honorable words that were then in my power; and afterward I recited to her succinctly, and point by point, how I fled the Dragon’s fury, and with what pain and difficulty I had reached that place; at which she marveled beyond measure, and likewise all the ladies. Now it happened by chance, and without thinking, that I had sat upon the circle of Mercury: and I saw, upon turning around, how his benignity, his good aspect, and influence are diminished and depraved when he finds himself in the tail of the Scorpion. the musical maidens approached, seven on each side, dressed in cloth of gold embroidered in the style of **Nymphs**: as the dishes were brought in, they changed their instruments; and while we ate, they played in such melodious chords and pleasing harmonies that they would have made the gods eager to listen. Immediately the tables and trestles were brought and set up almost without one noticing: for each maiden was wonderfully quick and skilled in performing her duty, attentive to the service, diligent and well-advised in everything she had to do.

First, before the Queen, a trestle was brought in the form of a tripod made of three gold pillars, fixed into a circle of <term>jasper</term> <note>a smooth, opaque gemstone, usually red or green, highly prized in antiquity for decorative arts</note>: the base of these pillars was formed into lion's paws spread upon the jasper, from which emerged a continuous pattern of foliage from one side to the other. A little higher than the midpoint, against each of these pillars, was the head of a small Angel between two wings, from which hung festoons or bundles of greenery, tapering at the ends, at the tops of these pillars tied with cords or tresses, the whole made of fine burnished gold. At the very top was an overhang or projection in the shape of clamps to secure the round table that was placed upon it, which was changed at every course just as the linens and the dishes were; but the tripod stand itself was never moved.

[Woodcut illustration of a decorative pedestal or stand with a cross-like top, foliage, and a bird at the base.]

Soon after, the Queen's table was brought, likewise round and made of fine gold, measuring three feet in width and a full inch in thickness: of this same form and measure were all the others where we ate, but the material was of ivory, and the trestles were of fine ebony. Upon each of these was spread a tablecloth of green <term>armozeen</term> <note>a heavy, plain-woven silk fabric used for luxury garments and furnishings</note> silk, hanging all around to within a foot of the ground, bordered with embroidery made in **arabesque** <note>an ornamental design consisting of intertwined flowing lines, originally found in Arabic decoration</note>, enriched with precious stones two inches wide, and beneath this a fringe of thread of the same silk, twisted and mixed with filaments of gold and silver: such were all the tablecloths. Then came a beautiful maiden carrying a golden basket, filled with all the fragrant flowers of springtime, which she scattered upon all the tables, except for the Queen's, where none were placed. When everything was ready, the Queen removed her royal mantle and remained in a corset of crimson velvet, decorated with small animals, both little birds and other species, along with flowers and leaves raised in embroidery neatly arranged with pearls; and over this was a somewhat saffron-colored crepe, so fine and delicate that one could easily see through it the crimson velvet, the embroidery, and the entire costume, which was (certainly) unique, rich, excellent, and imperial. The maidens brought an infinite fountain, artificially constructed in such a way that the water falling into a gold basin rose again through hidden pipes to the same place from which it had come. This revolution was achieved (at least as I conjectured) by two pipes, one more slender than the other, and a partition inside the vessel which was pierced in the middle; by which the air enclosed in this vacuum drew the water like a sponge, then by constraint and force made it rise upwards. It was first presented upon the Queen's golden table by the two girls, bowing their heads and bending their knees almost to within an inch of the ground. Similar reverence was made in the same instant by the other serving damsels, both in setting down and lifting the dishes, and consequently in all the services. The two girls were followed by three more damsels. The first held a golden ewer, the second a basin of the same, and the third a towel of white silk, exquisitely delicate and fine. The Queen washed in this fountain; and the damsel who carried the basin received the water so that it did not return to the source; but she who held the ewer replaced it with an equal amount of other scented waters, just as much as had left it; then the third held out the towel to dry the hands. The receptacle of this fountain was placed on four small wheels, by which it was rolled across all the tables to serve everyone. The middle was embossed and slightly raised, crafted with <term>gadroons</term> <note>a decorative border of repeated oval or curved shapes, common in metalwork</note> of fine grace; the border was enriched with precious stones and beautiful sculptures.

[Illustration of a decorative vessel or fountain on a wheeled carriage]

The pillar was composed of two vessels placed one atop the other, differing in fashion, joined and assembled by two handles. At the tip of the point of the lid of the last vessel, which ended in a flower, there was a large pear-shaped Diamond, its narrow end fixed in the flower, of unusual size, of a value in no way estimable, and shining with great wonder. The water, according to the judgment of my nose, was made of roses, lemon peels, ambergris, and <term>benzoin</term> <note>a sweet-smelling balsamic resin from trees in East Asia</note>, duly proportioned, yielding a most sweet odor.

In the middle of the place was set a perfume burner, exquisite not only for its rich material, which was of purified gold, but especially for its beautiful invention and the noble workmanship with which the craftsman had decorated it. It was a triangular base supported by three feet of <term>Harpies</term> <note>mythological creatures with the heads of women and the bodies of birds</note>, ending toward the top in foliage which embraced one another.
