[Woodcut illustration of three nude female figures standing on a decorative base, supporting a circular platform on their heads and hands. On the platform are several small vessels.]

Between the three Angels <note>The author often refers to these classical-style figures as "angels" or "genii"</note>, right at the center of the base, was fixed a pillar made in the style of an **antique candelabrum**, at the top of which was a cup identical to the others and of the same size, which filled the empty space that the six made in their midst. The serving maidens had placed burning coals covered with ash there, and in each cup a golden vial was boiling, full of water or some other liquor, which they (in my judgment) renewed every day. It seemed to me that these were all various waters, such as **Rose, Myrtle, Elderflower, Mint, Orange blossom**, and others similarly well-known, mixed with several fragrant substances, which exhaled a scent so sweet that the like was never felt.

The Queen was served by three very beautiful and graceful maidens, dressed in a cloth woven of gold thread and silk; however, they changed their clothing at the changing of the tablecloths, which occurred at every course. For they came in the form of **Nymphs**, dressed in cloth of the same color as the tablecloth they brought, tucked up above the waist with a pleasant fold in their attire, draped over their shoulders and drawn across the breast to reveal the beautiful valley that divided their small breasts—so round and perfectly white that the eyes of the onlookers were too sparingly satisfied, even though they gazed upon them without ceasing. Their footwear was open over the top of the foot in the shape of a crescent moon, fastened with gold buckles and straps. Their blonde and copious hair hung down to their knees, but was bound around the forehead with a garland of large, fine pearls, all of equal roundness. These three assisted before the Queen, humble in their bearing and countenance, expert in their offices, prompt and fit to serve, although they served only at one table and for one course; for when the next came, they remained standing with arms folded, and then the three newcomers served in their turn. Thus, in order, they served each setting of meat. Those who were seated at the table each had three servants: one carried the food to the mouth, another accompanied it with a plate so that nothing would fall, and the third wiped the mouth with a white and clean napkin, making a reverence each time, and afterward throwing the napkin on the floor, which was immediately lifted and gathered up by another.

When they wished to change courses, two maidens brought into the center of the space a chariot on four wheels, the front made in the fashion of a ship's prow and the back like a triumphal chariot, all of fine gold, carved with **Scyllas** <note>monstrous sea creatures from Greek mythology</note> and little sea monsters, and on all sides enriched and sown with gemstones, distributed so appropriately that they sparkled everywhere, meeting the luster of the mirror-jewels situated in various parts of the Palace, so that it seemed like sunbeams striking well-polished steel. The work was so ingenious that I could not find anything worthy enough (it seems to me) to compare it to. Inside this chariot were the items necessary for the changing of the tables, namely: tablecloths, napkins, cups, plates, dishes, forks, meat, sauce, and the beverage, distributed by the maidens of the chariot to the others who served the tables, who then placed all the remains back inside. When the chariot departed, the musical maidens began to play oboes and trombones; then they did the same when it returned. And as they ceased, the singers began a harmony that would have put the **Sirens** <note>mythological creatures whose song was irresistibly enchanting</note> to sleep. Wherefore, two sounds and chords like celestial ones were continually heard: a delectable melody heard, a very sweet odor smelled, and an unparalleled delicacy tasted; for all things there were suited to dignity, grace, and delight. At the first course, all the dishes were of fine gold, like the Queen's table; and we were served a cordial confection, made (from what I could understand) of **unicorn shavings** <note>original: "razure de Licorne" – ground narwhal tusk or similar material believed to be unicorn horn, prized for its medicinal properties</note>, the two sandalwoods, with pearls cooked and extinguished in **aqua vitae** <note>original: "eau de vie" – a potent distilled alcohol</note> until dissolved, manna, pine nuts, musk, and gold ground in rosewater, preciously composed and assembled into a mass with sugar and starch. We were given two morsels each without drinking; this is a food meant to preserve one from all poison, deliver one from fever or **melancholy humor** <note>in medieval medicine, "black bile," associated with sadness or depression</note>, and preserve health and youth. The opening of this last vessel surrounded a rich mountain, or heap of precious stones, all without cut or polish, gathered together in one pile and pressed against one another, roughly, without art or order: because of this, the mountain seemed rugged and difficult to climb, and it gave off a sparkling of various strange colors. Upon its point and summit grew a pomegranate tree, whose trunk and branches were of gold, the leaves of emeralds, and the fruit of natural size, the skin of which was of unpolished gold, and the seeds of oriental rubies, each the size of a bean. The membrane or skin which separates the seeds was of appropriate silver.

The noble craftsman of this masterpiece had adorned it in certain places with split and half-open pomegranates, the seeds of which seemed not yet to have reached maturity, and he had fashioned them from large oriental pearls. A certainly superb invention, almost putting nature to shame.

Furthermore, he had placed there pomegranate blossoms or flowers, carved from vermilion coral: the opening in the shape of a calyx, notched, and full of small filaments of drawn gold: then he had passed a small pillar above the tree, fixed like a pivot into the axle of the chariot, and passing through the hole which was hollow inside.

This pillar turned incessantly and supported a **Topaz** <note>a precious gemstone, often yellow or golden</note> vase, wide at the bottom, surrounded near the middle by two gold bands, fashioned with the molded heads of four small children, each having two wings, casting water from their mouths.

The neck of the vase was twice as long as the rest of the body, tapering and rising to a point, covered above with overturned foliage, upon which was placed another almost round vase, also covered with beautiful foliage.

At the bottom of this last vase, dolphin tails touched each side, meeting the slender part of the neck of the vase. Their heads, which were covered in foliage, descended down to the gold bands or belts, between which were the heads of the small children, bent almost in the shape of **handles** <note>original: "aſes"; referring to *ansae*, the decorative handles of a vessel</note>, with a beautiful grace, because the dolphin heads were curved and arched, and the tails low and pressed against the vase: this was made with such artifice that when the chariot moved, the vase and the pillar supporting it turned incessantly (as was said), throwing water over the pomegranate tree. I thought that this occurred by a wheel of the chariot which turned another laid flat and pegged, striking the bottom of the pillar, where a **lantern gear** <term>lantern gear: a type of mechanical gear consisting of two disks connected by rods, common in early clockwork and mill machinery</term> was made.

The wheels of the chariot were half-covered, up to the hub, in the form of two extended wings of fine gold, engraved with small monsters like **Scyllas** <note>mythological sea monsters, often depicted with a woman's torso and a tail of dogs or serpents</note>, masks, and foliage. So great and vast were the pomps, riches, triumphs, treasures, and delights of the Palace of this noble Queen, and her display so sumptuous, that one must not wonder if I have been unable or known not how to write of it distinctly and perfectly: for I do not think there is in the world so fine a spirit nor a tongue so eloquent, prompt, and well-spoken, who could satisfy the task: so far am I from being sufficient, considering especially that my heart was occupied with other things than thinking of Lady Polia <note>Polia is the object of Poliphilo's obsessive love and the goal of his journey</note>, besides that I hold for certain that all human understanding (however excellent one might choose) would have been troubled and confused among so many wonders impossible to believe, and more difficult to recite. And even if in my fantasy there had been no other thought or imagination than that one, it would have been enough to overwhelm and darken all my senses. 

But who is he who could—I do not say recite, but only remember—all the rich finery and perfect beauties of the maidens? The great prudence, beautiful and wise speech, along with the sense, knowledge, and liberality of the Queen? The exquisite arrangement of Architecture, the suitable proportion of the building, the excellence of the paintings and tapestries of silk and gold thread, the richness of the plate <term>plate: <note>original: "vaisselle" – expensive household vessels made of gold or silver</note></term>, the unparalleled work of the sculptures, and the infinite multitude of precious stones? Certainly it seemed to me that all those of the world were assembled there. 

The ornaments of the chambers, halls, galleries, cabinets, wardrobes, kitchens, baths, steam rooms <term>steam rooms: <note>original: "estues" – small heated rooms used for sweating or bathing, similar to a sauna or sudatorium</note></term>, and courtyards, were so sumptuous and well-appointed, that in all the kingdom of Faerie <note>original: "Faerie" – the mythical land of magic and folklore; the author suggests the palace surpasses even legendary enchantments</note> none were ever seen like them. The invention and undertaking of this manor was an incredible thing: for it was so harmonious and consistent in all its parts, that there was nothing to find fault with. 

But among the most excellent works, there was a floor made with compartments—round, square, oval, triangular, hexagonal, and other shapes all of one size, separated by a band or border edged with two moldings or intervals like strings of rosebuds, the corners of the compartments embraced by acanthus leaves, otherwise called bear's breech <term>bear's breech: <note>original: "Branque vrsine" – the Acanthus plant, whose leaves are a staple motif in classical Corinthian architecture</note></term>: the inside filled with Arabesque foliage in half-relief. The relief was gilded, and the background was of Acre blue <note>original: "azur d’Acre" – a high-quality, deep blue pigment, likely ultramarine or a fine cobalt blue associated with the Levant</note>, so beautiful that one could call it singular and without equal.

POLIPHILE. 41

The door and the windows of her house are at all times closed, and she does not allow in any way for men to know her. Likewise, it is neither lawful nor permitted for bodily eyes to look upon a thing so sovereign. That is why the outcome of her effects is at all times uncertain. She changes and transfigures herself into many very strange forms: then she manifests herself when one does not desire it at all, and when one thinks of it the least. At the opening of each of the three doors she will come to present herself before you; however, you will not be able to recognize her, except by conjecture, which foresees and considers her immediately, even though she changes her face and dress at every turn to make knowledge of her doubtful. This doubt and uncertainty often causes man to remain without improvement, being deceived by hope. These two maidens of mine, then, to whom I entrust, recommend, and give you in charge, will teach you at which of the doors you ought to stop, and you will be able, by virtue of the ring I give you, to govern yourself by whichever of the two seems good to you. Having said this, she signaled to them to approach me. Then by gestures and acts (it not being in my power, boldness, nor knowledge to speak), I thanked her most humbly for all her graces and benefits. Then my two companions took me familiarly, each by a hand: then with the leave of the Queen, and likewise of all the ladies, we went out through the same door by which I had entered. I turned back at every step, like one who could not satisfy himself with seeing this triumphant dwelling, so sumptuous that it is impossible to believe it was a building made by human hands, but that nature had made it to show off and display an excellent masterpiece of her craftsmanship, full of beauty, grace, wealth, security, blessedness, happiness, and perpetual duration. Therefore I would have willingly stopped for a little while longer, but it was necessary for me to follow my guides. Passing then along my way, I cast my eyes across and saw written on the frieze above the door an inscription saying thus:

THE WEALTH OF NATURE. <note>original Greek: "Ο ΤΗΣ ΦΙΣΕΩΣ ΟΛΒΟΣ"</note>

These small towers that you see built here and there are distant from one another by about seven circuits or revolutions of the paths; and there are ten of them in total, not counting the one in the center and middle. The danger into which those who enter fall is that in the center tower stays an invisible dragon, but one that is greatly cruel and hideous. It is true that not seeing him at all provides some small comfort; nevertheless, it is a thing far too terrifying to be unable to avoid him. Sometimes, right from the entry itself, or on the path by chance or by deliberate purpose, he devours those who have entered therein. And if he does not swallow them into his belly along the way or around the perimeter, they safely pass all the revolutions and see all the towers one by one until they reach the center where this monster makes his home; and there, they inevitably fall into his throat, and there is no release."

Know that the first stone is known only to itself: and although it is diaphanous <note>transparent or translucent</note> or transparent, it is not totally clear to us. Nevertheless, he who has a better spirit climbs higher and ingeniously considers the color of the round figure: then searches further forward and passes even to the third figure, which is of a dark color: and finally comes to contemplate another figure with three faces: and from there forward, sight and knowledge always go on diminishing and failing like a pyramid: for notwithstanding that man may be learned and expert, he can learn nothing else of it except that it *is*: but *what* or *how*, that cannot enter into his brain.

From these holy remonstrances that Logistica <note>The personification of Reason or Logic</note> made to me, taken from the secret of divine nature, I had more pleasure in my heart than from all that I had seen before: and in fact, I set myself to contemplate the Obelisk of such great mystery, upright, firm, and level, composed of incorruptible matter, eternally persevering, seated in the middle of this meadow among several fruit trees of sweet taste and salutary effect, planted in order and properly placed in grace, beauty, delectation, pleasure, and marvelous utility, indeed incessantly sustained by the sun, which never ends. After we had stayed there some time, my two companions took me again by the hands and led me out of this enclosure. Then Thelemia <note>The personification of Will or Desire</note> said to me: "It is time to go to the three gates that we seek." To which consenting, we set ourselves on the way through this beautiful country, where the air was clear and the sky as serene as possible: but this was not without passing the time in familiar and delectable talk, such that I, desiring to know and understand particularly the great riches and inestimable treasures of their Queen Eleutherilide <note>The Queen representing Free Will; her name is derived from the Greek 'Eleutheria' meaning Liberty</note>, made this honest request of them. "I pray you, O happy maidens, if my inquiring is not troublesome to you, tell me what history is carved inside the Diamond which hangs from the necklace of the Queen your mistress? For among all the precious stones that I have seen in her palace, that one seems to me so rich that I repute it beyond all esteem: and I think it is impossible to assign it a suitable price, seeing that it is such that the Jasper of the Emperor Nero where his figure was engraved, the Topaz of Queen Arsinoe of Arabia, and likewise the stone for which the Senator Nonius was sent into exile <note>A reference to a famous opal mentioned by Pliny the Elder</note>, were never worthy to be compared to it. It is true that because it was a little far from me, and by reason of its great clarity and brilliance, I could not see it at my ease: and that is why (if it would please you) I would very much like to learn what is there."

Following her <note>The Queen</note> were six young ladies of incomparable beauty, adorned with everything required to give grace to the excellence of their persons. The first was named Rhastone, the second Chortasine, the third Idone, the fourth Trophile, the fifth Etosie, and the sixth Adie.

The presence, the grace, and the attractive beauty of these six young ladies contented my eyes more than any of the others. Seeing this, Logistica <note>The personification of Reason or Logic</note>, my good and loyal counselor—noticing that I was already inclined and slavishly devoted to the love of this lady—piteously admonished me, saying: "Ha, Poliphilo! The beauty of this one is feigned, false, and painted. If you had seen the back of her shoulders, you would be forced to vomit; you would recognize the treason and smell a carrion stinking beyond measure. You would see her as so utterly abominable that you would be filled with great horror. Certainly, these young ladies will hardly remain with you, but will abandon you immediately, and you will be quite stunned to see them vanish from your presence. Pleasure passes, and shame remains, accompanied by repentance. Believe me, these are nothing but vain hopes and most certain harm: a very short joy and perpetual regret, mixed with sighs that trouble the rest of a miserable life. It is a counterfeit sweetness, preserved in dangerous bitterness; the birdlime <note>A sticky substance used to trap birds; here, a metaphor for a snare</note> where the wretched are caught, and the end which consumes all good."

Such and similar words my Logistica spoke with a grieving and angry heart; then, wrinkling her beautiful face, she threw her lyre against the ground and broke it into many pieces. However, Thelemia <note>The personification of Will or Desire</note>, who made little account of such remonstrances, did not care in the least; rather, smiling, she signaled to me that I should not stop for the preachings of this troublesome woman. Logistica, recognizing my evil and perverse inclination, sighing with vexation, turned her back on me and retreated at a run.

And so I remained with my dear Thelemia <note>Thelemia represents "Will" or "Desire" in Greek</note>, who, having won the battle, spoke to me in flattering words: "Poliphilo, my friend, here is the place where you will shortly find the thing you most desire in this world, which is yours, and of which your heart incessantly dreams." Then I began to presuppose that it was Lady Polia: for no other thought could enter my heart; therefore I was greatly rejoiced. Shortly thereafter, Thelemia, seeing that I was resolved and firm in my purpose to remain in the company of these young ladies, kissed me graciously, taking her leave of me, and returned toward the Queen.

[Woodcut illustration depicting several women in classical dress standing in a wooded landscape.]

The doors were closed after her, and I remained alone among these beautiful Nymphs: who entertained me most lovingly with all manners of pleasure, so much so that love began to renew itself within me through their sweet words, attractive glances, and great endearments. Their eyes were so very sharp that they would have pierced a breast of steel, and moved not just a simple and changeable young man like myself, but even the good old man Socrates. If one among them had been in the place of Phryne <note>A famous ancient Greek courtesan known for her beauty</note>, she would have warmed the cold Xenocrates <note>A Greek philosopher known for his extreme self-restraint</note>, and he would have had no cause to call her a stone statue: for they were accomplished in every perfection of nature, dressed in rich costumes decorated in diverse fashions. Their hair had the color of gold thread, puffed and curled around the forehead, perfumed with an odor sweeter than musk or ambergris. Some had it tied behind with ribbons of gold thread and silk; others had it corded, twisted, and braided into three or four strands, in the manner of lace-work. Their speech was most sweet, and of such great efficacy that it would have subjugated all resistance contrary and rebellious to love, softened bitterness, and tamed rusticity.

Then, looking here and there, I saw from afar a gathering of young people, men and women in several groups, in the middle of a field that was wonderfully large and spacious; some were dancing, others were passing the time in various acts of pleasure. As soon as I had discovered them, I stopped, falling into doubt as to which I should do: whether to go further toward them, or rather to wait and not move from there. Then, as I was in this thought, a beautiful Nymph left the troop, carrying a burning torch in her hand, and took her path straight toward me. I waited for her with great affection <note>In this context, "affection" implies a strong emotional yearning or intense interest.</note>, hoping to have some news of what I went seeking. The great mass of her tresses descended along the neck, where it was tucked up with good grace; and leaving the ears uncovered, which were round and small, it hung down as far as her knees, sparkling in the sun like threads of gold: for it was more beautiful and better variegated than the tail of a Peacock when he makes his wheel. She had a high, broad, and smooth forehead: then beneath it two laughing eyes, bright as the rays of the Sun, composed of two black pupils surrounded by a whiteness such that if one had placed milk against it, the milk would have appeared as black as ink. They were covered by two slender eyebrows, arched in the fourth part of a circle, separated and distant from one another by the width of two good inches, blacker than fine velvet. Her cheeks were vermilion, embellished by two small dimples, having the color of fresh roses gathered at the dawn of day and placed in a vessel of Crystal. Appetite contradicted this, prizing above all things her golden hair, wide, thick, arranged in beautiful waves, twisted in the fashion of ringlets. I knew well within myself that this dissension could not cease without losing the pleasure of looking at the beautiful Nymph: which was impossible for me: wherefore I was like a man pressed by hunger finding himself among a great abundance of meats which he desires all together, but he is satisfied by none that presents itself.

If Zeuxis <note>A famous Greek painter of the 5th century BCE, known for his realism.</note> had seen her when he created the image of Venus, in my judgment he would have taken her as his model above all the maidens of Agrigento <note>original: "Agrigẽte"; Zeuxis famously selected the five most beautiful virgins of Agrigento to composite the perfect form of Helen/Venus.</note>, indeed, of the entire universal world, judging her accomplished in every perfection of beauty. In contemplating her, I lost my senses, my spirit, my understanding, and my total awareness; and I knew not how to do anything else except present to her my heart, wide open. Of this heart she has since made her own heritage, disposing of it at her pleasure and choosing it as her perpetual dwelling. Since then, it has become the quiver for Cupid's arrows, and the workshop where he forges and tempers his sharpened darts. I felt my heart beating incessantly within my chest like a muffled drum. Now, notwithstanding that by her gracious look she seemed to me to be Polia, whom I so greatly desired, yet the strange dress she wore and the place which was unknown to me kept me for a long time in doubt. She carried her left hand pressed against her breast and held a burning torch, rising a little higher than her head. When she was near me, she extended her right arm, whiter than a lily, upon which the veins appeared like little lines of vermilion drawn on white paper; and taking my left hand in her right, she said to me: "Poliphilo, my peer, come now with me, and make no difficulty of it." At this word, I felt all my spirits troubled, and was almost turned to stone, marveling how she could know my name. I was, in good faith, all ablaze with an amorous ardor; and my voice, held back by fear and shame, did not permit me to answer her. Thus, I did not truly know how to honor her; therefore, without more words, I reached out my hand to her, unworthy (so it seemed to me) to touch her own.

Upon taking her hand, it seemed to me (and it was true) that I touched something other than human: at which I felt a great fear, for I knew nothing beyond the common natural world, and did not yet know what was to happen to me. I found myself in a poor state, poorly dressed, and of a heavy countenance, quite different in form, status, and quality from such an excellent creature: whereby I deemed myself unworthy of such company, knowing well that it is not permitted for the mortal inhabitants of the earth to enjoy the delights of heaven. I was all red with great shame, and filled with amazement, complaining within myself of my low condition. Nevertheless, I set myself to follow her, not having yet entirely recovered my senses, but believing nonetheless that the outcome could only be most blessed, considering that I was being led into such a beautiful place by so singular a guide: for her sweet, amorous gaze could have withdrawn from the hands of Rhadamanthus <note>In Greek mythology, Rhadamanthus is one of the judges of the dead in the Underworld, known for his stern and inflexible justice.</note> the souls condemned and lost: indeed (what is more) restore to their first nature bodies consumed and converted into ash. Thus I went along after her, my heart always beating, and trembling more than a lamb between the teeth of a wolf, marvelously inflamed with sweet amorous passion. "Oh," (said I then) "blessed above all lovers is he who might be, if not entirely, at least in some part, a participant in the grace of this so exquisite damsel." Then all of a sudden I blamed my foolish desires, saying: "Alas, I could hardly believe that such a nymph would deign to acquaint herself with things as low as mortal men, who have nothing similar to her. Certainly she deserves to be loved by the highest celestial gods, and to make Jupiter descend, disguised from his own form." On the other hand, I consoled myself by offering her my heart and my soul, having nothing else more worthy of which to make her a present, estimating that this is what the gods find most agreeable. Thus I found myself troubled and confused by a diversity of thoughts, so much so that my heart was variably moved by applying itself too willingly to such hidden imaginations, ready and prepared to serve as a firebrand or a log within the powerful fire of love, in which I suffered with such sweet pleasure that torment was my recreation. The gaze of this Nymph did to me as the lightning does to the oaks and other trees that it splits, breaks, and scatters, so much so that I dared no longer lift my sight to contemplate her eyes: for when her light met mine, for a long time afterward all things seemed double to me, and I was dazzled, like those who have looked firmly and with a straight eye at the sphere of the sun. In this manner I was taken, bound, and vanquished: quite ready to cry out to her, "My Lady, I surrender myself to you": which I had already for a good while concluded, confirmed, and resolved within myself, and given my heart as a hostage: which soon recognized the accustomed flame, which had only been covered and dormant: whereby it was promptly rekindled, like a firebrand which has been in the hearth and felt the fire. That love entered into my heart like the wooden horse into Troy, namely full and stuffed with hidden enemies, who have entirely burned it and turned it to ash, wounding me with incurable wounds, from which I never hope to recover, if it is not by means of this Nymph: toward whom I thought to embolden myself to declare to her the pain that I could no longer suffer, almost lost in a blinded desire: and I was on the verge of making her hear this speech in a full voice: "O divine Nymph, whoever you may be, moderate a little the ardor with which, without any misdeed, you consume my sad..."

Alas, she entertained me so familiarly, and I did not dare tell her of my misfortune. Certainly, I did everything possible to appease my heart, pulling it back from all hope that could have comforted it; notwithstanding this, never was a coal so extinguished that, upon approaching the fire, it did not reignite itself by the conforming disposition of its nature. Thus my eyes, finding my heart unarmed and devoid of defense, set it ablaze from hour to hour, and more and more, with an extreme affection for the Nymph, whom they showed to be always more beautiful, more gracious, and more worthy of being adored. Then all in a moment I came back to myself, and said: If the gods knew that with evil intention I crave the rarest things, forbidden and interdicted to humans, could it not happen to me as it does to a profane person, and as it has happened to several others who have rashly and presumptuously offended their goodness? Like **Ixion** the audacious <note>Ixion was punished in the underworld for attempting to seduce Hera.</note>, and the ill-advised Thracian <note>Likely referring to Lycurgus or a similar mythological figure punished for offending the gods of wine and sea.</note> for having indiscreetly joined and mixed through adultery the savory **Bacchus** with the goddess **Thetis**, unworthily meddling in their divine state. In like manner, **Galanthis**, the royal handmaid, would not have given birth to her children through her mouth if she had not lied to the goddess **Lucina** <note>In myth, Galanthis was turned into a weasel (which was folk-believed to give birth through the mouth) for deceiving the goddess of childbirth.</note>. Perhaps this Nymph is reserved for some Demigod, who could with good cause be indignant against me if I attempted to commit such sacrilege. Finally, I presupposed that those who lightly embolden themselves, lightly also perish; and for such people, it is easy to fail and be deceived: for it is commonly said that fortune is not always propitious to the over-bold; furthermore, it is not easy to know the heart of another. Therefore, just as **Callisto**, ashamed to see her belly grow, withdrew from the company of the chaste **Diana**, so I withdrew in shame, distancing myself from this importunate desire; nevertheless, always having my eye open to contemplate the beautiful Nymph, and disposing myself to love her forever.

**F**eigning to give me liberty, Cupid instead placed me in extreme servitude; and having accepted him as my lord, he governed me like a cruel tyrant. I found myself tightly bound by the chains of love, submitted and subjected to the privilege of his harsh laws (however pleasant they may seem), full of uncertain joy, and utterly oppressed by sighs. Seeing this, the beautiful Nymph cast a sweet gaze upon me to reassure me; and with a slight smile, she said to me: "Poliphilo, I wish for you to know that true love has no regard for outward appearances; therefore, let your clothing <note>Poliphilo is often depicted in humble or disheveled attire during his trials</note> in no way diminish your courage, which (perhaps) is noble, magnanimous, and worthy of seeing these holy places. Cast all fantasy from your mind, so that you may freely contemplate the great, inexplicable blessings prepared for those whom the goddess Venus has chosen to be crowned, and who manfully labor, persevering in her service, to acquire her good grace."

After she had said this, we walked at a brisk pace, and as we went, I said to myself: "O valiant Perseus, for this woman you would have fought the horrible monster more boldly than for the beautiful Andromeda. O Jason, if this Nymph had been offered to you in marriage, I believe that for her love you would have exposed your body to greater peril than that of conquering the Golden Fleece; and I would have rightly esteemed her more than all the treasures of the world, even were Queen Eleutherilide <note>A character encountered earlier in the book representing Free Will and immense wealth</note> there with her marvelous opulence."

I walked step by step with her, and sometimes lowered my eyes to see her feet, shod in soles of red leather, tied above the foot with ribbons of gold thread and silk, adorned with oriental pearls. Sometimes it happened that the wind, stirring her garment, revealed her legs, which seemed composed of scarlet, milk, and musk mixed together. These were the nets, ropes, and threads by which I was caught and held; even the knots by which I was bound were more difficult to undo than that of Gordius <note>The Gordian Knot</note> cut by Alexander the Great. **R**easonably, everyone can estimate that nothing is difficult for the gods, and that all things are easy for them; for which good and just cause they are called almighty. The hub was made of fine gold, as was the rim of the wheel, because that metal can be consumed neither by fire nor by rust; yet, it is the poison of virtue and the deadly venom of peace <note>The author reflects on the dual nature of gold: its physical incorruptibility versus its power to corrupt human morality and social stability</note>. This chariot was greatly honored and celebrated by those who followed it, dancing and rejoicing in great, solemn displays of pomp. The Nymphs seated upon the Centaurs sang in sweet melody, harmonizing with their instruments and celebrating the occasion of this divine and sumptuous mystery.

POLIPHILUS.                                                                    61

The following chariot was drawn by six tigers, dappled with reddish spots, harnessed with vine branches laden with clusters of grapes, which served as offensive weapons; and they moved along at a slow, steady pace. In the middle of the upper platform there was a golden base, one foot and four fingers in diameter, and three palms in height—specifically, one palm for the round plinth or torus, half a palm for the echinus <note>a rounded molding</note> and its small square member, and the remainder divided between the trochilus <note>a hollow, concave molding</note> or scotia, the reversed cyma <note>an S-shaped molding</note>, and the upper torus, all enriched with their small squares. The surface of this base was slightly recessed and hollowed out to make room for four eagle tails that rested upon the edge, made of *Aetite psane* stone <note>Eagle-stone, traditionally believed to be found in eagles' nests and to possess magical properties</note>. They had their backs turned toward one another and joined their wingtips to form a point, upon which they supported an antique vase of Ethiopian Hyacinth <note>likely a deep orange-red zircon or garnet</note>, variegated with veins of emerald and several other precious stones. Its height was two and a half feet, and its diameter one and a half at its widest point. Its circumference was three diameters and a little more <note>The author is describing the mathematical constant Pi (3.14...)</note>. The foot of the vase rose four inches above the wings of these eagles. At the widest part of its body, it was encircled by a frieze one palm wide; from which, up to the beginning of another vase-like spout <term>Gargoule: a throat-shaped vessel or spout</term> joined to the first, there was another palm. This latter vessel was one foot high and began to widen at the top by about a good palm and a half; this half-palm was used for a small frieze made of flowers and foliage in half-relief, pierced through and almost standing out from their background, carved from the same stone. The diameter of the vessel at its widest was two and a half palms, and it was fluted below the frieze with narrow gadroons <note>decorative convex moldings</note> toward the bottom and wide ones at the top. The neck, from the frieze to the mouth, was two and a half palms long, making the total height of the vessel's foot, including the palm and a half below the frieze, decorated with gadroons turning in the shape of lilies. The rim of the mouth was flat, adorned with moldings: cyma, ogee, echinus, and others; the borders of the friezes were similarly finished. In the frieze of the spout, on the lower molding, half-rings were soldered across each side, which two lizards were biting; these were made from a vein of emerald. Their four feet rested on the cover of the large vase that supported the spout; it was joined to the frieze in the form of an ogee or reversed cyma, carved with scales, of the same Hyacinth stone, and was one palm high, as I have said. The tails of the lizards, which lay upon the belly along this cover, were twisted to form rings upon the molding of the frieze, with another below, which served as handles. The base finished in foliage that entered half a foot into the frieze on each side and was almost entirely in full relief, so that one could easily see the Hyacinth background. Thus, this foliage occupied two feet of the vase's circumference. It remains now to speak of the space left in the frieze. Between the two pieces of foliage, measuring one and a half feet long on each side, were the sculptures that I shall describe hereafter; but first I will speak of the belly of this vase, which was covered with a vine. Its trunks, shoots, and branches were carved from a vein of topaz suited for this purpose; the leaves were of emerald and the grapes of amethyst, set upon a background of Hyacinth so round and polished that one would have judged it had been made on a lathe; for it seemed as though the leaves were separate from it.

The second had her transmutation only from the waist down: and so on for the others. Notwithstanding this, all showed some sign of transformation in the head.

[Woodcut illustration depicting several figures. On the left, three figures are in various stages of transforming into trees. In the center, three figures are dancing. On the far right, a figure (Jupiter) stands atop a decorated altar.]

On the other side was carved a young, plump god, resembling a girl in the face, crowned with two Snakes, one white and the other black, so well imitated that one would have taken them for natural. He sat beneath a trellis covered with a Vine-stock, where little children climbed to gather the vintage, and then brought their baskets full of grapes before this young god, who received them laughing. Some trod the vintage, others remained doing nothing, except that they beat a tambourine and sang out of tune. Several lay on the ground, stretched on their backs, asleep from having swallowed the wine and drunk from the Sibyl <note>original: "Sibille du pressoir" - likely a reference to a large wine-vessel or vat named after the prophetess</note> of the wine-press. And although the figures were very small, yet they were made to their proportion and measure so perfectly that there was nothing to find fault with: and the craftsman had applied the precious stones according to the colors, by marvelous dexterity joined with industry and great intelligence.

From the vessel issued a vine of gold, most abundant in leaves, laden with grapes made of oriental amethyst, and the leaves of Persian Selenite <note>A variety of gypsum or transparent stone, named for its moon-like luster</note>, which is not at all subject to the file, and pleases Cupid, insofar as it maintains the health of him who carries it upon himself. It served both as a trellis and as shade for the entire chariot, which had at each corner a candlestick seated upon three feet of coral, singularly profitable to laborers for the reason that it drives away thunders, lightning bolts, tempests, whirlwinds, and other evil winds. The pillar of one was of Portuguese Ceraunite <note>A "thunderstone," historically believed to fall from the sky during storms</note>, of celestial color, a friend to tempests, and greatly loved by the goddess Diana. It was fashioned in balusters, assembled with little pommels and other ornaments of fine gold, in filigree work. The second was of black Onyx stone, spotted with vermilion drops, which has the odor of incense when it is rubbed. The third was of Medea stone <note>A legendary stone named after the sorceress Medea, said to be black with gold veins</note>, of a dark gold color. The last was of precious Nebride <note>Likely a reference to a stone resembling a fawn-skin, sacred to Bacchus</note>, of black, white, and green color: all mingled together, and sacred to this god Bacchus. They each had a height of two feet, and upon the point a flat bowl, where there continually burned a flame of fire, which could not be extinguished.

Then my guide, perceiving my weakness, without me asking what it was, said to me: "Do you see that goddess?" Afterward, she showed me a large assembly of maidens, led by three matrons, walking before the whole company: and she said to me, somewhat troubled and changed in her countenance: "My Poliphilo, I truly wish for you to know that none of those who are born on the earth can enter here without having their torch lit by burning love and violent labor, just as you see me carrying mine. Furthermore, it must be through the means and direction of these three matrons." Then she said, sighing: "It will be necessary for me, for your love, to offer and extinguish mine within the holy temple." This word penetrated my heart: so much power did the pleasure have when I heard myself called *hers*, for by this word she gave me a suspicion that she was my desired Polia: and (in truth) such was my ease, that the soul which makes me move was on the point of abandoning my body and withdrawing into hers: of which the color of my face accused me, joined with a low and burning sigh that I cast out, whether I wanted to or not: but when she perceived it, she promptly changed the subject, saying to me: "Oh, how many there are in the world who would wish only to catch a glimpse of what you are permitted to contemplate in full view! Within these meadows was found an infinite multitude of country folk, such as I had never been accustomed to seeing. They seemed to me dressed rustically in the skins of Fallow Deer, Roe Deer, Ounces <note>An archaic term for a snow leopard or similar wild cat</note>, and Leopards. Their buskins <note>High boots worn by hunters or actors in antiquity</note> were made of Sorrel and Dock, bordered with flowers, for they were solemnizing a feast with the Hamadryad Nymphs <note>Nymphs who live in trees and perish when the tree dies</note> around Vertumnus <note>The Roman god of seasons, change, and plant growth</note>, who wore a hat of Roses, and had his lap full of little flowers. Beside him was his Pomona <note>The Roman goddess of fruit trees and orchards</note>, crowned with fruitage, her hair hanging over her shoulders: both seated in a triumphal chariot, drawn by harnesses of branches and foliage by four great horned Fauns. At their feet was a Chantepleure <note>A vessel used for watering gardens, or a funnel-like device</note>: and Pomona held in her hand a horn of abundance, full of leaves and fruits. Before the chariot went two beautiful Nymphs acting as ensign-bearers, one having in her device plowshares, mattocks, hoes, scythes, sickles, flails, shovels, and other instruments of labor, all hanging at the end of a lance. In the other, there were I know not what grafts or shoots with a small pruning hook, and a tablet whereon was written that which follows:

When we had passed further on, I saw through the forest certain Oread, Napaea, and Dryad nymphs <note>Nymphs of mountains, glens, and trees respectively</note>, along with the Nereids <note>Sea nymphs</note>, dressed in the skins of seals, and others in flowers and leaves, dancing with Fauns and Satyrs crowned with reeds and rushes. Likewise, the god Pan was there, and Sylvanus <note>God of the woods</note>: then Zephyrus <note>The West Wind</note> with his beloved Chloris, and all the other gods and goddesses of the woods, mountains, valleys, and fountains: together with several musical shepherds, sounding old instruments made of stalks and reeds, bagpipes of raw hide, pipes of bark, and others of such strange resonance, with which they celebrated the holy floral feasts. I leave it to those who can understand it to imagine the pleasure I had in seeing such novel things. 

We had not traveled far, my guide and I, when I perceived through the tops of the trees a high pinnacle like a small round tower, which did not seem very far from that seashore where my guide was taking her path, and to which all the streams we had passed came to empty themselves. When I had approached a little closer, I saw more clearly something like a round vault shaped like an oven-dome <note>original: "cul de four"</note>, covered in lead (as it seemed to me) and enriched with a lantern with eight pillars: and above it another similar vault, supporting another lantern likewise of eight square pillars, in which was fixed a rod and a very shining ball. I suddenly desired to see this beautiful building, which always seemed to me all the more exquisite the closer I approached it. Judging by its appearance from afar, I thought it was an ancient structure: therefore I deliberated whether to pray my guide that she might wish to lead me there, although we were already traveling toward the place where it stood: but I repressed my will, saying to myself: "Alas, I dare not ask for the thing I most desire <note>Likely referring to his lost love, Polia</note>, and which would make me more content than any man in this world if I could obtain it; how then shall I ask for this, which is neither necessary nor urgent for me?" 

Thus I went walking along, my fantasy always filled with such amorous variations, until we arrived on the shore of the Sea at a very pleasant place, where a sumptuous temple was built,

<margin>Phyzoé: the life of nature. <note>From the Greek "Physis" (nature) and "Zoe" (life)</note></margin>

consecrated to Venus Phyzoé. Its form was round, and it was as high as the diameter of its circle: and to design it well, the Architect had first made a circle on the plan, and within it a square: then he had divided the diameter of the circle into five parts, from the circumference to the side of this square, and had added a sixth part at the center. Upon this he had drawn another circle, and upon that erected this beautiful edifice as to its principal parts, indeed finding all its measurements, as much for the thickness of the walls and pilasters as for the space between the wall forming the enclosure of the temple and the columns supporting the central vault. Afterward, he had drawn ten lines equally from the center to the circumference, distant from one another like rays or semi-diameters: upon which he had made ten arches or vaults seated upon ten pillars of Serpentine stone <note>A dark green mottled stone</note>. Inside the work, against each of the pillars which were two feet wide at their face and supported the arches of the vaults, was placed a Corinthian column of Porphyry <note>A rare purple-red stone</note>, of Ionic height—that is to say, of nine diameters—not including the capitals which were of gilded copper, and likewise the bases, upon which were seated the architrave, the frieze, and the cornice, which had

because they are dangerous if they fall: therefore such an inconvenience must be avoided. Furthermore, the gutter hollows out the ground around it: and if the water falls upon the stone, it splashes back and rots the base of the wall. Indeed (what is more) the water falling from these gutters, blown by the wind against the wall, blackens it, covers it with earth, deforms, and ruins the moldings: it even engenders various weeds, mosses, or shrubs, which loosen and cause the stones to fall. The height of the exterior wall did not exceed at all that of the keystone of the arches, excluding the cornice above, which was hollowed out at the top in the fashion of a channel, where the slope of the roof came to rest, from the central dome down to the wall. This roof was made of gilded copper plates, fashioned like scales: and its slope began on the outside directly opposite the last line made on the inside, upon the cornice of the frieze and architrave: and it declined toward this gutter which received the rainwater, and emptied it into the pipes of the pillars through which it was conducted into the cistern, furnished with another secret conduit to discharge it when it was too full, and when the water overflowed, retaining only what was necessary for the sacrifice. The faces of the pillars were made in half-relief <note>original: "demytaille," referring to mezzo-rilievo sculpture</note>, with antique candelabra, birds, foliage, and small beasts, continuing up to the height of the exterior cornice placed opposite the interior one being above the figures of the Muses, upon which the great round vault began. From this cornice up to the height of the pillar, there was as much slope as the roof below carried, which was of copper scales, as I have said. On the exterior cornice, upon which was the <term>half-dome</term> <note>original: "voulte à cul de four," a vault shaped like the bottom of a bread oven</note>, began a flying buttress furnished with the same moldings as the architrave, corresponding to the height of the pillar: the corners of which rested upon two square half-pillars, projecting by a third of their width, one from the wall, and the other from behind the height of the pillar, in which on the outside niches were made above the capital to house ten figures in full relief <note>original: "boffe entiere," or ronde-bosse, meaning fully three-dimensional statues</note>, all in diverse poses. On the two sides the pillar was carved with sculpture just as on its face. The slope therefore began at the belt beneath the vault, and descended to the top of the pillar with such moldings as those of the enclosure, which was a denticulated and bordered cornice, the underside recessed with rosettes. The surface of the cornice at the point where it joined the vault was hollowed out all around, to serve as a gutter, and receive all the water that descended from it, which then flowed through the flying buttresses, and from there into the pillars, like that of the other roof, then cast itself into the cistern. These flying buttresses were covered with a <term>scroll</term> <note>original: "cartoche ou rouleau," a decorative architectural element resembling a roll of paper</note> (which some call a vault) in the form of a paper rolled at both ends, one contrary to the other: namely, that which touched the wall toward the bottom: and that which was against the pillar, toward the top. From their folds emerged pods of Beans, Peas, and Carobs, half-open, so that one could discern their fruit for ornament. The top surface was divided by a flat ridge, carved with scales on both sides, and over it a well-wrought artichoke leaf, slightly turned over at the end: which vaults are easily made by this practice. At the top of each pillar there was a chandelier of gilded bronze, made in the form of antique vases with a wide opening and two handles. They were provided with a substance that can neither be consumed nor extinguished by wind, rain, or any other accident: for they burned endlessly and without diminishing. From the handles of one to the other were attached curved festoons <note>decorative garlands of flowers or leaves</note>, which were much thicker in their middle than at the ends. These festoons were made of all sorts of leaves and flowers, filed and pierced through <note>original: "percées à iour," referring to openwork or filigree metalwork</note>, of the same material as their candelabras. The craftsman had tied them by the middle, and upon the binding branched an eagle having its wings extended and looking up into the air, toward the vault of the aisle—that is to say, the space between the row of columns and the outer wall, which was decorated on the inside with mosaics depicting beautiful histories. I have said before that the height of a round temple is determined by the line of its diameter: and to find this height up to the final cornice, one must divide the same diameter into six parts. In doing so, four of such divisions will give the height of the columns, architrave, frieze, and cornice, up to the beginning of the vault. The diameter of the large circle makes the total height: and that of the small circle the remainder of the height, which is the round vault. The slope of the roof or covering of the aisles is found by taking the distance from one wall to the other: and from that making two perfect squares, of which the diagonal shows how much slope it must have.

All the measurements and proportions of this sumptuous edifice had been so well ordered and arranged that the interior and the exterior agreed and corresponded with one another in pillars, columns, and moldings. O unhappy times! O our unfortunate age, in which such beautiful and worthy invention is so grossly ignored. Certainly, we must consider that we could never have understood what an <term>architrave</term><note>The main beam resting across the tops of columns.</note>, <term>frieze</term><note>The decorative band above the architrave.</note>, <term>cornice</term><note>The projecting molding at the top of a wall or building.</note>, base, capital, column, pillar, pavement, <term>entablature</term><note>The entire superstructure of moldings and bands that lie horizontally above columns.</note>, proportion, partition, and measurement were, if the ancient Architects had not taught us through drawing and writing. In the middle of this temple was raised the mouth of a cistern made of stone, around which was shown, carved in <term>half-relief</term><note>Also known as mezzo-rilievo, where the sculpture projects significantly from the background.</note>, a dance of Nymphs, who lacked nothing but speech, so well were they depicted with their gracefully fluttering garments. At the <term>keystone</term><note>The central stone at the top of an arch or vault.</note> of the vault, in the middle of a circle of leaves, was figured in the same casting and material the head of Medusa, open-mouthed as if she wished to cry out in great rage. But the thing that seemed to me most marvelous to behold was a battle of little children mounted upon dolphins, striving one against the other, no more nor less than if they had been produced by nature. They were engraved around the large crystal vessel, which did not seem sunken <note>intaglio</note>, but carved in relief <note>original: "entaillé de boſſe"; high relief sculpture</note>, and so aptly expressed that by the trembling of the light and flame of the aforementioned lamps, it appeared to the onlookers that the work was moving. Certainly, the one that Psammetichus, King of Egypt, made for his god Apis, was in no way comparable to it.

They hung equally at the midpoint of the sphere, and at the end of each was attached a round cymbal, notched from the middle downward with small slits like the teeth of a comb, in which there were certain small steel beads to give them sound. These cymbals, shaken by the wind, struck against the belly of the large sphere, so that their resonance, mixed with the deep echoing of the sphere, composed a graceful and lofty harmony—quite different from the chains and vessels hanging at the top of the Temple of Jerusalem <note>The author refers to the legend that golden chains or bells were hung on the Temple to frighten away birds so they would not soil the roof.</note> for the purpose of chasing away the birds. To conclude the summary of this temple, I shall set down its measurements here, in order to satisfy the craftsmen. The wall where the eight windows were was one and a half feet thick, and the vaulting was the same; even the projection of the pillars that supported the square showed this thickness on every side, that is to say, three feet in diameter. The door was Doric, carved from fine oriental jasper, upon which, on the flat surface of the frieze, was written this word in letters of gold, filed and fitted together: <margin>Cylopera, a place where women drink in order to conceive children</margin> CYLOPERA <note>original: "ΚΥΛΟΠΗΡΑ" (Kylopera). This is a pseudo-Greek term likely meaning "the pouch of the womb" or "vessel of conception."</note>. The gate was of gilded metal, enriched with beautiful openwork; however, we found it closed from the outside with a powerful bolt, upon which my guide dared not lay her hand without the leave of the Prioress and her seven maiden guardians of the temple, to whom the right of entry belonged. 

But when they had come and had heard from the Nymph the reason for our arrival, they immediately received us with a kind countenance. Then they had us climb seven steps of porphyry, set from the level of the pavement up to the door, where we found a beautiful landing made of a single black stone, so polished that there is not (I believe) any such to be found on Mount Briance <note>Likely a reference to the "Mont de Brance" or "Brianza" region, known for its stone and marble.</note>. It was worked in a marquetry of mother-of-pearl. There the maidens stopped, and we did also. Then the Prioress began to say certain prayers; wherefore the Nymph, my guide, bowed in all reverence, and for my part, I did the same. However, I could never hear what she was saying, because in lowering my head, I cast my gaze upon the feet of my guide, who had part of her right leg uncovered, because in moving, her garment had been pulled back a little. 

After the venerable Prioress had finished her orisons addressed to the gods Foriculus, Limentinus, and to the goddess Cardea <note>original: "Foricule, Limentin, & à la deesse Cardine." These are Roman "threshold" deities: Foriculus for the door-leaves, Limentinus for the threshold, and Cardea for the hinges.</note>, the Nymph and I rose. Then the bolt was unlocked by the Prioress, and the doors opened without any noise, except for a sweet and pleasant sound. Wishing to see from whence it was caused, I perceived beneath the gate, at each side of its jambs, a metal pipe, round and hollow, turning upon a polished axle; this, rubbing upon a Serpentine stone as smooth as ice, caused the gate to open more easily than it otherwise would have, and from this came that graceful echoing. But one of the things that amazed me most was that the gate, on one side and the other, without being pushed or pulled by anyone, opened as if by itself. Therefore, having entered inside, I stopped on purpose to learn if it was thus pulled by counterweights or some other engine, and I saw that in the rebate where one of the doors closed upon the other, there was a small steel blade, quite narrow, soldered onto the metal; then, that in the wall and the recess of the door on each side, there was inset a tablet of Lodestone <note>original: "Ayemant" (Magnet/Lodestone).</note> of a dark indigo color, fearing the Garlic and the A— <note>The text cuts off; it refers to the ancient belief that garlic (ail) destroys the magnetic power of a lodestone (aimant).</note>

Then, by means of a golden key, she opened the cover with very great devotion and unparalleled ceremony. Thereupon the young nun gave the candle she was holding to the one who had brought the Mitre, and took the book, which she opened in all reverence to hold it before the Prioress, who began to read softly in the Etruscan tongue <note>original: "langue Hetrurienne"; likely referring to an ancient or liturgical form of Italian/Tuscan used in the mystery rites</note>. Shortly after, she took the holy salt-vessel, over which she performed several priestly blessings, and thus scattered it into the cistern. This done, she commanded that the candle or torch of the Nymph, my companion, be lit; and she had the flame turned downward toward the middle of the cistern, questioning the Nymph in this manner: "My daughter, what do you ask?" "My Lady," she said, "I ask grace for this man" (pointing to me) "and desire that we may go together to the blessed kingdom of the great divine mother, to drink from her holy fountain." Having heard this, the Prioress turned toward me and said, "And you, my son, what do you ask?" To which I responded very humbly: "My Lady, I ask for nothing more than to have the grace of the sovereign mother, but especially, that this woman—whom I believe to be my most-desired Polia, and yet I am not certain—no longer keep me in doubt nor in this amorous torment." Then she replied to me: "Take then, my son, with your hands this torch that she carries, and say thus three times after me: 'Just as the water shall extinguish this flame, may the fire of Love kindle her cold heart.'" I uttered these words three times after her in those exact terms, and with the same ceremony.

It is certainly impossible for a man of no learning and of poor speech, as I am, to declare sufficiently and in worthy terms what my heart was doing in the midst of the great fire that had then seized it; for if my soul had departed from my body at that instant, it would have left me greatly satisfied. But to come to the point, the Prioress said to Polia: "Let us continue, my daughter, to accomplish the interior sacrifices which we have so happily commenced." ### How Polia offered the two turtledoves, and of a little angel who arrived there: whereby the Prioress makes her prayer to the goddess Venus: then the roses were scattered, and two swans sacrificed: upon the ashes of which miraculously grew a Rosebush full of flowers and fruit, of which Poliphile and Polia ate. [Large decorative initial I] I cannot believe that Numa Pompilius <note>The legendary second king of Rome, credited with establishing many of its religious rites.</note> had ever invented such beautiful and devout manners of sacrifice, nor the great Jew <note>A reference to Moses and the Levitical laws of sacrifice.</note> likewise: for (in truth) one does not use such at Caere in Tuscany, nor in all the country of Etruria: also the priests of Memphis never performed them in such humble reverence to their god Apis <note>The sacred bull of ancient Egyptian religion.</note> when they threw the golden cup into the Nile. Even I dare well assure that the image of the goddess Fortune was not honored with similar solemnity within the city of Rhamnus, nor (certainly) the sovereign Jupiter in Anxur: and that those who celebrated the feast of Feronia, walking upon burning coals without injury, approached in no way to these women here. Polia then, having understood the sign that the Prioress made to her, rose promptly to her feet, all the others remaining on their knees: and was led by the good mother straight to a pitcher of Hyacinth <note>Likely referring to a deep blue or purple gemstone or glass.</note>, placed at one side of the chapel. I took careful heed of all their acts: and as she had turned her face toward me, it seemed to me I saw the Sun when it shines upon the beautiful Aurora <note>The Roman goddess of the dawn.</note> at the break of day. I saw her put her hands inside this pitcher, and draw from it a sweetly smelling liquid, with which she washed her face, which was by this means purified. Before the step of the altar there was a large golden candelabra, of rare and singular workmanship, adorned with precious stones: upon the top of which was a round plate, a little hollow, containing about an ell <note>A historical unit of measurement, roughly 45 inches.</note> in circumference, in which was put Amber, Musk, Camphor, Labdanum, Thymiame <note>An ancient incense blend.</note>, Myrrh, Mastic, Benzoin, Aloeswood, Blactebifantis <note>A rare aromatic substance, possibly related to onyx or a specific resin.</note>, and other odors that Happy Arabia <note>Latin: *Arabia Felix*, the fertile southern region of the Arabian Peninsula famous for spices.</note> produces, duly composed by weight and measure: to which Polia, being admonished to do so, approached the burning candle, and after having lit these odors, extinguished it immediately, then set it aside, and furthermore threw into the flame of these scents a branch of dry Myrtle: and when it had caught fire, she carried it back onto the altar of sacrifice, to light from it all the other branches that were there. Thus these nuns surrounded the sacred altar, singing and dancing in measure while the sacrifice was consumed, and they continued until the flame was extinguished, and nothing remained but smoke. I think that these sweet odors and perfumes were placed there to cover the bad smell of the burning flesh.

Immediately after, they all prostrated themselves upon the pavement, except for the Prioress; and it was not long before I saw clearly emerge from the smoke a little spirit, beautiful in all excellence, who had upon his shoulders two wings so shining that my eyes could not look well upon him. I felt my heart fail me, and was dazzled by the rays of his brightness, like a lightning bolt created from water, fire, cloud, and wind. But the Prioress, taking notice of me, made a sign that I should not be afraid, and that I should only remain silent. This beautiful child held in one of his hands a crown of Myrtle, and in the other an arrow, sparkling with burning fire. His head was covered with small golden hair, curly, and crowned with a fillet of Diamonds. He fluttered three times around the altar, then at the third time vanished, and turned into smoke, so much so that I lost sight of him, and remained trembling and greatly pensive, seeing these miraculous things and such an admirable vision, which had (certainly) filled me with a devout horror.

Shortly after, the Prioress made them all rise, and began to read inside the book which was held open before her by the little Novice. The holy lady carried a golden rod in her hand, with which she then commanded Polia to gather the ash remaining from the sacrifice, and put it in a golden sieve prepared for this purpose; which she did, and sifted it upon the first step of the altar, so neatly and with such discretion that she seemed to have been born for this office. When that ash was sifted, the Prioress made her write and portray within it, with the first finger of her right hand, certain characters in the form of those that were in the book; then she made her kneel again, and likewise all the others.

Believe me, I trembled like a leaf upon a tree: and nevertheless, my eyes never moved from her person, but carefully noted everything that she and the prioress did: who, taking the book, again made several terrible signs, conjuring, anathematizing <note>To formally curse or excommunicate.</note>, and exorcising all things contrary to Love, and which might cause it trouble.

She sprinkled all the nuns with it, and me likewise.

Then the beautiful women gathered all their branches of Myrtle, along with that of Rue, which were carried into the cistern by one of the professed <note>A nun who has taken her final vows.</note>, to whom the prioress thus commanded it, giving her the key to do so: then she herself took a brush of Hyssop <note>A plant used for ritual purification.</note>, tied with gold thread and gray silk, and swept the ash with it, gathering it into a heap, and locking it in a box.

O goddess of love, merciful mother, recourse and refuge of all lovers, foundation and principle of all gracious assemblies and unions <note>original: "cōiunctiōs" (conjunctions)</note>, certain and infallible aid to those who loyally serve you: I pray you, be pleased at this hour to receive the humble prayers of this young lady, who has this day vowed, given, and dedicated herself to you. Then she prostrated herself: and no sooner was she bowed down, than a smoke began to rise from this water, and mount little by little toward the vault: whereupon all in an instant the earth began to tremble, moving in the air, and inside the temple a whirlwind of storm so terribly frightening, that it truly seemed as if some great mountain had been plunged into the sea. During this, the doors and windows clashed one against the other with such impetuosity that the noise represented a great thunder, caused by wind enclosed within a cavern without exit.

If I was terrified on my part, it is no wonder. It was abundantly sown with crimson roses intermingled with a round, white fruit, slightly colored with red. Upon this fruit-tree appeared three Doves, and certain other flying birds, which hopped from branch to branch, sweetly warbling their song; whereby I presumed that the goddess showed herself to us in this form, and as if by a divine vision. Then the priestess gathered three of these miraculous fruits, ate the first, gave me the second, and the third was for Polia.

Thus (certainly) I began to burn in flames more amorous than before, and with a softened torment, by being (by means of this miracle) transformed into a new quality.

around which, in the time when it was in its full state, were held fairs and markets, where every year came innumerable multitudes of people from all nations; and there were celebrated many kinds of games and pastimes, so much so that for the excellence of its structure, and for the abundance of sacrifices, it was greatly renowned and devoutly visited. But because its magnificence has fallen away, you see it at this hour deserted and lying in ruin. It was anciently called <term>Polyandrion</term> <note>original: "Polyandrion"; a Greek term for a collective burial place or cemetery</note>, <margin>Polyandrion, sepulchre of many.</margin> consecrated to Pluto, god of the shadows: and therefore there are a great number of tombs where are buried those who, by the importunity of unhappy love, have miserably ended their days. Each year, on the day of the Ides of May (which is the fifteenth of the month), all those who served love, or were under its protection, both men and women, from various regions both far and near, assembled in this temple to celebrate the solemnities of the funerals and annual obsequies of their friends who had thus deceased. And they sacrificed to this three-bodied Pluto <note>A reference to Pluto's power over the three realms or his association with the three-headed dog Cerberus</note>, to the end that they themselves might not fall into the misfortune of being the cause of their own death, and advancing their appointed days. For this reason, they reverently made him funeral offerings of black sheep, which had not yet borne a lamb, and burned them upon an altar of copper, presenting the males to the god, and the females to the goddess Proserpine, his wife, ordering the <term>lectisternia</term> <note>original: "lectisternes"; an ancient Roman propitiatory ceremony consisting of a meal offered to gods and goddesses whose statues were laid on couches</note> for three nights; then they extinguished the flame of the sacrifice with roses and <term>arserie</term> <note>A term likely referring to a type of aromatic water or lye used in ancient rites</note>. So it was, that you still see there a great rosebush, from which if anyone had then plucked a rose, he was reputed sacrilegious, having committed a marvelous offense against this god. But the priests could give them out in exchange. The sacrifice being completed, the high priest, dressed in pontifical robes and having before his breast a rich clasp of a precious stone called <term>Synochite</term> <note>A legendary stone believed by ancients to have the power to summon spirits</note>, gave to each a little ash which he carried in a golden <term>Simpulum</term> <note>original: "Simpule"; a small vessel or ladle used in Roman sacrifices to pour wine into a cup</note>, and it was received with great devotion. After having thus scattered it, they also threw the cane into the sea, and spat there three times, saying at each time, "fu, fu, fu": and they returned back, sowing roses throughout the temple, especially upon the graves, singing in a piteous and funereal tone, accompanied by complaints, tears, groans, and the sound of certain <term>milvine pipes</term> <note>original: "chalemyes miluiennes"; shrill, kite-like sounding pipes used in mourning</note> suitable for such a sacrifice. And after having taken their refreshment, they called upon the souls, and left for them around the graves the remainder of the meat. Besides these anniversaries, the secular games were held, which being finished, they left the temple, and each bought a <term>Pancarp</term> <note>original: "Pancarpe"; literally "all-fruit" or "all-flower," here meaning a garland</note>, that is to say a wreath of flowers, which they put upon their heads, and took in their hand a branch of Cypress, used for funerals. There we sat down upon the fresh and flowery grass. Then my eyes turned to contemplate the great perfection and excellence of beauty with which my companion was adorned, so much so that they found no pleasure nor contentment in any other thing. Wherefore my heart, refreshed by a secret joy, left behind all lowly thoughts and simple fantasies, and my understanding rose to consider her admirable virtues. Nevertheless, it happened at times that I returned to consider the situation of this place, beautiful (certainly) and delectable. The air was serene and favorable, the greenery pleasant, the little hills shaded with groves, bedewed by fountains and streams flowing through the beautiful valley, bordered by all manner of fruit trees. The winds rendered themselves gracious, the earth abundant and fertile, resounding with the song of birds: so that I would have almost thought these were the much-renowned Elysian Fields <note>The paradise of the afterlife in Greek mythology</note>: for the beautiful fields and river of Thessaly <note>Likely referring to the Vale of Tempe, famous in antiquity for its beauty</note> are in no way to be compared to it.

Notwithstanding this, my eyes were always fixed upon my companion, without being able to look elsewhere, considering that my brain occupied itself with nothing else; and I knew not on which part to rest my sight, for each was most beautiful and delectable. Yet it is true that I looked willingly upon a little valley situated in the middle of her breast, between two breasts rounder than apples and whiter than flakes of snow, truly (in truth) more sumptuous than the tomb of King Mausolus <note>One of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World; the origin of the word 'mausoleum'</note>: at least so it seemed to me, because there was the tomb of my soul. Sometimes she cast her gaze upon me, and I felt it run through my whole body, like a flash of lightning, so much so that I shivered for an hour afterward. 

That having passed, I began again as before, pressed by an insatiable desire through a harsh and importunate love, saying, without moving my lips, many words of piteous prayers, founded on plausible reasons, by which I asked for that which would have rendered me the most content in the world, which I obtained in imagination; and I found myself in the midst of the treasures of the goddess Venus, stealing there (just as Mercury did) the jewels of abundant nature. But (alas) I found myself touched too deeply by that contagious malady, besieged by the divine mother <note>Venus</note>, and assailed by her son, the great firebrand <note>Cupid/Amor</note>, indissolubly bound and ensnared under the bait of two beautiful eyes, marvelously sparkling: against which it served nothing to make an effort to withdraw: for that was to enter even further in, and it was no longer in my power to resist these diverse thoughts, seeing that my patience was almost conquered. 

So I deliberated (in whatever way it might be) to extinguish this insupportable ardor, and putting all wise counsel aside, to tempt my Polia with a furious audacity, wishing nevertheless to say to her beforehand in a humble voice: "Madam, I would esteem dying for you as eternal praise, and death would be (in my opinion) tolerable, sweet, and glorious. I say this because my soul is oppressed by too violent an ardor, which increases incessantly and strengthens within my heart so much that I cannot have a single hour of peace nor rest." I thought well by this way to give an end to my grievous martyrdom, but suddenly another counsel came to me, which said: "What will you do, Poliphilo? Think a little what end came of the violence done to Deianira, to Lucretia the Roman <note>Famous historical/mythological victims of unwanted advances or rape, used here as a moral warning</note>, and many other such renowned ladies. Consider that the Gods have often been refused by their earthly loves. What then should a poor simple person like you do in this matter?"

Bring back, bring back to your memory that every long duration comes to a certain end, at least for one who can wait for it: indeed, even Lions and other savage beasts are tamed by persistence: even the tiny Ant <note>original: "Formy"</note> hardens the path by passing over it many times: therefore, with even greater reason, a celestial spirit hidden in a human body might well feel some small spark of love. In this manner, then, approving and blaming my own opinions, I withdrew from these wearying fantasies, hoping to reach the fruit of my long quest, and in the end triumph with the victory acquired through my patience. I remembered also the holy prayers and sacrifices of Polia, where she had made special mention of me, and extinguished her burning torch to show favor to her Poliphile. I thought it better and safer to wait, enduring a happy (though late) reward and obtaining the perfection of my desire, than by perilous importunity to increase my pain and lose all hope for the future. Polia perceived that I changed color too often, and saw me altered, troubled, and almost out of breath, sighing stroke upon stroke from the depths of my chest: to counter this, she cast me a sweet look, which chased from me all these impetuous thoughts, so much so that from then on my soul maintained itself in more tranquil hope amidst the flames of love, like the Phoenix which burns itself in order to be renewed.
