These were six columns of Porphyry <term>Porphyry: a hard igneous rock, typically purple or red, prized in antiquity</term>, seated upon a hexagonal plinth of ophite <term>ophite: a green, snake-like patterned stone similar to serpentine</term>, or a base with six faces. Upon this was placed a round vault, made entirely of a single piece of massive stone, tapering to a point in the shape of a chimney, pierced to let in light. It covered a large cellar which had no light except through a round opening, closed with a copper trellis located in the middle of the six pillars. Directly beneath the center of the vault, through which I looked, it seemed to me that I saw a square space below; therefore, I was seized by the desire to descend there.

At first glance, the place seemed dark to me, but as soon as my eyes were a little accustomed to it, I began to see a large round cave, vaulted and supported by six natural columns <note>original: "nayues," likely meaning monolithic or carved from the living rock</note>, placed directly beneath the six standing above, all made of grey marble <note>original: "marbre biz," a brownish-grey or dark stone</note>, as was the vault. The blocks were so very well joined that the vault and the columns truly seemed to be of a single piece. It is true that the cave was entirely full of saltpeter <note>original: "Aphronitre ou baurach," referring to mineral crusts or efflorescence found in damp ruins</note> and fouled with the droppings of Little Owls <note>Athene noctua</note> as well as bats.

In the middle of these six natural columns was found a copper altar, composed of two perfect squares making six feet in length and three in height, including the ordinary moldings. It was hollow in the manner of a tomb, but in the opening on top, two good inches deep, there was a lattice of the same casting, and on one of the sides a window, made (as I could understand) to put the fire beneath the sacrifice and to draw out the extinguished ash. What made me presume this was that the said lattice, along with the surface of the altar, were all blackened by smoke, which (in my judgment) exited through the round opening above, and then through the small pipe that was in the vault seated upon the six columns, made in the Egyptian fashion. On the last face of the altar was written in well-carved Roman letters:

Every man of good judgment can imagine that where two lakes of contrary natures happen to meet, a marvelous thunder must be engendered there, by reason of the contrariety and perpetual discord of their differing qualities: for where they join, they both lose themselves in a profound abyss, terrifying beyond measure. To tell the truth, the depth of this Hell was so ingeniously represented that it seemed a natural thing <note>original: "nayue" - meaning lifelike or realistic</note> opened for those of evil life: so well and artistically had the craftsman (to show his intention) known how to vary his colors and conduct the lines of Perspective by measure.

Whoever looked at this portrait for a long time could without difficulty recognize that it held much verisimilitude: for the noble master had figured the souls in bodily form: among which, some stopped up their ears for fear of hearing the terrifying noise.

Others covered their eyes with both hands, not daring to look at the abysses so hideously sunken and filled with abominable monsters.

The majority were pale and discolored, clutching their arms against their chests as if frozen with cold.

Some, to express the burning heat they suffered, vomited a thick smoke from their mouths.

Many had their hands clasped one inside the other, or else their fingers interlaced like the teeth of a comb, as a sign of their sadness, accompanied by too vehement a pain.

These souls met upon the bridge already specified, and there came to confront and rudely strike one against the other, without having any means of retreating, because of the press of those following behind; nor (what is more) of going forward, because of the resistance of the others coming against them. And then this bridge would split in two (as has been said) to overturn each one into its torment, then would reassemble itself, and in an instant was recharged with new souls, without ceasing or delay: whereby the poor, desperate souls wished for their annihilation, which would have been less grievous to them than these insupportable Furies. This excessive torment, and this unlucky hell, was so well represented in painting, that those who paused to contemplate it fell into a marvelous horror.

->**To the Divine Manes** <note>original: "D. M." (Dis Manibus). A standard Roman funerary dedication to the spirits of the deceased.</note><-

Those whom the pirates' greed did not keep, nor the lion's gluttony devour, and whom the immensity of the sea refused to take, the narrowness of this little urn now holds together. # BOOK ONE OF

[A decorative architectural frame with a pediment at the top containing a circular emblem.]

O Reader, come hither; this unhappy monument calls to you, and then asks you to read where human pleasure falls. Here are the ashes of two lovers, who lately burned with an unaccustomed and itching love; driven by a wicked and unbridled impulse of pleasure, they met in a deserted place among ruined stones, where by chance the broken walls and rough ruins of sacred buildings stood. There, as we were both urgently pressed to pay the desired gifts to Venus <note>The goddess of love; the "gifts" refer to their romantic tryst.</note> and I, Lopidia, lying on my back, saw a snake fallen from high above, threatening us. "Alas, stop what you have begun," I said, "my Chrysanthes! Rise, flee! Behold a serpent about to devour us; I see him about to hurl himself from the wall." Soon he, looking up terrified, said: "O my Lopidia, please take your way, flee your way; let me, though dying, attack the Dragon." 

Hardly had I risen. Alas, sad and wretched me! I saw my Chrysanthes, my life, ensnared to his destruction; and tightly encircled in the serpent's coil, I saw him now gasping for breath. And suddenly, the throat of my Chrysanthes was bitten and wounded by its teeth: then I watched my Chrysanthes be suffocated. Ah, I have perished, unhappy woman, I feel my Chrysanthes dying! Immediately, in a fury, I rushed at the serpent: and seizing a club, I hastened to strike it. But the serpent turned away its struggling neck, nor was I able to drive it away from its tight embrace. At last, missing my aim carelessly, I killed my own Chrysanthes, most unhappy woman. 

Alas, I am lost! What have I done? What shall I do? Shall such a wretched woman survive? Or the serpent and I? By no means; but with Herculean daring—or rather with the snarling fury of a ghost—with that same staff, with a turned blow, I struck and killed the beast coiled around the fallen corpse. What then was I, a lost and dead girl, to do? I carried my Chrysanthes and the beast—witnesses to my crime—thrown over my shoulders into the city. And so as not to escape punishment, repeatedly bedewing them with sighs, heartache, and tears, I climbed a certain platform <note>original Latin: "suggestum"; a raised rostrum or public speaking stage.</note> in the public forum, and sighing, I made the matter known openly. A crowd of citizens rushed in a throng to the cruel and hated spectacle; they wondered pityingly at the misfortune, they blamed Fortune, and they damned Venus. I bear witness to my crime: I invoke the spirits of the underworld. "Come then," I said, "receive me to pay the penalty together with my Chrysanthes: now I take all the guilt upon myself." Then, in despair, in the public sight of everyone, I seized a sword and pierced my breast, and gave myself, most wretched, to be buried eternally in this tomb with his body. Farewell.

O Reader, come here, I pray you. This unhappy monument calls to you, and furthermore requires that you read to what end human pleasure <note>original: "volupté"</note> falls. Here are the ashes of two lovers, who once, scorched beyond measure by love for one another, at the troublesome persuasion of immoderate pleasure, found themselves in a deserted place, among the ruins of an old destroyed temple, ardently desiring to fulfill their vows to Venus the goddess. Then he looked up, quite terrified, and cried out to me: "Ah, Lopidia, save yourself, leave me to die with this beast." No sooner had I risen (alas, wretched me) than I saw my friend and my life, Chrysanthes, mortally enveloped and bound most tightly by the coils of this serpent, so much so that he could no longer breathe, for it held him by the throat. Alas, I saw my dear Chrysanthes suffocated in my presence. Alas, unhappy woman, I am lost: my Chrysanthes is dead. Then suddenly I took up a staff, as if in a fury, and ran at the serpent; which, even as I hastened to club it, turned its head, gnashing its teeth, and I could not drive it away: wherefore, wishing to strike again with another blow, I missed and killed my friend Chrysanthes. Alas, alas, ill-fated one, I am dead <note>Meaning her spirit is broken or her life is forfeit.</note>. But what have I done? What shall I do? Who shall remain, the serpent or I? Having said this, with a Herculean boldness, or rather by an infernal rage, I took up that staff again, and struck again at the cruel beast encircling the body which lay dead upon the ground, until I likewise struck it dead. What could a simple, distraught girl think or do then? I placed my Chrysanthes upon my shoulders, and the beast slain by me, as witnesses to my crime: then I carried them into the city, watering my friend with tears, and accompanying him with the anguished sighs of my heart. Afterward, I climbed to a high place in the public square, where, weeping, I recounted the event: all the people ran to this hideous spectacle, and the folk looked upon me with pity, blaming Fortune and cursing Venus. I confessed my crime, and said, invoking the lower gods <note>The gods of the Underworld, such as Pluto or Proserpina.</note>: "Come now, receive me with my friend Chrysanthes, to suffer worthy pain, and to be punished according to my duty: for I alone am guilty of everything." Then, being in despair, in the presence of all the common multitude, I struck myself with a knife in the chest, and miserably gave my life as a prey to be buried with this other body. Farewell.

->[Illustration of a classical monument with a pediment and a central laurel wreath. Two birds are perched on the pediment. care, concern.</margin>

Whoever you approach to read this, take care if you love: but if you do not love, consider, you wretch, that for one who lives without love, nothing sweet ever comes forth. But I, breathing in such sweetness, incautiously lost myself, and Love was the cause. While on horseback, desiring to please the most beautiful maiden Dyruionia with the greatest care <note>original: "Polyoria" — the marginal note explains this as "care" or "concern," personifying the effort the rider took to impress his lady.</note>, I fell by chance; my foot caught in the stirrup, and I perished being dragged along.

Which is to be understood thus in common speech:

Whoever you are who comes here to read me, guard yourself if you love: and if you do not love, think (wretch) that without love there is nothing sweet. But in seeking this sweetness, I have inconsiderately lost myself. Love, also, was the cause of it. I was upon a horse, and desired with all my heart to please Dyruionie, a young maiden of perfect beauty: so I fell by chance, my foot remaining in the stirrup: whereby I was dragged and put to death.

My desire to see increased more and more when I entered another gallery, which was completely in ruins except for the wall on the right side. There, I saw a **tomb of Porphyry** <term>Porphyry: A rare, hard purple-red stone used in antiquity for royal and imperial monuments.</term>, excellent in its invention and of most singular workmanship; indeed, it was of marvelous expense, being made in this manner. At each of the sides, it had a square fluted column with its base and pedestal. On each face of the pedestals were three Nymphs, carved almost entirely in high relief, weeping and turned toward the center of the tomb. Upon the capitals of the columns were the architrave and the frieze, entirely carved with foliage, and then the cornice. Between the two columns was a throne recessed into the stone, like a nest between two semi-relief columns with their own bases and capitals, and above it a semi-circular vault, separated from the throne by a small molding that sprang from the capitals atop the half-columns. Between the two square pillars was a Greek inscription, which made me realize that this was the monument of the good Queen of Caria, and it read as follows:

THE ASHES OF QUEEN ARTEMISIA. <note>original: "ΑΡΤΕΜΙΣΙΔΟΣ ΒΑΣΙΛΙΣΣΑΣ ΣΠΟΔΟΣ." Artemisia II of Caria was famous for her extraordinary grief after the death of her husband, Mausolus.</note>

*That is to say:*

*The ashes of Queen Artemisia.*

Beneath the throne, upon a plinth, were four lion paws made of gilded copper, which supported an antique chest serving as a bench; it appeared to be covered with a cloth of gold pattern. There sat a Queen in robes of majesty: and upon the hem of her gown—which was fashioned in the shape of three semicircles hanging lower than the waist—was written in Greek capital letters made of gemstones and pearls:

THE DISHONORED MAUSOLEUM. <note>original: "ΜΑΙΣΟΛΑΙΟΝ ΑΤΙΜΙΤΟΝ." The word "Atimiton" can mean "unvalued" or "without honor," perhaps suggesting that without her husband, the great tomb—one of the Seven Wonders—held no value to her.</note>

*That is to say:*

*The Mausoleum without honor.*

In her right hand she held a cup, as if she intended to drink <note>History recounts that Artemisia mixed her husband's ashes with her daily drink to become a living tomb for him.</note>; and in the other she carried a scepter. Her hair hung down upon her neck, and she was crowned with a closed, double crown, around which part of her hair was pulled back and interwoven. In the corner of the vault of her throne was an oval shape, inside of which was carved a crowned head with a grave face, a long beard, and curly hair. This led me to guess that it was the true likeness of her husband, portrayed from life, held up by two small flying children <note>Often called "putti" or "cupids" in classical art.</note> perched upon the last molding of the vault. With their other two hands, they held a small cord of gilded copper hanging beneath the head. Strung upon this cord were several small beads of the same material, like prayer beads. Upon the flat surface of the final cornice supported by the square pillars was a plinth, wider at the bottom than at the top and decorated with moldings. Above it was a roundel of gilded copper, in which was encased a shiny black stone adorned with such characters.

I then realized it was a memorial to the naval victory this Queen won over the Rhodians. It featured the ram of a galley along with part of the prow, upon which stood a tree trunk dressed in ancient armor. The branches passed through the armholes; from one branch hung a small shield, and from the other, the handle of a bilge pump <note>original: "trompe à vuyder la sentine." I also believe they were carved by the very same craftsmen who worked on the **Mausoleum** <note>The Mausoleum at Halicarnassus, the monumental tomb of Artemisia's husband Mausolus, which was one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World.</note>.

Just as Aeneas had lost his Creusa while fleeing the great fire of Troy, and in the very same way I had left my Polia far from me in a deserted place by the seashore. Alas, how I experienced in 그hat hour what grievous anguish there is in the condition of lovers. In truth, I was not so distraught even when I saw myself ready to be devoured by the dragon <note>Referring to an earlier episode in the book where Poliphilo is pursued by a monstrous dragon through a dark tunnel.</note>: therefore my stay was not long; rather, I immediately abandoned that undertaking and set myself to running across the ruins and heaps of stones, through the briars and thorns, without regard for my threadbare robe, of which shreds remained at every turn on the snags of the bushes: for I had impressed upon my imagination that I had come to my final misfortune, to my ultimate fear, and to the loss of all my hope. Thus, running with all my might, I happened by chance to fall near the lap of Polia, out of breath, drowned in tears, half alive, and so lacking in courage and strength of limb that I could only with great difficulty reach her: she was (certainly) a little moved to see me so greatly terrified: and she lifted me in her arms, wiping my face—all wet with tears, tarnished with sweat, and grimy with dust—with a linen cloth: then she lovingly asked me the cause of this accident, in words so sweet and so amiable that she could have resuscitated a dead man. Hearing this gracious request, I suddenly came back to myself and found myself in her lap, free from all doubt and unease: then I recounted my misfortune to her point by point: at which she began to smile and kissed me sweetly, saying that Cupid our master would soon come, and that meanwhile I should remain patient, considering that suffering is often the cause of great good. I found myself greatly consoled by these gracious words and such kind remonstrances: therefore my color of boxwood <note>original: "Buys"; boxwood was a common Renaissance metaphor for a pale or sallow complexion.</note> returned to its natural luster, and my excessive fear changed into firmness of heart, so much so that my eyes returned to their accustomed duty to live upon their ordinary pasture <note>A poetic way of saying his eyes could once again delight in looking at Polia's beauty.</note>.

I had certainly stayed in that place for almost no time at all when Polia rose from where she was sitting and, bowing honorably, made a very gracious, humble, and honest reverence: then she knelt down: at which I was completely astonished, for I did not know what moved her, and I looked at nothing else but her great unparalleled beauty, in which my eyes were so occupied that it was impossible for me to turn them away: nevertheless, for my part, I did just as I saw her doing, without knowing why or to whom: and I knelt down beside her. Then suddenly I perceived Cupid, completely naked, who was coming in a boat, and approaching the shore, he turned the stern toward the ruined pier. My eyes could never endure the sparks of his divine brightness; rather, I was constrained to put my hand between the two <note>Poliphilo must shield his eyes from the blinding light of the god's presence.</note>. When we were far from the land, the nymphs checked their oars and turned their faces toward their master, who was at the prow, making him the most humble reverence they could devise; then they sat with their backs toward us. No sooner were they in such order than Cupid, our captain, extended his wings, calling upon Zephyrus <note>The personification of the gentle West Wind.</note> to blow into them in place of sails. This he did with such strength that we began to lose sight of land, and we sailed on the high sea with singular calm—truly in such pleasure that I know of no heart so fierce that it would not have been tamed there: no lust so extinguished, or desire so lost and disgusted, that it would not have been ignited, regaining its natural appetite. It was enough to make Diana fall in love, to convert the chaste Hippolytus, and to force the prudent Pallas <note>Athena, the goddess of wisdom, usually depicted as eternally virginal and armored.</note> who is always armed. Now consider how mortal men must have felt, being so close to it, apt and disposed to burn.

I was then like the little fish born in warm water, which, when put into another to cook, can neither heat up nor boil <note>Poliphilo suggests he is so accustomed to the "heat" of his love for Polia that this new external stimulation cannot increase his internal temperature.</note>.

I contemplated the wings of this divine spirit, upon which there were some downy feathers, trembling in the wind, and representing the plumage of a sea-egret not yet emerged from the nest.

O, how beautiful and shining they were, of a gold color inclining toward red, and in other places toward azure or violet. There were some tending toward emerald, the colors so well assorted that it is not possible for painting to imitate them so naturally.

It seemed, to tell the truth, that all the jewels of nature had been brought from her treasury to sparkle in this place; for they shone like plates of fine burnished gold, hung in the wind and swaying against the sun, so that the water seemed to be painted with their colors, which were suddenly erased by the instability of the waves spreading out in great circles.

The air was clear, the sea calm, the water clear as crystal, so much so that one could see the bottom all paved with beautiful golden sand, and several little reefs or islets covered with trees—especially the Sporades islands, so green and so fertile that <margin>Sporades, scattered.</margin> none are more so—together with several other distant places as far as the eye could see, which resembled little black spots upon the water. LOVE CONQUERS ALL.
<note>original: "OMNIA VINCIT AMOR"</note>

*Love surmounts all things.*

I often forced myself to look at our patron <note>Referring to Cupid as the captain or master of the vessel.</note> with a steady eye, but it was not at all possible for me, for my eyes could not endure the sparkling of his rays. Yet when I held them half-closed, with my hand held open above them, I perceived him a little, though always in diverse ways: for at one moment he seemed to me entirely double, at another imperfect; then a child, and afterwards a decrepit old man; in such a manner that I could not establish any certain knowledge of him. Then our crew <term>Churme<note>A term usually referring to a galley's rowing crew, here used poetically for the group of nymphs.</note></term> (the six nymphs) began a song, with a voice totally different from the human. First with two voices, then three, then four, and finally six, in proportioned music, with the delicate <term>prolations<note>A technical musical term referring to the rhythmic phrasing and duration of notes.</note></term> of love, pauses, and sighs of good grace, accompanied by passages trilled through their nightingale throats, in accord with the instruments, which were two lutes, two viols, and two harps, resonating so melodiously that it was enough to make one forget all the passions and necessities to which nature inclines humans. These beautiful women sang of the qualities of love, the joyful thefts of Cupid, the savory fruits of Hymen <note>The god of marriage.</note>, the abundance of Ceres <note>The goddess of the harvest, symbolizing plenty.</note>, and the amorous kisses of Bacchus <note>The god of wine and ecstasy.</note>, composed in beautiful rhythm. Nevertheless, I can infer by good reason that if you have been cruel toward yourself, I should have no hope of obtaining mercy, nor expect any pity."

Shorten then (my lord) this waiting, anticipate this tiresome hope: for help tarries far too long for whoever has need of it. 

Then I accused most-just Nature; for notwithstanding that she has wisely composed everything, yet I said that she had forgotten or failed to assemble the will and the power. Meanwhile, we always made progress on our way, and the nymphs sang without ceasing, from the Phrygian to the Lydian mode <note>Ancient musical modes: the Phrygian was often associated with excitement or passion, while the Lydian was seen as soft and intimate.</note>, without discording in any way, expressing the sweetnesses of Venus, mixed among the frauds and deceits of her son who was present there. But Polia sang a thanksgiving for the graces she had received from him, and sometimes she asked me what I thought of that company. Afterward, she told me all the names of these nymphs, affirming that perseverance alone carries away the crown as a reward. In such a height of all solace, we arrived at the island of Cythera.

## How they arrived at the Island of Cythera, THE BEAUTY OF WHICH IS DESCRIBED HERE, along with the form of their boat: and how upon landing, several Nymphs came before them to honor Cupid, their master.

**V**oyaging then in this manner—not by the hull or the mainsail, but with the wings of Cupid, which he had stretched to the wind, as has been said—Polia and I, united in our desires, both wishing to reach the place determined for our bliss with the greatest ease that human sense could ever feel or tongue express, sighing with a sweetness kindled by love, and heated like a boiling pot over too great a fire which overflows the top, we arrived at the port of the holy island of Cythera <note>The mythical island birthplace of the goddess Venus, dedicated to love and beauty.</note> in the boat of Cupid. This vessel was neither ballasted nor loaded with freight <note>original: "laytage"—referring to commercial cargo or heavy ballast; the author emphasizes the boat's supernatural lightness.</note>, but bobbing upon the waves, and fashioned as follows:

Of its four parts, two were used, one for the stern and the other for the prow, and the other two for the midsection <note>original: "mizane"—here referring to the proportions of the ship’s waist or middle breadth.</note>, where it was wider by a third. The gunwales <term>postices: the raised edges along the ship's sides</term> were two feet high above the deck, and the benches one foot and a half. The hull and the sides were covered in plates of gold; which extended out at the prow and rose at the stern in the shape of a crook, curving back into a scroll, within the round of which was a rich ornament of pearls. From the scroll emerged a running foliage across the surface of the seat, made of fine gold and carved after nature. The thickness of these scrolls formed the width of the oar-locks <term>Palescalme: the reinforced part of the ship's side where oars are supported</term>, made of the same metal and chiseled with a frieze four inches wide, adorned with precious stones, and the thole-pins <term>scalmes: the wooden or metal pins that hold the oars in place</term> were of ebony. The entire body of the ship was so well made that one could not see a single joint; rather, it seemed to be of one piece, without any caulking visible on the surface, except for the composition I previously described. This was the mixture with which it was pitched or coated, and the painting on top consisted of Arabesques of ground gold.

This place was so beautiful, so pleasant and delectable, that Eloquence herself would find herself too poor in terms, figures, and colors of Rhetoric if she wished to amuse herself by describing it; any comparison would be ill-suited, for there was nothing fitting except to compare it to the places I had seen previously. For this was the true retreat of solace and blessed delights, fashioned into gardens, orchards, and little groves, arranged as the goal and finishing touch of all pleasure. There were no rocks, mountains, nor anything that could bring annoyance to the sight, the body, or the mind; rather, the land lay as flat as a palm <note>A common Renaissance expression meaning perfectly level.</note> all the way to the steps of the theater, entirely planted with fertile and fragrant trees and watered by fountains and streams. Along these waters were trip-wires, traps, and little surprises <note>These "surprises" (original: *petites surprises*) refer to hidden water jets or "wetting sports" popular in Renaissance gardens, designed to playfully soak unsuspecting guests and "prepare them for laughter."</note> to provide amusement for the people. There were no dark shadows there, nor somber turns without light, because the climate was in no way subject to the inconstancy and change of the weather, nor to the danger of ill winds, heat, frosts, or mists; instead, it was always flourishing and healthful, dedicated to eternity and producing all the goods that nature can make grow. Therefore, I deem it too high and difficult an undertaking to try to define it in our common tongue <note>original: "termes vulgaires"—referring to the vernacular French language as opposed to the "higher" classical languages like Latin or Greek.</note>. Nevertheless, hoping that my memory will serve me with what it has been able to retain, I shall try to describe it in few words.

That region is dedicated to merciful Nature, as the habitation and dwelling of the gods and blessed spirits. It contains in its circumference (as well as I could guess) about three thousand paces. Its position is in the middle of the sea, which encloses it with clear water, without rocks, mud, or pebbles; instead, the bottom is sown with a mineral substance shining like crystal, mixed—in place of pebbles and other useless things—with precious stones of every kind that one could imagine. Upon the shores of the sea is found a great quantity of Amber <note>original: "Ambre"—likely referring here to ambergris, a precious substance found on beaches, though it could also mean fossilized resin (yellow amber).</note> produced by the sea.

Then, the space found between the half-diameter and the end of the crossing line will be the tenth part of the circle; divide this in two, and you will have twenty parts.

And because the circumference of any circular or round figure is as great in measure as three of its diameters—specifically if the said circumference is divided into eleven parts, and one subtracts one of the diameters, the remainder makes two portions—the diameter of this voluptuous island contains one mile in length, and two parts of the eleven mentioned above. <note>Poliphilo is describing an approximation of Pi ($\pi$). In his calculation, the circumference is equal to $3 + 2/11$ times the diameter, which is approximately 3.18.</note>

Next is another circular enclosure, running all around the center, made of Orange and Lemon trees, which is a good eight paces high and one foot in width; and it is so thick with leaves that one cannot see through it, because its branches are so joined that it truly resembles a painting laden with fruit and flowers. In truth, it is a work all the more excellent because it rarely happens that men see the like.

Beyond that enclosure, one encounters an orchard so sumptuous that the best mind in the world would not know how—I dare not even say to order it, but even less—to imagine it; so much so that he could not declare by what artifice it was conducted, a thing which makes it known that none other than Nature made it for her own pastime.

This delicious garden extends toward the center for a length of one hundred and sixty-six paces, half of which is divided into beautiful meadows; and this division is arranged by paths tending straight to the center, and others crossing circularly, which are five paces wide. The first meadows in the first line of their <term>quadrature</term> <note>The geometric "squaring" or layout of a space.</note> tending toward the partition can contain fifty paces. But the fourth line toward the center continually diminishes, and upon it, the first of the second meadow takes its dimension or measure; and by the same means, the third is squared, because the force of the lines tending to the center causes the curvature, along with the narrowing of the said meadows and the passages for going around; and thus the square is formed, while the crossing lines remain totally in their entirety.

These ways are covered with vaulted trellises or arbors. At each crossroads, there is a small turret seated upon four <term>Ionic columns</term> <note>One of the three classical orders of Greek architecture, characterized by the use of volutes (spiral, scroll-like ornaments) on the capital.</note> of white marble. On either side of the paths is a low wall having projections in the form of a pedestal or <term>stylopode</term> <note>original: "ſtylopode"; a continuous base supporting a row of columns.</note>, fashioned from the same marble. Upon these rest the columns, distant from one another by three diameters of their base. Within the low wall, which is hollow in the middle, are planted rosebushes which fill and populate the space between the columns with beautiful greenery, above which rest the architrave, the frieze, and the cornice, made of <term>Porphyry</term> <note>A rare, hard igneous rock. BOOK ONE OF
<note>original: "LIVRE PREMIER DE"; this refers to "The First Book of the History of Poliphilo"</note>

These meadows are bounded by the river, which is enclosed within its banks, constructed from the bottom of the water up to three feet above the surface with masonry of beautiful **green marble** and of **Doric structure** <term>Doric structure: the earliest and simplest of the classical Greek architectural orders, known for its strength and restrained decoration</term>. The river is confined between these two walls, just as the Tiber once was in Rome by the will of the Emperor **Tiberius** <note>Tiberius (42 BC – 37 AD) was the second Roman Emperor; the text refers to historical efforts to channel the Tiber to prevent flooding</note>. The river is ordinarily clear, pure, and clean, without canes, rushes, reeds, or any other weeds or shrubs, but is entirely surrounded by flowers. It springs from a living fountain and flows with few turnings; it is then conducted through certain pipes specifically made to bring it into the enclosure to water the entire place, and from there it flows into the sea through small streams all around the island. Because of this, the river can never overflow, but remains always in one state, neither rising nor falling, because as much water as the springs pour out, just as much leaves through the pipes. It is twelve paces wide and four feet deep. The water is so purified, clear, and subtle that it causes no disproportion or hindrance between the sight and its object; for all things are seen there even to the bottom in their proper form and nature, neither larger, nor more elongated, curved, slanted, nor in any way distorted. The sand at the bottom is mixed with **gold flakes**, and instead of pebbles, it is adorned with **precious stones**. Along the banks grow **Irises** <note>original: "Glaieulz"; likely referring to the Yellow Flag or Iris, common in Renaissance water-gardens</note> of all colors, namely blue, white, red, and yellow. Swans fly there in great flocks. On both sides are planted **Orange** and **Lemon trees**, spaced three paces from one another; but at one pace from the ground they begin to put out their branches, which join together with one another, creating a vault of foliage three paces high. The other higher branches are bent over the river, forming another vault for shade in the fashion of a **trellis** <note>original: "berceau"; an arbor or pergola-like structure formed by trained branches</note>, which is seven paces high from the water upward. The foliage is so thick and so even that not one leaf surpasses the other by anything, except when they stir in the wind, which gives them a singular grace. In short, everything there is covered with fruit and flowers; it is also a true dwelling for **Nightingales**, who hide themselves within and hold there their chapel, as delightful and pleasant as possible.

Between this boxwood enclosure and the third step specified above, there was a sumptuous work to astonish all human understanding, for at first glance it seemed to me that the entire ground was covered with Turkish carpets, matching in all colors according to the craftsman's invention, arranged in various types of interlacing and foliage, both Moresque and Arabesque <note>Ornate decorative patterns of intertwined lines or leaf-work, often found in Mediterranean art</note>, some brighter and clearer, others a bit darker—or rather, less prominent—but artistically harmonized in a variety of figures. Beyond this forest there were yet another seven steps, and above them another peristyle or circuit of columns, like the one that was near the river, made in the same fashion and material as the others: then a beautiful, wide, and spacious plaza, paved with mosaic in foliage and antique Moresque interlace, perfectly portrayed and furnished with colors so life-like that nothing more could be added. Having received all his instruments, Cupid mounted a chariot of gold specially prepared for him. <margin>Pastophores: carrying the **canopy** <note>original: "poille" (poêle). A ceremonial cloth or veil carried over figures of high status</note>.</margin>

First came the Pastophores, then the Trophigeres, the Pyrgophores, and those who carried the bundles of **rods and axes** <note>original: "faiſſeaux de verges & cognées." Then came those who sounded instruments, namely: lutes, viols, rebecs, flutes, harps, oboes, cornets, trombones, lyres, **shawms** <term>chalemyes: a medieval and Renaissance woodwind instrument, the precursor to the modern oboe</term>, and others of all sorts, harmonizing with the voices of the female singers who accompanied them, crowned with wreaths of flowers and leaves of all colors mixed with pearls and other precious stones amidst beautiful gold foliage. This produced a harmony so melodious that Apollo never made the like for the Muses when he sang with his lyre, nor **Arion** <note>A legendary Greek minstrel who was saved from drowning by dolphins who were charmed by his music</note> when the dolphin carried him, nor the Sirens to deceive the sailors. The beauties did not walk all together in a crowd, but in order, three by three, each in her rank, in the places assigned to them; so much so that I would hold as foolish and too presumptuous any tongue, of whatever eloquence it might be, that would undertake to express the smallest part of this triumph: the divine bearing of the beautiful nymphs, their singular beauties, their sumptuous clothes, their gracious countenances, and the abundance of treasures, riches, great delights, and pleasures that, by the special grace of Cupid, I was permitted to see in that moment.

Thus was triumphant Cupid accompanied, Polia and I led behind him, bound by chains of flowers and ropes made of roses. The nymphs entertained us with romantic conversation and courteous words, their faces joyful and full of grace, like kind and elegant maidens. Finally, in this superb array and magnificent pomp, this great Lord marched among so many victory banners following the imperial standard, in the midst of so much music, through beautiful rosebushes scattered with fragrant flowers and under the cover of so many rich trellises, until we reached a large square before the gate of an excellent and marvelous amphitheater, the likes of which was never seen. It was a marvel and a prodigy of architecture, and rather a divine work than one made by the hands of mortal laborers. Our arrival was by the great way, along which, on either side, there were small hidden pipes that incessantly sprayed musk-scented water, so perfect that a sweeter odor was never smelled. When we arrived at the gate of the amphitheater, I began to contemplate it in detail, to describe its particularities. [A woodcut illustration depicting several figures, possibly mythological or allegorical, in a classical architectural setting with columns and a landscape in the background.]

Above this frieze, accompanied by its cornice, was another vault <note>original: "voulture" — referring here to the upper story or arched tier</note> entirely similar to the first. And although the art of architecture requires that columns placed in a building atop other columns be smaller by a fourth part than the lower ones upon which they are set—and even that the third layer placed upon the second should decrease by a fifth portion—yet this was not observed in this sumptuous and well-proportioned edifice; rather, they were all of one size and thickness, whether high, low, or middle. But to tell the truth, the third tier consisted of square and fluted pillars <note>original: "pilliers quarrez & cannelez" — fluted pilasters</note>, protruding from the wall by a third of their thickness. Between two of these pillars there was a window, not square like those of temples, but arched, as they are made for private houses. The royal cornice was without projection or overhang <note>original: "sans faillie ne forget" — meaning it did not jut out significantly from the wall</note>, but above it there was only a small wall a pace and a half in height. This entire magnificent structure was built of fine Indian Alabaster, as transparent as glass, masonry without cement or any mortar; rather, the stones were so well squared, joined, and locked together that one need not fear their dissolution, but should instead judge them to be durable for eternity. The surface was not blackened by smoke, nor scorched by the sun, nor fouled by the rain, but remained in its natural and original polish, without spot or blemish in any of its parts. The space within the work contained a length of thirty-two paces in diameter. The width of the enclosure and the aisles running around it was eight paces. This department or division of the roundness of the edifice and the columns was first made into four, each fourth part divided into eight, which made in all thirty-two divisions: and as many columns in a circle: for upon each eighth part a column was placed.

The enclosure was vaulted with double vaults, which formed two paths or aisles encircling the building. The pillars in the middle were closer to one another than those on the outer facade, and there was even less space between those on the inside; just as the lines approached closer to the center, the more they narrowed. The space from one pillar to the next decreased in width according to the proportion of the curvature, while the height always remained at an equal measure. The pavement of these beautiful aisles was of mosaic, as was the ceiling <note>original: "fons des voultes" — the interior surface or "back" of the arches</note> of the vaults, all done in the same fashion, so that the work of one corresponded to the other. It was all laid out in compartments <note>original: "compartimens" — decorative panels or framed sections</note> enriched with antique foliage <note>original: "fueillages antiques" — likely classical acanthus leaves or scrolls</note>, so skillfully and with such grace that the whole seemed to be made of a single piece, rather than of joined stones. Within these compartments were depicted, through beautiful stories, all the effects and operations of Love.

In this marvelous edifice, one could easily recognize the fine spirit, the quick discourse, the excellent art, the ingenious design, the profound knowledge, the marvelous diligence, and the supernatural invention of the master craftsman <note>original: "ouurier" — while it translates to 'worker', in this context it refers to the architect or master builder</note> who had made it,

Indeed, in comparison to this work, the sumptuous Temple of Ephesus <note>The Temple of Artemis at Ephesus, one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World</note>, the Colosseum or Amphitheater of Rome, or any other structure renowned in history, was nothing or very little. But to return to my subject: when we arrived at this great Royal gate, all the nymphs remained outside, and only Cupid entered with his beloved Psyche. Then Polia, myself, and the nymphs who held us bound, after passing through the two vaults, entered the space of the theater. This area was paved with a single stone of **jet** <note>original: "Iayet" — a dense, black gemstone-like form of coal capable of a high polish</note> made of one entire piece, round and complete, so black and so polished that when the nymphs leading us pulled me inside, I had no sooner set foot upon it than it seemed to me I was stumbling into an abyss, precipitated into a great, dark, and terrifying pit. Nevertheless, the walls surrounding it made me somewhat recognize where I was. Despite this, fear caused me to misstep, and I twisted my foot slightly. In this stone, one could clearly see the color of the sky and the clouds, as well as the walls that formed the enclosure, just as one sees in the sea when it is calm <note>original: "boñasse" — a maritime term for a dead calm sea</note>. In the middle of the place, directly above its center, was the exquisite fountain of the divine mother of our master <note>Poliphile refers here to Venus, the mother of Cupid</note>, excellently beautiful and well-adorned. But before describing it, I wish to speak of the incredible structure and layout of the amphitheater, which exceeded not only the grasp of my mind, but all mortal thought; and I would say it was miraculously built.

The steps made all around the space began at the level of the pavement and were arranged in three orders. In each order were four steps, which were not solid <note>original: "massifz"</note> but hollow, being six palms in height and two and a half feet in width, filled with earth and sown with all manner of flowers, which grew no higher than half the height of the following step. On the fourth step, there were no flowers, for it was made for a passage or walkway, covered by a **trellis in a cradle-vault** <note>original: "treille en berceau" — an arched garden trellis</note>, measuring five feet in width and a pace and a half in height. This trellis did not obstruct the view of the fifth step, where the second tier began, being a little more elevated than the others while keeping suitable proportion; and so it was with the others, both for the third and fourth orders, for the same measure was observed in everything. 

The armrests or supports <note>original: "accoudoers ou appuys" — parapets or railings</note> of the first walkway were of black stone, shining like glass; the second were of <term>Spartopolia</term> <note>A grey-and-white marbled stone described in classical texts</note>; the third of <term>Hieratite</term> <note>A "sacred stone" mentioned by Pliny, likely a type of black or red ironstone</note>; and the fourth of <term>Cepronite</term> <note>A stone mentioned by ancient authors, possibly a variety of malachite or a stone with "cloud-like" patterns</note>. These were so shining that it would have seemed to you, looking through the trellises, that it was the sky itself presenting itself to your sight, and not a stone wall. At the edge of these armrests, the trellis began to turn into a vault; the whole was so well-conducted by architecture that all the squares of the steps corresponded to the level of a line drawn from the highest to the lowest, by an excellent artifice, a divine invention, and almost incomprehensible. 

Higher than the fourth trellis, there was a wall a pace and a half high and just as wide, hollow, and then filled with earth, surrounded both inside and out by a molding made of **Alabaster**, as was the rest of the edifice—save for the steps, which were of oriental **Jasper** of several colors confused and mixed together. These were bordered at the top by a molding of fine gold. This wall formed the cornice of the amphitheater, within which were planted Cypress trees, two by two.

I gazed, as if stunned, at the grace and majesty of this place, its excellence, the ingenious distribution, and the arrangement of all its members, perfectly harmonized with one another, along with all the particulars specified above, so much so that I remained confused and almost outside of myself—like one who, while dreaming, thinks he is dreaming, and is uncertain whether he sleeps or wakes. All my senses were occupied and surrounded by an inexplicable pleasure, and my heart was set ablaze by an ardent flame of love, lit by the matchless beauty of my best-beloved Polia, so that I no longer knew who I was, nor to what place I had been transported.

To form this seven-sided outline <note>A heptagon</note>, one must first draw a circle and divide it into four by a perpendicular line and a transverse line, which intersect exactly at the center point. Then, divide one of these parts into seven equal portions with a compass, and encompass four of these portions between the two legs of the compass; then, pass this measurement over the line of the circumference: and one will find it very accurately divided into seven.

POLIPHILO. 127

Driven by a blinded affection to see the goddess Venus, I broke through the beautiful curtain; and in that instant, it seemed to me that I saw Polia change color and feel a deep distress in her heart. Then, the majesty of the holy goddess was fully revealed to me, as she bathed in the fountain, adorned with all the beauties that nature could imagine. As soon as I cast my eyes upon this divine object, and heard the sound of such an unexpected sight, Polia and I—moved by extreme sweetness and a long-awaited pleasure—remained as if ravished, losing all awareness, and almost in an ecstasy. We were filled with great fear and dread, especially myself, because there came to my memory the pitiful fortune of poor Actaeon <note>In Greek mythology, the hunter Actaeon was punished for seeing the goddess Diana bathing by being turned into a stag and torn apart by his own hounds.</note>, who, for having seen the goddess Diana bathing naked in the fountain in the valley of Gargaphia, was by her transformed into a stag and immediately devoured by his dogs. For I feared that the same might happen to me. 

The goddess Venus was submerged up to her hips in the water of the fountain, which was so clear and subtle that the entire form of her body could be discerned in its natural perfection. This is contrary to the effect of all other waters, which represent everything plunged into their moisture as double, rendering them larger, curved, deformed, distorted, or diminished from their whole. Furthermore, this water produced a light foam along the banks, smelling like musk melted with ambergris, or very nearly so. There sat that celestial body, shining like a carbuncle <term>Carbuncle|A gemstone believed to emit its own light</term> exposed to the rays of the sun. Her hair sparkled like little threads of gold and was entwined around her forehead, then hanging over her shoulders where it made a graceful fold, and from there descended to the water, upon which it floated all around the goddess. 

She wore on her head a wreath of flowers mixed with precious stones; her eyes were amorous and laughing, her cheeks rosy, her mouth small and delicate, her neck straight, round, and smooth, her chest raised and polished like alabaster, and her breasts round with a great space between them. From her ears hung two large oriental pearls, more beautiful and richer than those of Queen Cleopatra ever were. For such beauty, I could find no comparison among humans, for only the glorious and celestial gods can enjoy such a noble vision. 

Between the joints of the steps grew the beautiful flower into which her lover Adonis was once transformed <note>The anemone flower</note>; and on the left side, the herb called Thelygone, and on the right, Arsenogone. Around the goddess hovered several small birds, which moistened their beaks in the clear waves and sprinkled that divine body with a fine rain of small, round drops that resembled oriental pearls. At her side stood her good and loyal servant Peristera. Outside the fountain, on the right side upon the pavement, were three other maidens joined together, embracing one another; two of them, Eurydomene and Eurymene, were turned toward us, but the third, Eurymedusa, showed us her shoulders and her back covered by her blonde hair. These maidens always accompanied the goddess, who held in one hand a shell full of roses and in the other a burning torch. 

One descended into the fountain by six steps, upon the first of which the columns were planted. The water reached up to the fourth step. The first two steps, made of black agate camletted <note>original: "camelottée" — meaning a wavy, variegated pattern resembling camlet fabric</note> with white waves from the veins of the same stone, were dry and out of the water.

I stood before them on my knees, almost as if in a trance, my mind entirely troubled, doubtful of what was before me; I could not rightly imagine how, by what merits, in what manner, or by what stroke of good fortune this grace had befallen my eyes, which were unworthy to see such high divine excellence and such secret mysteries.

However, at last I presumed that it was by the sole will of the immortal gods, the gracious consent of Polia, and the intercession of her holy prayers. Above all, it displeased me that among so many divine persons, I found myself a clumsy fellow, poorly dressed and wrapped in a worn-out, threadbare robe, utterly poor and of no value, different in every quality from this noble company. Nevertheless, I secretly praised in my heart the divine kindness for permitting an earthly man to see and contemplate the great treasures of nature.

The Nymphs of the trellises continued their dances and songs, leading a perfect joy for the victory that their master Cupid had obtained over me. Meanwhile, it seemed (so I believe) to the goddess that the hour was convenient and the time had come to put our affairs in order: therefore she signaled to the instruments to cease, and for everything to be held in silence. She then turned toward us, saying: "Polia, my loyal servant, your good services, your humble sacrifices, and your devout prayers have merited and obtained that I should be favorable to you, and indeed make you worthy of my good grace. For this reason, inclining favorably to your reasonable requests, I wish to liberally recognize and reward them, by accepting the solemn ceremonies through which you have vowed, given, and dedicated your heart to me. It is decreed that your friend Poliphilo here, equally smitten and inflamed by your love, shall be counted among the number of true, loyal, and blessed lovers, purged of all common and base conditions, as well as all faults and shameful acts, if he had in any way fallen into them. Hardly had he released the string when I felt the bolt <note>original: "vire" - a heavy arrow or crossbow bolt</note> pass entirely through my heart, and with the same stroke (the arrow being still all red and smoking with my blood) strike into the breast of Polia, where it remained fixed, after having wounded me with a wound for which there was no longer any place for medicine, remedy, or any cure. This done, Cupid approached Polia and withdrew his arrow, which was halfway out. Then he washed it in the fountain to clean it of our blood, with which it was soiled. 

Alas, alas! I was at that moment so seized by an excessive heat that spread throughout my veins that my understanding became clouded. Nevertheless, I felt my heart open, and the figure of my best-beloved Polia engraved therein, adorned with her chaste and laudable virtues; and the trace was so deep that it is not possible to erase it, but rather it is a necessary thing that the imprint remain there all my life, and that my lady take such possession of it that no other may ever have a part, let alone pretend to enter there. Upon me, certainly, there was neither nerve nor artery that was not burned by this fire like a dry straw in the middle of a great furnace, so that I almost no longer knew myself and thought I was transformed into another form. Indeed, I staggered, unable to understand in what state my heart was. The Boar that had killed him in a rage lay slain. The goddess Venus appeared there fainting, supported in the arms of three Nymphs who wept with her, and Cupid wiped her eyes with a beautiful bouquet of roses. Between Venus and Adonis was a round medallion similar to the previous one in both material and workmanship; but the letters decorating it contained nothing but this Greek word, **ADONIA** <note>original: Α Δ Ω Ν Ι Α, referring to the festivals of Adonis or things pertaining to him; the text translates it here as "pleasure"</note>, which signifies pleasure. This pitiful scene was represented so vividly in sculpture that, while looking at it, heavy tears were forced to fall from my eyes.

The upper side of the masonry was set perfectly plumb with the edge of the fountain, and in the middle, a small cavern was hollowed out between stones that seemed to be split open. Inside was a large serpent of bronze or gilded copper, emerging from the depths of the cavern and gliding on its belly in a winding, wavy motion. Its head was slightly out of the opening that delivered the water into the basin; the ingenious craftsman had made it curved in this way on purpose to moderate and hold back the flow of the water, which was too forceful. Had it found a straight conduit and pipe, the water would have shot out beyond the edges of the basin. 

Upon the tomb, the goddess Venus was sculpted in relief <term>en bosse: a technique where the sculpture stands out significantly from the background, almost in the round</term>, life-sized, made from a fine three-colored Sardonyx stone. She was seated upon an ancient chair, in the manner of a woman who has recently given birth. The body of the goddess was carved entirely naked from a white vein found in the onyx, and was only adorned with a small cloth—carved from a red vein occurring in the same stone—which covered her below the navel along with part of her thigh. It is true that this cloth passed over her right breast, which seemed almost to push it away. Venus had thrown it over her shoulder, so that it hung behind her over the fountain and on the other side down to the base of her seat. Certainly, it was crafted and draped with such great skill that beneath it one could easily see all the muscles, joints, and movements of her person. 

She held her son in her arms, who was nursing at her left breast, looking at his mother while she looked at him so graciously that everyone took great pleasure in it. The cheeks of the goddess and the child, along with the small nipple, were slightly colored vermilion, thanks to a vein in the stone that was found in exactly the right place. It was (believe me) an excellent and, truly speaking, miraculous work, for in these two bodies nothing was lacking but a soul. The hair of the goddess was parted by a straight line in the middle of her forehead, curled along the temples in the form of small rings, then tied behind in a bundle, spreading out from there down to the seat. There, the hair seemed held and caught in small openwork waves; all the hair was carved from a vein of the onyx that was perfectly suited to its color. She had her left foot drawn back slightly toward her seat and the other extended to the edge of the tomb. There, the Nymphs, kneeling, kissed this foot with great reverence and marvelous devotion. Polia and I, seeing this, began to do the same; and in the meantime, I saw that on the cornice of the tomb, beneath the foot of the goddess, these two verses were written and engraved:

# THE FIRST BOOK OF

When Polia had heard the Nymph Polyoremene <note>The name Polyoremene is derived from Greek, likely meaning "much-praised" or "widely remembered."</note>, she rose immediately to her feet with a venerable bearing, her cheeks slightly tinted with a modest blush <note>The original Middle French "vergogne honneſte" implies a virtuous shyness or a sense of "honorable shame" appropriate for a noblewoman.</note>, ready to obey and satisfy the desire of the petitioner. She wished, nonetheless, to somewhat dissemble, as if she were ignorant of what was being asked of her. But she could not feign so well that a small, half-suppressed sigh did not reveal how she was struck. This sigh truly passed through the center of my heart—or to speak more accurately, through hers—because of the great harmony between the two, just as it happens with two flutes tuned to the same pitch and chord <note>This is a beautiful Renaissance metaphor for "sympathetic resonance." It suggests that the narrator (Poliphile) and his beloved (Polia) are so perfectly in tune that their hearts vibrate as one.</note>. Then she gently cast her beautiful eyes upon all the ladies and, with humble assurance and a voice resonating low, she courteously saluted them. Then, having made a kind reverence, she sat down again upon the grass, where after a short pause she began to speak thus.

In the time when the Romans ruled over all that can be known of the habitable earth, the noble house and family of **Lelius** was in great power and renown, holding the principal offices and high dignities of the Republic through their virtuous acts and many victories obtained against the enemies of the Roman name. He was also very far from my thoughts: for at that time my heart and my understanding were entirely indisposed to receive the gift of love, considering that I could have no knowledge of the good or the evil that one can acquire through it. Therefore, from so many pains and labors, and even from so many steps spent and lost by him in vain, nothing came to him but displeasure, boredom, vexation, despair, and a life of unease in all sadness and affliction of mind.

long and tedious languishing: and if I am destined to die for you, I hold my death well employed, and give thanks to Cupid <note>The Roman god of desire and erotic love, often depicted as a powerful and sometimes cruel tyrant in Renaissance literature.</note> for making me die so gloriously. Therefore, if in the great heat of my evils, through impatience or too harsh pains, I have blasphemed or murmured against his divine power, I ask his pardon for it with all my heart, knowing and confessing of my free will that it has too often happened to me to speak ill of him—indeed, even to curse his benefits, which I called **malefices** <term>malefices: evil deeds or enchantments intended to cause harm</term>, saying that tyrannically and wrongly he had oppressed me and subjected me to his false and iniquitous laws, robbed of rest, and stripped of liberty. Why does he deceive, by such baits, simple lovers of easy belief who loyally trust in him? O gods all-powerful, he presents honey and gives them poison. He gives them a gracious welcome, and then leads them to the **slaughterhouse** <note>original: "eſcorcherie," literally a place where animals are skinned or slaughtered; used here to describe the brutal end of a lover's hope</note>, so that all his art is but feigning and simulation, so much are his effects different and contrary. But I see in your face no sign of pity to suggest that my ill displeases you; this makes me believe that you are consenting to the outrage he does to me, and that the sweetness shown in you is a hidden bitterness to the detriment of my life, which will remain no longer with me—and in this I comfort myself. Alas, I can well call myself unhappy, since she who should have sustained my life is the cause of it taking so soon an end. Ha, Polia, help me: for without you I cannot help myself. 

Then, in uttering these words, he cast a great sigh and fell as if dead at my feet, having lost the use of all his senses, except for his tongue, which served him to make long, anguished lamentations, more piteously than I have been able to tell you. And notwithstanding this, there was never found in me any spark of sweetness—no, what is more, not a single sign that his trouble displeased me. For I did not deign to answer him a word, nor lower my eye toward him, but remained obstinate, my ears closed to his prayers, and deafer than the solid rock, persisting in my severe will. Whereby (as I have told you) his heart broke with grief, and he died of it.

Sometimes I said, trembling: "Alas, have I been brought here by the will of the gods to be slaughtered as a sacrifice? Have I deserved a punishment so cruel? What land so savage can produce and nourish beasts so furious and fearsome? What inhumanity can be compared to this? Never was such a thing seen or heard. O horrible vision! Since I had thus vowed and dedicated my virginity to the goddess <term>Diana</term><note>The Roman goddess of the hunt and protector of virgins; Polia represents the classical ideal of the chaste maiden.</note>, and had by profession bound and obliged myself to serve her all my life, the service of <term>Venus</term><note>The goddess of love and beauty, and the mother of Cupid.</note> seemed to me grievous and intolerable, as something entirely different and contrary to my first institution—especially seeing as I had declared myself her enemy and adversary. Recognizing this, my good nurse—desiring above all my health and fearing (as she said) that worse might befall me—used this speech toward me to remedy it to the best of her power:

"My daughter, it is a common saying, and one sees it by experience, that he who takes counsel from others in his affairs cannot fail all alone. For this cause, I pray you, take heed of yourself, and consider whether by any simplicity, thoughtlessness, contempt, or rashness of heart, you have offended the gods. Certainly, there is no doubt that those who deny their power, or disobey them, are in the end bitterly punished; and the punishment is all the greater the longer it is delayed. Therefore, one should not be astonished if their Majesties are angered against any of you young ladies, who very often through imprudence and lightheartedness, or through a foolish and superstitious opinion that you hold, run into an infinity of errors. This has caused many to come to a piteous and miserable end, as I could prove by various histories, which would be too long to recite.

Furthermore, you must consider that Love is a cruel tyrant, endowed with such power that he wounds, burns, and consumes without any regard or mercy—not only mortal men, but (what is more) the sovereign Gods, even the great <term>Jupiter</term><note>The king of the gods, also known as Jupiter Pluvius, the bringer of rain.</note> who makes the rain and the fair weather. For such difficulty has he found (my daughter) in all his amorous enterprises: there is nothing so true as that he could not exempt himself from this servile subjection, but rather, to achieve his intentions, was constrained to transfigure himself even into the form of a beast. Now let us leave the other deities and speak only of <term>Mars</term><note>The god of war.</note>, who is unceasingly armed in every piece: he never had the power to resist love, let alone defend himself—far be it from me to say, to rebel. If he ever intended to do so, he immediately found himself bruised and mangled with wounds. Believe me (my daughter) that Love's virtue is great. And if he can outrage the gods, what do you think he can do against humans, who are tender and fragile—especially those he finds fit for his service, who, although they are powerless and weak, have the audacity and presumption to resist him? Alas (my daughter), not only this **Apollo**, but infinite others of all qualities and conditions have run into similar trouble because they wished to resist the power of this great lord, by whom (as I believe) these visions have been shown to you as a warning of the evil that must befall you. Do not wish to oppose one stronger than yourself, nor flee from that which you cannot avoid; for being beautiful of body, discreet of understanding, well-mannered in condition, wise and accomplished in all virtues—indeed (to say it in few words) the matchless one among the young ladies of this country, so much so that you seem to be the true masterpiece of the **perfect Artisan** <note>A reference to God as the creator of all things.</note> who gave essence to all things, insofar as he has decorated you with singular and extreme beauty—it is to be presumed that the holy goddess **Venus** wishes to withdraw you into her temple, and by such secret admonishments shows that you must enter into her service. Even divine disposition, which has care and cure of your tender youth, has destined you for such <term>mysteries</term><note>In this context, "mysteries" refers to the sacred rites and experiences of love.</note>, and warned you of this in dreams, making known through occult revelations the danger that can befall you, as it has done to many like you who have opposed her immutable decree. For he shows and declares himself an enemy of the gods who despises the <term>offices of nature</term><note>The natural duties of humankind, specifically love and procreation.</note>, or is negligent in exercising them. And this I will presently make you understand through the history of a beautiful young lady whom I saw and knew—a gentlewoman like yourself, of a great, noble, and ancient race, endowed with all the virtues and good graces required of a person of her quality. This young lady was noble, joyful, lively, and always pompously dressed; she also showed herself careful of her appearance, as one ordinarily nourished in the height of riches, pleasures, and the prosperities of fortune. When she was in the flower of her age, she found herself many times sought in marriage by several young gentlemen, and especially by one among the others, equal to her in age, lineage, wealth, beauty, and good grace, as valiant, wise, and virtuous as possible. Nevertheless, she never deigned to condescend to him in any way, whatever prayers or promises he knew how to make her; rather, persevering in this foolish <term>overconfidence</term><note>Original: "oultre-cuydance," meaning excessive pride or arrogance.</note>, she passed the best part of her time (which is brief and marvelously scarce) without considering (my daughter) that there is nothing in this world more agreeable than the correspondence of equal and reciprocal love. In this manner, the young lady remained hardened in her detestable and perverse obstinacy until she passed the age of twenty-eight. He had sunken cheeks, hanging lips, and eyes that were red, raw, and watery. His hands were trembling, and on the back they resembled a sheep's stomach <note>original: "caillette de mouton," referring to the wrinkled, curdled texture of the fourth stomach of a ruminant.</note>. His nose was flat, snotty, and full of crust; his voice was hoarse, and his neck wrinkled like the face of a marmoset. His gums were thick and pale, where there were only the roots of two hollow teeth above and as many below—long ones in the front, wobbling and eaten by canker, which had given them a yellow color spotted with black. He wore a cap on his head because it was scabby, resembling the spine of a mangy dog. His robe was all slobbered upon his chest; he was bent over as if seeking the grave <note>original: "cherchant la fosse," a common idiom for the extreme elderly.</note>, and his beard was as rough as the hair on a donkey's ears. The rest of his body was rotten and turned to dung; and when he moved his clothes, there came an odor of urine such that no living man could approach him. Never did this old man think of anything but greed.

I believe that on the morning of his wedding the crows sang him the morning-serenades <note>original: "aubades." Wherefore, when she came to think of the ease, solace, and contentment that other young brides receive, lying in the arms of those they have loved, and receiving the <term>guerdon</term> <note>A reward or recompense, often used in courtly literature for the consummation of love.</note> of their sweet affections by the fulfillment of wishes, it was to her an aggravation of grief, which tormented her all the more because that imagination returned to her memory at every turn. From this she came to conceive a furious rage and enmity against herself, so great that she became the mortal enemy of her own life; to put an end to which, she one day secretly took a knife and stabbed herself in the stomach <note>original: "estomach," referring here to the chest or heart-center.</note>, like a woman abandoned by hope and confidence, a homicide and murderer of the body she should have held most dear.

Alas, my daughter, if at the age you are, such a misfortune happened to your person (as it might happen for some similar offense, from which nonetheless the gods wish to guard you), I would die of grief before my days. Alas, is there any calamity or misfortune in this world that could so much trouble me as if my eyes had seen you fall into the piteous end of this miserable damsel? Therefore (my daughter) know and hold for certain, that the ire of the gods is inevitable, and that sooner or later those who despise them are infallibly punished. Of this the beautiful Medusa can give testimony, whose hair, for having used rigor toward those who loved her, was changed into living serpents; wherefore she was afterwards fled by the heroic personages who had sought her, even though she followed them and desired to become acquainted. 

Thus young damsels, being in this fair age where you are, take little account of celestial dispositions and well-ordered causes, which induce and incline young persons to fall in love at the time determined for it; which is a kind of rebellion and disobedience. For it seems that they wish to presumptuously resist the holy laws and decrees of Mother Nature, doing her shame, for which things often turn out badly for them. ...and the riches of the world: for our life is far more fleeting than the winds, and vanishes sooner than the bubbles that form upon the water when it rains. And then we strive to seek it again, <term>painting</term> <note>original: "fardãt," referring to the heavy application of lead-based cosmetics common in the Renaissance to hide aging</note> our faces, stretching and smoothing our dry and wrinkled skins by every means possible to us, longing for time past and displeased with the present, in which we are refused by everyone, banished and deprived of sweet glances, good cheer, and the gracious conversation of young men, who know our worth <note>original: "portée," here meaning one's attractiveness or social standing</note> and perceive well enough that we are young in paint, but quite old in nature. 

Alas, my God, youth does not think of the end because it seems far away; and when it approaches, then the desire to live increases. Therefore (my daughter), I pray you above all else, as you love your life, take heed of these signs that have been shown to you, lest they be omens of the wrath of the gods conceived against you for some foolish opinion that you have too stubbornly maintained in the past. Without any doubt, it is necessary to appease them by amending your perverse will, if you have had any, and resolving to obey them henceforth in all humility. And if you have carelessly used their graces, see to it (my dear) that from now on they may be content with you and your service. 

Now, to accomplish all these things, and so that you may better understand how you should conduct yourself, I am of the opinion that you go immediately to the temple of the goddess Venus, where you will address yourself to the <term>Prioress</term> <note>The author uses Christian monastic titles like "Prieuse" (Prioress) for the attendants of pagan deities, a common stylistic choice in 15th-century humanism.</note>, to whom you will declare and confess point by point the reasons for which you believe the gods are indignant with you, and what might be the occasion of such threats made in the visions that have come to you. You must not fail, as I tell you, to recount everything to her word for word, revealing furthermore all the faults and errors you may have committed. Doing this, I hope she will give you good and salutary counsel, so that you may avoid the doubts and suspicions in which you find yourself, and prevent divine punishments, if by misdeed or carelessness you have deserved any.

After my nurse, who was wise and expert in such affairs, had thus explained and taught me all she could gather from my dreams and visions—indeed, giving me counsel on what she felt I ought to do—she went about the business of the house, for it was already broad daylight. Meanwhile, finding myself alone, I began to think upon her words, and I realized she had touched upon the very points where I had failed. Therefore, I resolved to deliver myself from such <term>scruples</term> <note>original: "scrupule," referring here to her hesitant moral doubts regarding her religious vows of chastity</note>, fearing that what my nurse had so fully demonstrated and made me understand through examples might later happen to me. 

In the midst of these thoughts, Love found a small path to enter my heart, which until then had been forbidden and closed to him. Through it, this little god passed into the depths of my breast, where he nourished himself on my consent, and in a short hour grew so great that it was no longer in my power to resist his strength. Nevertheless, in this pondering, many doubts came upon me; I considered the marvelous misfortunes that had befallen a great number of those who had followed the path of Love. Specifically, there returned to my memory Queen <term>Dido</term> <note>The legendary Queen of Carthage who committed suicide when her lover, the Trojan hero Aeneas, abandoned her to fulfill his destiny</note>, who killed herself for Aeneas when she saw he had abandoned her. Likewise, the grieving <term>Phyllis</term> <note>In Greek mythology, she waited for her lover Demophoön; when he missed his return date, she despaired and took her own life</note>, who, through impatience for the return of her beloved Demophoön—he having exceeded the term he had promised her—despairing of his arrival, hanged and strangled herself with her own hands. I also recalled the piteous accident that befell poor <term>Thisbe</term> and her partner <term>Pyramus</term> <note>A pair of ill-fated Babylonian lovers who both committed suicide; their story is a famous precursor to Romeo and Juliet</note>; nor did I leave behind the unhappy death of poor <term>Byblis</term>, who was the murderer of her own body. Did I not also think of the nymph <term>Echo</term>, and of countless other poor ladies whose lives ended so cruelly? And to further swell the account, I thought of the troubles, thefts, violence, and destruction caused by the love of the beautiful <term>Helen</term> <note>Helen of Troy, whose abduction or flight with Paris led to the Trojan War</note>. Then I said to myself: "Alas, could it be that I would expose myself to such dangers? Is it possible for me to enter such a perilous passage without a guide, safety, support, or any experience? Have I not dedicated my body to the chaste goddess Diana? Certainly I have; I cannot deny it. And yet, Polia, you must..."
