Alas, it was a great regret to me to have borne a grudge against one who wished me so much good. I would have wished—certainly—to find him in his former state: that is to say, alive, healthy, and of good will. On the other hand, I feared being surprised alone with a dead man; for perhaps the blame would have been imputed to me, especially since a wrongdoer is frightened by the slightest noise and cannot hide their crime, but easily accuses themselves. I remained for a long time in this troublesome perplexity, but Love conquered fear and made me follow the urgency of my desire, so that I set myself to run alone to the temple where my Poliphile had remained. 

As soon as I had entered, I did not go to kneel before the altar as was my custom, but ran straight to the place where he had been dragged by me. There I found him still dead and wan, colder than marble, since he had remained there all through the past night. Seeing him so greatly changed, I became quite pale with fear and pity, which moved me immediately to weep and to wish that I might participate in death with him, to keep him company in this final passage. I continued my grief so long that my strength abandoned me, and I fell upon his body in a swoon. 

But after coming to myself, I began to say: "O Death, who ends all goods and all evils, all joys and all sadnesses, come to me I pray you, to join me with this man here, whom my cruelty and harshness have delivered into your hands, only because he loved this wretched woman too much—indeed, more than his own soul, as he has well shown. Alas, it is he who considered me his only good and perfect contentment. Am I not then the most unhappy person in the world, not being able now to find the end of this life? POLIPHILE. 150

...[in the] temple of Diana, where some solemnity was being held; and it was at the hour of the morning when the <term>holy women<note>original: "religieuses," here referring to the priestesses or attendants of Diana's temple</note></term> of that place were celebrating the divine office. I glimpsed her by chance among them: and as soon as I set my eye upon her, it happened to me just as it does to an extinguished firebrand: which, if it is brought near the fire, is instantly revived and lit. On the other hand, I felt her image reform within my heart, no more and no less than upon a smoothed wax which is placed back into its mold. My eye (to tell the truth) could not pull itself away from such a pleasing attraction, but rather contemplated her attentively like a goddess among her nymphs: and then it seemed to me that her eyes lit up the entire temple with a light that set my heart ablaze: whereby I became like a man of stone, and held my gaze fixed upon her without wavering, being marveled by her beauty, especially by her eyes, which were large and brown, covered by two small black eyebrows, arched in the shape of the <note>The "fourth part of a circle" (a 90-degree arc) was a Renaissance ideal for perfectly shaped eyebrows.</note>fourth part of a circle, and as fine as a thread of silk. Her complexion resembled vermilion roses mixed with a handful of lilies: and her lips like incarnate coral: between which breathed a breath sweeter than all the compositions of the perfumers. This made me say silently: "O gods, if I could acquire the love of this damsel, I would not only be satisfied, but would consider myself the happiest man in the world: and I would hold it a great felicity to adventure my life for her service, provided however that she could know the affection I bear for her." 

Meanwhile, my Lady, I enjoyed (as it seemed to me) an entirely divine vision. And if, in her singing, speaking, or other ceremonies, she sometimes turned her eyes toward me—even though they were <term>adorned<note>original: "ēpēnez," literally "feathered" or "fledged," as if her gaze were a modest arrow</note></term> with modesty and good grace—they nonetheless dazzled me like a ray of the sun, so much so that I felt a fire of sweetness run through all my veins, which caused me a marvelous fit of fever. Then when it was her turn to perform the divine office, her voice awakened my half-asleep soul and summoned it to follow her. This my soul strove to do, despising its natural home <note>Poliphilo suggests his soul wished to leave his own body to join with hers.</note> to be forever united with a good so excellent and perfect. 

Now, notwithstanding that I knew this alteration proceeded from looking at her, I still could not pull my eyes away, for they were insatiable, and did so much that I granted their desire, saying: "I am resolutely devoted to this damsel: I have placed all my hope in her goodness. She is my whole treasure, and she alone whom I wish to perpetually serve and honor above all ladies who live: and I do not think I shall repent of it: for there is no love, hate, pleasure, nor trouble, however grievous, that could move me from it. She is my mistress, she is my lady: whom I strive humbly to obey. Never in the temple of my heart shall there be another adored image, because it is dedicated to her alone. She is my glory, she is my wealth, my contentment, refuge, aid, and help, through which I hope to attain the beatitude of loyal lovers." 

I was almost drowned in these abysses, content with what was harming me, and consenting to the pain that another had sought out for me: for Cupid, having usurped jurisdiction over me, held me subject to his tyranny, where I was so strictly bound that there only remained to me the power to complain, saying: "Alas, if I could at the very least discover my will to her, and make her understand the pain I endure, or else open my breast to her, so that she..."

Therefore, seeing that I could not set this in order, and that my pains were always increasing from bad to worse, I wished to write you this present letter, not through audacity or reckless presumption but through the great importunity of love, which I cannot resist: joined with the fact that I estimate you to be so prudent, that you will excuse my error if I have committed any by loving too affectionately. In truth (My Lady) I do not presume so much of myself that I think I deserve your good grace. Yet I dare well say, that if love is paid with reciprocal will, I deserve that you wish me well: a thing from which you could not excuse yourself without charging yourself with ingratitude: and it cannot enter my imagination that a lady so well-born, accomplished with perfect beauty, and of all praiseworthy conditions, should be devoid of pity: for without that, all other virtues do not shine at all in the person. The grace that I require of you (My Lady) is of such small importance, that by refusing it to me, you would do wrong and injury to your goodness, considering that I pretend to nothing else, except that you would please to hold me as yours, and believe that I will be such with pure heart and affection, as long as life shall last. Supplicating you moreover, to add faith to the contents of this present letter, and to weigh that it is a hundred times more than I can either say or write to you.

I thought indeed that after having read this letter, my lady would be somewhat moved, and show some sign of friendship: but I lost my time, my labor, and my writing, no more nor less than if I had addressed it to a stone: for just as much gratitude did I receive. Having said this, she threw her two arms around my neck, embracing and kissing me so amorously that I thought I would swoon <note>original: "trancir"; to pass away or be paralyzed by intense emotion</note> with joy. And for my part, I did no less, being seized by such extreme pleasure that I knew not if I was in heaven or on earth: so much so that I almost failed to recognize both myself and my Polia, into whose face, by the sheer force of love, a vermillion color had risen, mingled with her natural whiteness, which gave her such a beautiful luster that it was enough to strike dead a heart not even subject to death. In the midst of these events, and all in an instant, tears came forth from her eyes like crystal, or small round pearls, so that you would have said they were drops of dew upon the leaves of a crimson rose blooming at the rising of the Sun in the season of the month of May. And as I was at this height of bliss, that worthy figure vanished, rising into the air like a little puff of benzoin <note>original: "Beniouyn"; a fragrant balsamic resin used in perfumes and incense</note> smoke: and she left behind a scent so exquisite that all the perfumes of Arabia Felix <note>original: "Arabie heureuse"; the fertile southern region of the Arabian Peninsula, legendary in antiquity for its spices and incense</note> could not be compared to it: which caused me to awaken, and it seemed to me that I heard, as if in passing, "Farewell, farewell my friend Poliphilus."

[Floral ornament]

How Poliphilus brings an end to his **HYPNEROTOMACHIA**, <note>The title literally translates from the Greek as "The Strife of Love in a Dream"</note> COMPLAINING OF THE DREAM which was so brief, and that the Sun rose so soon to break his sleep, as if it were envious of his happiness.

[Large decorative initial T] Just as soon as this angelic spirit had vanished from my imagination <note>original: "fantasie"</note>, I awoke, weary and broken by the tight embraces with which she had strained me (as it seemed to me): and I remained full of bitterness, seeing the departure of her through whom I ought to live, and who had led and raised me to such high thoughts. Thus abandoned by all my supernatural felicities, except for the memory of them, I knew not whom I should complain of, if it were not the Sun, who (perhaps) out of envy for my well-being, shortened that blessed night, notwithstanding that it was in his power to delay yet a little longer, just as he formerly did for several others <note>A reference to mythological instances where the sun was halted, such as when Jupiter lengthened the night to stay with Alcmene</note>. Oh, how much I would have been indebted to him who might have sent me the sleep that the beautiful Psyche <note>In the myth of Cupid and Psyche, she is sent to the underworld to bring back a box of divine beauty, which instead contains a "Stygian sleep"</note> carried closed in her box! But (alas) at the height of this wish I heard the sweet...

...this Philomela, or Nightingale, lamenting the treacherous Tereus <note>In Greek mythology, Philomela was a princess who was transformed into a nightingale after being violated by Tereus; her song is traditionally interpreted as a mournful cry.</note>, saying in her warbling song: *Tereus, Tereus, he has forced me.* <note>original: "Tereus Tereus eme ebiasato"; a transliteration of the Greek phrase "Τηρεύς, Τηρεύς με ἐβιάσατο".</note> That is to say: *Tereus, Tereus has violated me.* And thus the dream and sleep left me, because I awoke as if with a start, saying:
"Now farewell then, my best beloved Polia."

# OBSERVATIONS ON THE STATE OF THE ARTS

## ON THE CAUSES OF THE DECLINE OF TASTE

It is certain that <term>mannerism</term> <note>In an art historical context, this refers to a style that prioritizes artificiality, elegance, and cultivated technique over the realistic representation of nature.</note> has triumphed over the natural. One no longer seeks truth, but rather effect. <margin>This is seen especially in portrait painting.</margin>

In examining the works of the ancients, such as those of <insert>Phidias and</insert> Praxiteles <note>Phidias and Praxiteles were the two most celebrated sculptors of Ancient Greece, representing the height of the Classical style.</note>, one senses a simplicity that we lack.

### Comparison of Artistic Schools

| School | Character |
| :--- | :--- |
| Italian | Grace and drawing |
| Flemish | Color and truth |
| French | Wit and <unclear>finesse</unclear> |

<column-break/>

The <term>chiaroscuro</term> <note>From the Italian for "light-dark"; the technical use of strong contrasts between light and dark to create a sense of three-dimensional volume.</note> is often poorly used by our contemporaries. They forget the old Roman proverb that *true art is to conceal art* <note>original: "ars est celare artem" — a classical principle suggesting that the highest level of craftsmanship is that which appears natural and effortless, hiding the labor involved in its creation.</note>.

If we wish to return to the path of beauty, we must study the masters of the previous century without imitating their faults. Nature remains the only true guide for the spirit.

<summary>This page presents a critique of 18th-century art, arguing that contemporary artists have abandoned natural truth in favor of artificial effects and "mannerism." The author compares various European schools of painting and advocates for a return to the simplicity of Classical Greek sculpture.</summary>

<keywords>Art criticism, Mannerism, Aesthetics, Chiaroscuro, Classical Antiquity, Art Schools, Enlightenment Philosophy</keywords>
